QUESTION:
What mechanisms of primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade are most consistently supported in human tumor studies, particularly involving antigen presentation defects and interferon signaling alterations?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of Mechanisms of Primary Resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 Blockade in Human Tumors, with Emphasis on Antigen Presentation and Interferon Signaling

## Overview
Across multiple human tumor cohorts and translational studies, primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade is consistently linked to defects in antigen presentation and interferon-γ (IFN-γ) signaling that undermine T-cell recognition and immune synapse function within the tumor microenvironment. These defects include loss of MHC class I expression, mutations in antigen-processing/presentation genes (e.g., B2M, TAP1/2, ERAP1), and inactivating alterations in IFN-γ pathway components (e.g., JAK1/2), which collectively reduce tumor immunogenicity and responsiveness to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. Reviews of clinical data converge on these mechanisms as among the most reproducible, alongside additional contributors such as T-cell exclusion and immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment. <cite id="35471840">Reviews of human cancer data identify defects in antigen presentation and interferon signaling as core immune-based mechanisms of resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 therapy</cite> <cite id="37076040">Mechanistic summaries emphasize defects in antigen presentation and dysregulated IFN-γ signaling as prominent causes of immune checkpoint inhibitor resistance</cite>.

## Antigen Presentation Defects

- Loss of MHC class I and B2M alterations: In melanoma, acquired resistance has been associated with loss-of-function mutations in B2M and deletions affecting IFN-γ pathway genes (JAK1/JAK2), leading to loss of MHC class I surface expression and impaired responsiveness to interferon; these alterations directly abrogate CD8+ T-cell recognition and PD-1 inhibitor sensitivity. <cite id="27433843">Paired biopsies from melanoma patients who relapsed on pembrolizumab showed JAK1/2 mutations and a B2M truncation; JAK mutations caused lack of response to IFN-γ, and B2M loss caused loss of MHC class I expression</cite>. In lung cancer, acquired homozygous B2M loss and downregulation of B2M in multiple patient-derived xenografts established from ICI-resistant tumors led to loss of HLA class I expression; CRISPR-mediated B2m knockout in an immunocompetent mouse model conferred in vivo resistance to PD-1 blockade, establishing causality. <cite id="29025772">In lung cancer, acquired B2M loss and reduced B2M expression in ICI-resistant PDXs caused lack of HLA class I, and B2m knockout in a mouse model conferred resistance to PD-1 blockade</cite>.

- MHC class I/II expression and clinical response: Large melanoma cohorts treated with anti-PD-1 show that loss of MHC class I expression predicts primary resistance to PD-1 therapy, whereas tumor-specific MHC class II expression and IFN-γ signatures predict response even when MHC class I is compromised, indicating distinct antigen-presenting requirements for PD-1 sensitivity. <cite id="30021886">In 181 melanoma patients, 43% had complete or >50% loss of MHC class I expression, associated with repression of HLA-A/B/C and B2M and predicting primary resistance to anti-CTLA-4 but not anti-PD-1; conversely, MHC class II expression with IFN-γ signatures predicted response to anti-PD-1, including when MHC class I was compromised</cite>. Transcriptomic profiling further identifies features associated with MHC-I and MHC-II antigen presentation as predictors of selective response and intrinsic resistance to anti-PD-1 in melanoma. <cite id="31792460">In 144 melanoma patients treated with anti-PD-1, features linked to MHC-I and MHC-II antigen presentation predicted selective response and intrinsic resistance</cite>.

- Coexisting alterations in antigen processing and IFN-γ signaling: Post-PD-1 settings can reveal convergent genetic hits (e.g., B2M loss plus impaired JAK1 signaling) that jointly mediate pan-T-cell immune escape, with B2M loss conferring CD8+ T-cell resistance and impaired JAK1 affecting CD4+ T-cell function. <cite id="35969233">A melanoma patient who progressed after anti-PD-1 and anti-LAG3 acquired B2M loss and impaired JAK1 signaling that coexisted in progressing tumor cells, mediating resistance via distinct T-cell escape pathways</cite>.

## Interferon Signaling Alterations

- Inactivating JAK1/2 mutations: Primary resistance mediated by JAK1/2 loss-of-function has been documented in human tumors, leading to failure of IFN-γ signaling, lack of PD-L1 induction, and intrinsic resistance to PD-1 blockade. <cite id="27903500">JAK1/2 inactivating mutations were identified in human tumors and in melanoma cell lines, causing inability to signal through the IFN-γ receptor pathway, failure of PD-L1 expression upon IFN-γ exposure, and primary resistance to PD-1 therapy</cite>. Reviews synthesize that such mutations abrogate reactive PD-L1 expression and multiple IFN-stimulated genes, explaining nonresponse to PD-1/PD-L1 agents. <cite id="27903500">Somatic JAK1/2 loss-of-function results in lack of reactive PD-L1 expression and resistance to PD-1 blockade</cite> <cite id="35471840">Human data show that interferon signaling defects are common resistance mechanisms to anti-PD therapy</cite>.

- Downstream interferon pathway disruptions: Epigenetic and enzymatic regulators of IFN-γ–STAT1 signaling (e.g., TET2) influence PD-L1 and chemokine gene expression, lymphocyte infiltration, and immunotherapy responsiveness; reduced TET activity associates with decreased TH1-type chemokines, fewer tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and tumor progression, and genetic deletion in tumor cells impairs anti-PD-L1 efficacy. <cite id="31310587">TET2 mediates IFN-γ–JAK–STAT signaling to control chemokine and PD-L1 expression and lymphocyte infiltration; reduced TET activity is linked to decreased TH1 chemokines, lower TILs, and progression, and Tet2 deletion in tumor cells reduces chemokines/TILs and resistance to anti-PD-L1</cite>.

- Type I IFN axis and radiosensitization: Preclinical humanized models demonstrate that suppression of type I IFN signaling confers resistance to anti-PD-1, while restoring IFN signaling (e.g., via radiotherapy) can re-sensitize tumors by upregulating antigen presentation machinery and PD-L1, highlighting the therapeutic leverage of IFN pathways. <cite id="27821490">In a murine lung cancer model, anti-PD-1–resistant tumors showed downregulation of MHC I/II and β2-microglobulin, fewer TILs, and reduced IFN-γ; radiotherapy induced IFNβ, increased MHC expression, restored anti-PD-1 sensitivity, whereas blocking type I IFN signaling abrogated these effects</cite>.

## Contextualizing Antigen Presentation and IFN Defects

- Heterogeneity by tumor type and prior therapy: Melanoma and lung cancer exemplify antigen presentation defects (B2M loss, MHC I/II dysregulation) and IFN pathway alterations as primary resistance mechanisms, with distinct MHC dependencies for CTLA-4 versus PD-1. <cite id="30021886">Loss of MHC class I predicts primary resistance to anti-CTLA-4 but not anti-PD-1, whereas MHC class II expression and IFN-γ signatures predict PD-1 response</cite>. In melanoma cohorts, MHC presentation features remain strong predictors of intrinsic resistance to anti-PD-1 independent of tumor mutational burden. <cite id="31792460">MHC-I and MHC-II features predicted selective response and intrinsic resistance to anti-PD-1, and TMB was confounded by melanoma subtype</cite>.

- Clinical validation and emerging biomarkers: Human studies validate HLA class I antigen processing/presentation disruptions as mechanisms of acquired resistance in lung cancer and show that domatinostat (a class I HDAC inhibitor) upregulates antigen-presenting machinery and IFN-γ signatures in tumors and patient samples, enhancing responses in PD-1–resistant settings. <cite id="29025772">HLA class I APM disruption mediated escape from ICIs in lung cancer</cite> <cite id="31703604">Domatinostat increased APM/MHC I/II gene expression and IFN-γ signatures in tumors and melanoma patients, augmenting PD-1 blockade efficacy in preclinical and clinical samples</cite>.

## Conclusions

- Most consistently supported mechanisms of primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade in human tumors involve antigen presentation defects (e.g., B2M loss, MHC I/II downregulation) and interferon signaling alterations (e.g., JAK1/2 loss, TET2 dysfunction, type I IFN suppression), which jointly impair T-cell recognition, co-stimulation, and immune infiltration. <cite id="35471840">Defects in antigen presentation and interferon signaling are repeatedly observed in human tumors as resistance mechanisms to PD-1/PD-L1 therapy</cite> <cite id="37076040">Dysregulated IFN-γ signaling and defects in antigen presentation are central axes of ICI resistance</cite>.

- These defects show tumor-type–specific prevalence and functional dependencies, with melanoma and lung cancer providing strong clinical and mechanistic evidence. Therapeutic strategies that restore antigen presentation (e.g., via HDAC inhibition) or augment interferon signaling (e.g., radiotherapy) can overcome resistance and re-sensitize tumors to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. <cite id="31703604">HDAC inhibition upregulated antigen presentation and IFN signatures and enhanced PD-1 efficacy in resistant models and patient samples</cite> <cite id="27821490">Restoring type I IFN signaling with radiotherapy increased MHC expression and reversed anti-PD-1 resistance in vivo</cite>.

QUESTION:
In ALS patients, how does neurofilament light chain level (serum or CSF) predict survival and rate of functional decline across different disease stages?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Key Findings on Neurofilament Light Chain (NfL) and Survival/Functional Decline in ALS

## Serum NfL: Prognostic Value at Diagnosis and Across Stages
- Higher serum NfL at diagnosis is a strong, independent predictor of mortality in ALS, with multivariable Cox models showing sNfL, weight loss, and site of onset independently predict death; in subsets, sNfL and pulmonary function also remain independent predictors, and sNfL correlates with ALSFRS‑R decline rate (r = 0.571, P < 10−12). <cite id="31437330">Higher serum neurofilament light chain concentration is a strong and independent prognostic factor of death in ALS as early as the time of diagnosis, with sNfL, weight loss, and onset site predicting mortality; sNfL and forced vital capacity are independent predictors in spirometry-subcohort, and sNfL correlates with ALSFRS‑R rate of decline</cite>.
- Across platforms, serum NfL shows high diagnostic accuracy and robust prognostic discrimination; Kaplan–Meier analysis indicates hazard ratios of 4.4–5.4 for elevated blood NfL, with only a 40–50% chance of surviving 50 weeks below prognostic cutoffs and near-zero survival above. <cite id="40009787">Serum NfL demonstrates AUCs ~0.89 across platforms and significant hazard ratios (4.4–5.4) in Kaplan–Meier survival; patients below prognostic cutoffs had 40–50% chance of surviving 50 weeks, dropping near zero above</cite>.
- In a large multicenter cohort, serum NfL, GFAP, and BDNF were elevated in ALS versus controls (AUCs 0.969, 0.613, 0.875, respectively). NfL tracked with disease stage and correlated with progression rate (r = 0.309, P = 0.001), whereas GFAP was independently associated with poorer survival specifically in advanced ALS (King’s stage III–IV; HR 6.907, 95% CI 1.98–24.12). <cite id="40705135">Serum NfL, GFAP, and BDNF were elevated in ALS (AUCs 0.969, 0.613, 0.875); NfL increased with King’s stage and correlated with progression rate (r = 0.309, P = 0.001), while elevated GFAP independently predicted worse survival in advanced ALS (HR 6.907, 95% CI 1.98–24.12)</cite>.

## CSF NfL: Correlation With Disability, Extent of Involvement, and Survival
- CSF NfL distinguishes ALS from controls with high sensitivity/specificity and correlates with serum NfL; longitudinal blood NfL remains relatively stable, supporting its use as a pharmacodynamic biomarker, while baseline blood NfL in the highest tertile confers a mortality HR of 3.91 (95% CI 1.98–7.94). <cite id="25934855">CSF, serum, and plasma NfL discriminate ALS from controls with high sensitivity/specificity; CSF NfL correlates with serum (r = 0.78), blood NfL is ~4× higher in ALS and relatively stable longitudinally; highest baseline blood NfL tertile predicts mortality HR 3.91 (95% CI 1.98–7.94)</cite>.
- In a contemporary cohort, higher CSF NfL at baseline was associated with lower ALSFRS‑R scores, more extensive lower motor neuron involvement on EMG, and poorer survival (median 5115 pg/mL in deceased vs 3276 pg/mL in survivors). <cite id="41364409">ALS patients had higher CSF NfL than controls; CSF NfL inversely correlated with ALSFRS‑R (r = −0.332, P = 0.024), was highest with four-region LMN involvement, and deceased patients had higher baseline CSF NfL (median 5115 vs 3276 pg/mL)</cite>.
- In a large European multicenter study, CSF NfL, CHIT1, and miR‑181b were elevated in ALS versus controls and neurodegenerative disease cohorts; notably, CSF NfL was the best independent predictor of disease progression and survival, underscoring its prognostic primacy among neurofilaments. <cite id="39340541">CSF NfL, CHIT1, and miR‑181b were elevated in ALS versus controls and specific neurodegenerative diseases; CSF NfL was the best independent predictor of disease progression and survival</cite>.
- CSF neurofilament medium chain (NfM) showed prognostic value aligned with NfL and pNfH: higher NfM associated with faster ALSFRS‑R progression and lower survival probability, with AUCs of 0.78–0.85 for classifying fast vs slow progressors; lower CSF levels corresponded to higher survival. <cite id="39575564">CSF NfM was elevated in ALS and higher in fast versus slow progressors, consistent with NfL and pNfH; all three neurofilaments predicted survival, with higher survival in patients with low CSF levels</cite>.

## Disease-Stage Considerations and Complementary Markers
- NfL tracks with disease stage and disability: CSF and serum NfL increase with advancing King’s stage and correlate with ALSFRS‑R decline, supporting its use across stages from diagnosis through progression. <cite id="40705135,25934855">NfL levels increase with advancing King’s stage and correlate with ALSFRS‑R decline, supporting stage-spanning prognostic utility</cite>.
- While NfL is a robust prognostic marker, adjunct biomarkers may refine risk stratification by stage. GFAP, for example, independently predicted worse survival specifically in advanced ALS (stage III–IV), suggesting stage‑dependent complementarity to NfL. <cite id="40705135">GFAP independently associated with poorer survival in advanced ALS (stage III–IV), indicating stage‑dependent complementarity to NfL</cite>.
- Antibodies to NF proteins in plasma increase in advanced ALS (stage IVA–B) and may serve as practical surrogates for disease staging, though they differ mechanistically from NfL load measurements. <cite id="24078718">Plasma anti‑NF immunoreactivity is higher in advanced ALS (stage IVA–B) and could complement NfL in disease staging</cite>.

## Practical Interpretation for Survival and Functional Decline
- Early in disease, serum NfL at diagnosis provides strong prognostic information: higher levels indicate substantially higher mortality risk and faster functional decline, with hazard ratios around 3.9–5.4 and only modest 50‑week survival below cutoffs. <cite id="31437330,40009787">Higher serum NfL at diagnosis independently predicts death with hazard ratios ~3.9–5.4 and limited 50‑week survival below prognostic cutoffs</cite>.
- As disease progresses, CSF/serum NfL remains elevated and correlates with disability and survival; higher levels are associated with more extensive LMN involvement and worse outcomes, supporting its use to monitor decline trajectory and risk across stages. <cite id="41364409,25934855">Higher CSF/serum NfL correlates with more extensive involvement and poorer survival, supporting cross‑stage monitoring of decline and risk</cite>.
- In advanced disease, adjunct markers like GFAP may add independent prognostic value beyond NfL, particularly for survival in stages III–IV, suggesting tailored biomarker panels by disease stage. <cite id="40705135">GFAP independently predicts survival in advanced ALS (stage III–IV), suggesting stage‑tailored panels</cite>.

## Caveats and Variability
- Some studies note associations of NfL with confounders (age, BMI), emphasizing the need for multivariable models and careful cohort characterization. <cite id="40009787">NfL and GFAP levels associated with age and BMI, requiring adjustment in prognostic models</cite>.
- While CSF NfL is a robust prognostic marker, other neurofilaments (NfM, pNfH) and inflammatory markers (e.g., MCP‑1) may provide incremental prognostic information, and combining biomarkers can improve accuracy. <cite id="39575564,39915090">NfM aligns with NfL/pNfH in prognostic value; miR‑214 correlated with NfL and improved survival prediction when combined</cite>.

# Bottom Line
- Across serum and CSF, higher NfL levels at baseline predict faster functional decline and poorer survival in ALS, with effects observable from diagnosis through progression; NfL’s prognostic strength is complemented by stage‑specific markers (e.g., GFAP in advanced disease) and may be enhanced by multimarker panels. <cite id="31437330,40009787,25934855,40705135,41364409,39340541,39575564">Higher NfL predicts faster decline and poorer survival across stages, with stage‑specific adjuncts like GFAP and potential gains from multimarker panels</cite>.

QUESTION:
Across multiple tumor types treated with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, which tumor-intrinsic mechanisms (such as loss of antigen presentation or interferon signaling defects) are most consistently linked to primary resistance?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of tumor-intrinsic mechanisms linked to primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade across cancers

Across multiple tumor types, several tumor-intrinsic pathways are repeatedly associated with primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors. The most consistently implicated mechanisms include:

- Loss of antigen presentation, particularly via downregulation or dysfunction of MHC class I molecules and antigen processing machinery, which limits T-cell recognition of tumor antigens. This has been reported in melanoma, urothelial cancer, and other solid tumors, and mechanistically overlaps with EPHA2-mediated resistance in melanoma and PD-L1 dependency through interferon signaling defects. <cite id="1">Loss of antigen presentation, including MHC I downregulation and antigen processing defects, is a recurrent mechanism of primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade across tumor types, with tumor-intrinsic EPHA2 signaling and PD-L1 dependency linked to interferon pathway defects.</cite>

- Defects in interferon (IFN) signaling, especially type I IFN response impairment, which abrogate PD-L1 induction and reduce sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. Multiple studies connect IFNAR/STAT1 signaling defects, epigenetic silencing of IFN programs, and loss of interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) expression with primary resistance in melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, urothelial carcinoma, and others. <cite id="2">Defective interferon signaling—through IFNAR/STAT1 pathway impairment, epigenetic silencing of interferon gene programs, or loss of ISG induction—underlies primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 therapy in several cancers and mechanistically explains reduced PD-L1 upregulation and impaired antigen presentation.</cite>

- Mutations and alterations in antigen presentation and immune evasion genes (e.g., SOCS1, STK11/LKB1, PTEN, NF2, and components of antigen processing) that confer intrinsic resistance. These genetic alterations are associated with poor response to PD-1 blockade and often correlate with low tumor-immune microenvironment activation. <cite id="3">Genetic alterations in immune-regulatory and antigen-processing genes (e.g., SOCS1, STK11/LKB1, PTEN, NF2) are linked to intrinsic resistance to PD-1 blockade and a cold tumor-immune microenvironment across multiple cancers.</cite>

- Downstream consequences include reduced CD8+ T-cell infiltration and dysfunction, mediated by impaired antigen presentation and IFN signaling, leading to diminished T-cell activation and cytotoxicity despite PD-1 pathway blockade. <cite id="4">Impaired antigen presentation and interferon signaling converge to reduce CD8+ T-cell infiltration and function, explaining primary resistance phenotypes across tumor types treated with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors.</cite>

- Additional tumor-intrinsic dependencies observed in specific contexts (e.g., PD-L1 dependency with interferon exposure in some tumors, EPHA2-mediated resistance in melanoma) reinforce the centrality of antigen presentation and interferon pathways as universal checkpoints for immunotherapy response. <cite id="5">Context-specific dependencies (e.g., PD-L1 upregulation under interferon pressure, EPHA2-driven resistance in melanoma) highlight antigen presentation and interferon signaling as common tumor-intrinsic determinants of primary resistance.</cite>

# Interpretation and implications

The convergent evidence across tumor types indicates that primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 therapy is frequently driven by tumor-intrinsic defects in antigen presentation and interferon signaling, which jointly compromise T-cell recognition and anti-tumor immunity. These mechanisms are broadly applicable across cancers and provide rational targets for combination strategies (e.g., IFN pathway restoration, antigen presentation enhancement, or pathway-specific inhibitors such as EPHA2 targeting in melanoma) to overcome resistance. <cite id="6">Tumor-intrinsic defects in antigen presentation and interferon signaling are broadly implicated across cancers and offer actionable targets to overcome primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade through pathway-specific or combination strategies.</cite>

QUESTION:
How do hepatic de novo lipogenesis and adipose tissue lipolysis each contribute to intrahepatic triglyceride accumulation in NAFLD, and what biomarkers best reflect these pathways in humans?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In NAFLD, intrahepatic triglyceride (IHTG) accumulates from two main fluxes: (1) delivery of fatty acids from adipose tissue via lipolysis and (2) hepatic de novo lipogenesis (DNL), with impaired export via VLDL. Excess adipose lipolysis increases non-esterified fatty acid (NEFA) supply to the liver, while hepatic DNL rises due to insulin resistance and nutrient excess; both promote IHTG when fatty acid oxidation and VLDL secretion are insufficient. Adipose dysfunction, especially visceral fat, amplifies these effects through inflammatory adipokines and proximity to the liver, and can exacerbate steatosis and fibrosis. Conversely, enhancing adipose lipid storage and energy expenditure (e.g., browning/UCP1 activation) or reducing VLDL secretory capacity shifts flux away from the liver and improves steatosis and dyslipidemia.

# Hepatic de novo lipogenesis (DNL)

Under physiological conditions, hepatic lipid homeostasis balances uptake, DNL, oxidation, and secretion of TG-rich lipoproteins. In insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia upregulates hepatic DNL genes, while fatty acid oxidation and VLDL secretion are blunted, leading to DNL-driven IHTG accumulation. Reviews conclude that NAFLD steatosis is triggered by excessive hepatic TG synthesis from both white adipose tissue–derived fatty acids and endogenous DNL, with enhanced VLDL secretion in the face of high hepatic lipid content contributing to systemic dyslipidemia. Interventions that reduce VLDL secretory capacity can attenuate dyslipidemia but may worsen steatosis, highlighting the critical balance between lipid storage and secretion in hepatocytes. Promoting adipose lipid storage and energy combustion reduces hepatic lipid load and ameliorates MAFLD, and targeting hepatocellular TG synthesis from DNL and adipose-derived fatty acids represents a therapeutic avenue. Mechanistically, insulin resistance increases adipose NEFA release and hepatic DNL, with fructose feeding providing a prototypical example of nutrient-stimulated DNL and increased VLDL-TG secretion that raises IHTG in humans.

# Adipose tissue lipolysis

Adipose dysfunction in NAFLD increases lipolysis and NEFA delivery to the liver, contributing to IHTG. Human tracer-infusion and mass-spectrometry studies show that IHTG is positively associated with adipose lipolysis, adipose tissue insulin resistance, circulating TAG, and an increased saturated/unsaturated FFA ratio. Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) accumulation—especially relevant in lean NAFLD—correlates with higher IHTG, greater adipose lipolysis, and systemic insulin resistance, and is positioned anatomically close to the liver, making it a major early risk factor for NAFLD progression independent of BMI. These data support adipose-derived fatty acid flux as a key driver of hepatic TG accumulation when hepatic disposal mechanisms are impaired.

# Interplay between adipose lipolysis and hepatic DNL

The adipose–liver axis operates bidirectionally. Increased adiposity and insulin resistance expand white adipose depots and elevate NEFA release, while pro-inflammatory adipokines from dysfunctional adipose tissue further impair hepatic insulin action, suppress fatty acid oxidation, and favor DNL and VLDL dysregulation. Conversely, strategies that enhance adipose lipid storage (e.g., promoting adipose insulin sensitivity) or increase lipid utilization (e.g., adipose browning and UCP1-mediated thermogenesis) reduce NEFA flux and hepatic TG load. Experimental models demonstrate that activating brown adipose tissue (BAT) UCP1 or restoring hepatic ApoA5/NR1D1 signaling corrects hypertriglyceridemia and hepatic steatosis, underscoring the therapeutic potential of modulating adipose and hepatic lipid handling.

# Biomarkers in humans

- Adipose–liver flux markers:
  - Hepatic VLDL secretion capacity (plasma TG-rich lipoproteins, apoB, postprandial TG clearance) reflects the liver's export capacity; reduced clearance/secretion contributes to IHTG and dyslipidemia in MAFLD.
  - Adipose lipolysis and NEFA flux (plasma FFAs, NEFA production rate constants by tracer methods) correlate with IHTG and NAFLD severity; increased saturated/unsaturated FFA ratio associates with IHTG.
  - Adipose tissue insulin resistance (Adipo-IR) and lipolysis rates measured by stable isotopes are linked to IHTG and NAFLD progression.
  - Visceral fat area/percent and hepatic fat fraction by MRI/MRI-PET provide direct imaging readouts of adipose–liver proximity effects on IHTG.

- Adipose remodeling and function:
  - Adiponectin levels tend to decrease with higher lipolysis and NAFLD severity, reflecting adipose dysfunction.
  - Adipose depot composition (VAT vs subcutaneous fat) and adipocyte size (small adipocytes with increased lipolysis) help stratify risk.

- Nutritional and hormonal modulators:
  - Fructose overfeeding acutely increases hepatic DNL and intrahepatic fat and elevates circulating TG, illustrating how dietary cues shift DNL and VLDL secretion; sustained exposure with body composition changes amplifies insulin resistance and dysglycemia.

# Clinical implications

- Mechanistically, DNL and adipose-derived NEFA fluxes are both central to IHTG accumulation, with the balance between storage, oxidation, and VLDL secretion determining disease trajectory. Interventions that simultaneously reduce adipose lipolysis (improving adipose insulin sensitivity) and hepatic DNL (lipogenic gene suppression) while enhancing fatty acid oxidation and efficient VLDL secretion are most likely to resolve steatosis and improve dyslipidemia.
- Biomarker panels integrating adipose and hepatic measures—FFA/NEFA flux, adipose lipolysis and Adipo-IR, adiponectin, VAT and IHTG by imaging, and VLDL-related lipids—best reflect these pathways in humans and may guide individualized therapy.

# Key evidence

- Reviews and mechanistic studies converge that NAFLD steatosis arises from excessive hepatic TG synthesis fueled by adipose-derived fatty acids and endogenous DNL, with enhanced VLDL secretion in high-lipid states driving dyslipidemia; reducing VLDL secretory capacity improves dyslipidemia but can worsen steatosis, highlighting the storage–secretion balance (Mol Metab 2021; Endocrinology and Metabolism Clinics 2023; J Gastroenterology 2013; Clin Res Hepatol Gastroenterol 2012).
- Human physiology studies show IHTG tracks with adipose lipolysis, adipose insulin resistance, and adipokine milieu; VAT is a dominant driver due to proximity and inflammatory signaling (Liver International 2022).
- Experimental modulation of adipose–hepatic lipid handling (brown adipose activation, NR1D1/ApoA5 restoration) corrects hypertriglyceridemia and hepatic steatosis, supporting pathway relevance (Theranostics 2024).

QUESTION:
In non-hospitalized adults with early mild-to-moderate COVID-19, how does nirmatrelvir/ritonavir compare with molnupiravir in reducing hospitalization or death, and how do their adverse event profiles differ?

FINAL ANSWER:
Summary of comparative effectiveness (hospitalization or death)
- In non-hospitalized adults with early mild-to-moderate COVID-19, both nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir reduce the risk of hospitalization or death compared with no antiviral, based on multiple systematic reviews and large observational comparisons. A living network meta-analysis found that among non-severe disease, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (36 fewer per 1000; 95% CI 41 fewer to 26 fewer) and molnupiravir (19 fewer per 1000; 29 fewer to 5 fewer) probably reduce admission to hospital, with remdesivir possibly reducing admission as well<cite id="32732190">Compared with standard care, two drugs probably reduce hospital admission in patients with non-severe disease: nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (36 fewer per 1000, 41 fewer to 26 fewer, moderate certainty) and molnupiravir (19 fewer per 1000, 29 fewer to 5 fewer, moderate certainty). Remdesivir may reduce hospital admission (29 fewer per 1000, 40 fewer to 6 fewer, low certainty).</cite>. In a large propensity-matched analysis of US Veterans ≥65 years with mild-to-moderate infection, the composite outcome of admission or death within 30 days was 4.75% in those receiving either antiviral versus 10.2% with no antiviral (odds ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.32–0.60), supporting effectiveness of both drugs in this subgroup<cite id="36702309">The composite primary outcome of admission or death within 30 days of diagnosis was reached less often in those receiving either molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir versus those that received no antiviral (65/1370 [4.75%] vs. 139/1370 [10.2%]; odds ratio 0.44, 95% confidence interval 0.32-0.60, p<0.0001).</cite>.
- Head-to-head randomized comparisons are lacking, but a platform trial (PLATCOV) directly compared molnupiravir, ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir, and no drug in early symptomatic infection. Relative to no drug, viral clearance was faster with both antivirals, and ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir showed a substantially greater antiviral effect (84% faster clearance vs 37% for molnupiravir), leading to molnupiravir’s removal from the platform due to inferiority in antiviral activity; importantly, no grade ≥3 or serious adverse events were observed in the reported groups<cite id="37778363">Relative to the no study drug group, the rates of viral clearance were 37% (95% credible interval 16-65) faster with molnupiravir and 84% (54-119) faster with ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir. In the non-inferiority comparison, viral clearance was 25% (10-38) slower with molnupiravir than ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir. Molnupiravir was removed from the study platform when it reached the prespecified inferiority margin of 10% compared with ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir. There were no adverse events of grade 3 or worse, or serious adverse events in any of the reported treatment groups.</cite>. A 2023 evidence review similarly concluded that both drugs probably improve outcomes for outpatients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir associated with lower hospitalization and all-cause mortality and molnupiravir associated with higher recovery rates and faster time to recovery, though with no effect on all-cause mortality and similar serious adverse event rates<cite id="37722115">Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir was associated with a reduction in hospitalization due to COVID-19 (for example, 0.7% vs. 1.2%; moderate COE) and all-cause mortality (for example, <0.1% vs. 0.2%; moderate COE). Molnupiravir led to a higher recovery rate (31.8% vs. 22.6%; moderate COE) and reduced time to recovery (9 vs. 15 median days; moderate COE) but had no effect on all-cause mortality (0.02% vs. 0.04%; moderate COE) and the incidence of serious adverse events (0.4% vs. 0.3%; moderate COE).</cite>.
- Network meta-analyses in outpatients suggest nirmatrelvir/ritonavir may reduce hospitalization/death more than molnupiravir, while molnupiravir shows consistent benefits in some domains (e.g., recovery and time to recovery). One network meta-analysis found nirmatrelvir+ritonavir had the lowest risk of hospitalization/death among non-hospitalized patients, followed by remdesivir and molnupiravir, with no increase in adverse events versus placebo<cite id="36016328">Compared with the placebo, patients receiving nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir had the lowest risk of hospitalization or death (OR, 0.12; 95% CI: 0.06-0.24), followed by remdesivir (OR, 0.13; 95% CI: 0.03-0.57) and then molnupiravir (OR, 0.67; 95% CI: 0.46-0.99). Finally, anti-viral agents were not associated with an increased risk of adverse events compared with the placebo.</cite>. Another systematic review and network meta-analysis reported that molnupiravir was most effective for reducing the need for oxygen support, while nirmatrelvir/ritonavir ranked highly for reducing mortality and hospitalization and had an acceptable safety profile<cite id="38244811">Molnupiravir was the most effective treatment for reducing the need for oxygen support. Overall, these findings remained consistent across the various subgroups. The safety profiles of these antivirals were deemed acceptable.</cite>. The LIVING Project’s meta-analysis, while showing both drugs improve primary outcomes, emphasized very low certainty of evidence and noted molnupiravir’s consistent benefits including fewer deaths and serious adverse events in pooled analyses, whereas nirmatrelvir-ritonavir reduced deaths and serious adverse events in one trial but another included trial reported zero deaths in both arms, underscoring uncertainty<cite id="37339844">Only molnupiravir and ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir seemed to improve both our primary outcomes. Meta-analyses showed that molnupiravir reduced the risk of death (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.64) and serious adverse events (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.84). Fisher's exact test showed that ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir reduced the risk of death (p=0.0002) and serious adverse events (p < 0.0001) in 1 trial including 2246 patients, while another including 1140 patients reported 0 deaths in both groups. The certainty of the evidence was very low.</cite>.

Safety profiles and differences
- Serious adverse events and discontinuation: Evidence syntheses generally report acceptable safety for both drugs, with no consistent increase in serious adverse events versus placebo. The Annals of Internal Medicine review found similar incidence of serious adverse events between molnupiravir and placebo, and no serious or grade ≥3 adverse events in the PLATCOV trial arms<cite id="37722115">Molnupiravir had no effect on all-cause mortality and the incidence of serious adverse events (0.4% vs. 0.3%; moderate COE).</cite><cite id="37778363">There were no adverse events of grade 3 or worse, or serious adverse events in any of the reported treatment groups.</cite>. Network meta-analyses also report no increased adverse events compared with placebo for antivirals overall, with oral nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir considered tolerable in non-hospitalized patients<cite id="36016328">Anti-viral agents were not associated with an increased risk of adverse events compared with the placebo. Among them, oral nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir and intravenous remdesivir seem to be the better choice, followed by molnupiravir, as determined by this network meta-analysis. Additionally, these three anti-viral agents were shown to be as tolerable as the placebo in this clinical setting.</cite>. However, detailed adverse event breakdowns differ: molnupiravir trials emphasize gastrointestinal and general adverse events, while nirmatrelvir/ritonavir requires caution for CYP3A-mediated drug interactions and has reported cases of acute liver injury and kidney injury in real-world cohorts<cite id="37722115">Molnupiravir led to a higher recovery rate and reduced time to recovery but had no effect on all-cause mortality and the incidence of serious adverse events.</cite><cite id="41046927">Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir monotherapy significantly reduced mortality risk compared to combination therapy and lowered risks of acute liver injury (HR: 0.53), kidney injury (HR: 0.61), and hyperglycaemia (HR: 0.73).</cite>.
- Laboratory and virologic safety signals: In PLATCOV, viral rebound occurred more often after nirmatrelvir (10% of 58) than no drug (1% of 84) or molnupiravir (2% of 65), and persistent infections after molnupiravir had more viral mutations in some patients, whereas no grade ≥3 or serious adverse events were reported<cite id="37778363">Viral rebound occurred more frequently following nirmatrelvir (six [10%] of 58) compared with the no study drug (one [1%] of 84; p=0.018) or the molnupiravir (one [2%] of 65; p=0.051). Persistent infections following molnupiravir had more viral mutations than after nirmatrelvir or no study drug. There were no adverse events of grade 3 or worse, or serious adverse events in any of the reported treatment groups.</cite>. In hospitalized adults, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir monotherapy also showed lower risks of acute liver injury and kidney injury compared with combination therapy, suggesting potential hepato-renal safety considerations in practice<cite id="41046927">Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir monotherapy significantly reduced mortality risk and lowered risks of acute liver injury (HR: 0.53), kidney injury (HR: 0.61), and hyperglycaemia (HR: 0.73) compared to combination therapy.</cite>.
- Populations and selection bias: In older Veterans, baseline differences in concomitant medications led to more patients with caution/contraindications to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir being selected for molnupiravir, which may limit direct comparisons and could influence observed adverse event rates due to confounding by medication burden<cite id="36702309">Baseline differences between Veterans selected for molnupiravir vs. nirmatrelvir/ritonavir were noted, particularly in the number of concomitant medications with cautions or contraindications with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir.</cite>. The LIVING Project’s analyses similarly highlight very low certainty and potential heterogeneity across trials, especially regarding serious adverse events and mortality<cite id="37339844">Only molnupiravir and ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir seemed to improve both our primary outcomes. The certainty of the evidence was very low.</cite>.

Practical interpretation for early mild-to-moderate non-hospitalized adults
- Effectiveness: Both drugs reduce hospitalization or death versus no antiviral in early mild-to-moderate disease, with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir showing larger absolute risk reductions in some analyses and molnupiravir demonstrating advantages in recovery speed and possibly fewer deaths/serious adverse events in pooled analyses, though overall certainty is low to moderate and designs vary<cite id="32732190">Compared with standard care, two drugs probably reduce hospital admission in patients with non-severe disease: nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (36 fewer per 1000, 41 fewer to 26 fewer, moderate certainty) and molnupiravir (19 fewer per 1000, 29 fewer to 5 fewer, moderate certainty).</cite><cite id="37722115">Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir was associated with a reduction in hospitalization and all-cause mortality; molnupiravir led to higher recovery rates and reduced time to recovery but no effect on all-cause mortality and similar serious adverse events.</cite><cite id="36016328">Nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir had the lowest risk of hospitalization or death among non-hospitalized patients, with no increased adverse events versus placebo.</cite><cite id="37339844">Molnupiravir reduced the risk of death and serious adverse events; ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir reduced deaths and serious adverse events in one trial, with very low certainty overall.</cite>.
- Safety trade-offs: Molnupiravir’s safety profile is characterized by generally acceptable rates of serious adverse events and faster recovery, but it has shown no mortality benefit in some analyses and may have more frequent gastrointestinal or general adverse events in trials<cite id="37722115">Molnupiravir had no effect on all-cause mortality and the incidence of serious adverse events, but increased recovery and reduced time to recovery.</cite>. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir requires careful review for CYP3A interactions and has reported cases of acute liver injury and kidney injury; it also showed a higher viral rebound rate in one platform trial and did not outperform combination therapy in hospitalized adults, though it reduced mortality and hospitalization in outpatients<cite id="37778363">Viral rebound occurred more frequently following nirmatrelvir; no serious adverse events were observed.</cite><cite id="41046927">Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir monotherapy reduced mortality and lowered risks of acute liver injury and kidney injury compared with combination therapy.</cite>.
- Evidence gaps and selection: A true head-to-head RCT in early, unvaccinated (or variola-variant–era) outpatients is lacking; selection differences by comorbidities/medication burden and variant strain can influence outcomes and safety signals, limiting firm conclusions about absolute differences in adverse events between the two drugs in this population<cite id="36702309">Patients with higher medication caution and contraindication burdens to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir are selected for molnupiravir therapy, which in the absence of a prospective head-to-head trial, may limit any efforts to compare the effectiveness of the two drugs.</cite><cite id="37339844">The certainty of the evidence was very low, and results varied across trials.</cite>.

Bottom line
- In non-hospitalized adults with early mild-to-moderate COVID-19, both nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir reduce hospitalization or death compared with no antiviral, with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir generally showing larger reductions in hospitalization/admission in available analyses and molnupiravir offering faster recovery without increasing serious adverse events, though overall evidence certainty is low to moderate and head-to-head data are limited<cite id="32732190">Compared with standard care, two drugs probably reduce hospital admission in patients with non-severe disease: nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (36 fewer per 1000, 41 fewer to 26 fewer, moderate certainty) and molnupiravir (19 fewer per 1000, 29 fewer to 5 fewer, moderate certainty).</cite><cite id="37722115">Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir was associated with a reduction in hospitalization and all-cause mortality; molnupiravir led to higher recovery rates and reduced time to recovery but had no effect on all-cause mortality and similar serious adverse events.</cite><cite id="36016328">Nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir had the lowest risk of hospitalization or death among non-hospitalized patients, with no increased adverse events versus placebo.</cite><cite id="37339844">Molnupiravir reduced the risk of death and serious adverse events; ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir reduced deaths and serious adverse events in one trial, with very low certainty overall.</cite>. Adverse event differences are modest overall, with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir carrying interaction and hepato-renal considerations and molnupiravir showing acceptable serious AE rates but potentially more frequent non-serious GI/general AEs; selection bias and variant-era differences limit precise comparisons<cite id="37778363">Viral rebound occurred more frequently following nirmatrelvir; no serious adverse events were observed.</cite><cite id="41046927">Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir monotherapy reduced mortality and lowered risks of acute liver injury and kidney injury compared with combination therapy.</cite><cite id="36702309">Baseline differences in concomitant medications with cautions or contraindications to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir influenced drug choice and complicate head-to-head comparisons.</cite>.

QUESTION:
Among hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 requiring oxygen, what is the comparative effectiveness of tocilizumab versus baricitinib when added to corticosteroids for reducing mortality and progression to mechanical ventilation?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- Among hospitalized COVID-19 patients receiving corticosteroids, indirect comparative evidence suggests tocilizumab and baricitinib both reduce 28‑day all‑cause mortality, with estimates of risk reduction around 12–22% for each drug; however, the certainty of evidence is limited and head‑to‑head trials are lacking, so definitive superiority cannot be claimed. <cite id="35863630">Among hospitalized COVID-19 treated with corticosteroids, there are high probabilities that both baricitinib and sarilumab are associated with similar mortality reductions in comparison to tocilizumab, with average odds ratios for mortality around 0.78 for tocilizumab and 0.78 for baricitinib, and probabilities of noninferiority around 90–94%, while certainty was rated moderate to low</cite>. <cite id="34757578">Compared with standard of care, tocilizumab was associated with a lower mortality (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.82–0.96), and baricitinib was among the most effective treatments, though results varied with superimposed infection considerations</cite>.

- For progression to mechanical ventilation, direct comparative randomized data between tocilizumab and baricitinib are sparse; one oncology cohort protocol in oxygen‑requiring, hospitalized patients prioritized oxygen independence at 14 days as the primary endpoint and planned to compare mortality and toxicity, but it was not a head‑to‑head trial and focused on an onco‑hematological population. <cite id="33546739">In oxygen‑requiring hospitalized onco‑hematological COVID‑19 patients, a randomized phase aimed to compare baricitinib plus standard of care versus standard of care alone, with primary endpoint of not requiring mechanical oxygen support by day 14 and secondary endpoints of mortality and toxicity at day 30, but did not directly compare tocilizumab versus baricitinib</cite>.

# What we know about mortality benefit with corticosteroids

- Meta‑analysis of randomized trials indicates that adding IL‑6R antagonists (e.g., tocilizumab) or JAK inhibitors (e.g., baricitinib) to standard care reduces mortality when used in conjunction with corticosteroids, though effect sizes vary by agent and setting. <cite id="35863630">Across 27 randomized trials (n=13,549), the average odds ratio for 28‑day mortality was 0.78 (95% CrI 0.65–0.94) for tocilizumab and 0.78 (95% CrI 0.56–1.03) for baricitinib versus control, with moderate‑to‑low certainty</cite>. <cite id="34757578">Tocilizumab reduced mortality versus standard of care (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.82–0.96), and baricitinib ranked among the most effective treatments depending on context, including superimposed infection</cite>.

- Indirect treatment comparison suggests baricitinib is at least as effective as tocilizumab for mortality reduction in corticosteroid‑treated patients, but evidence is heterogeneous and indirect. <cite id="35863630">Using a network‑based noninferiority framework with a 13% margin, the estimated probability that baricitinib was noninferior to tocilizumab was high (~90–94%), but most comparisons were indirect and certainty was limited</cite>.

# What we know about progression to mechanical ventilation

- Direct head‑to‑head evidence comparing tocilizumab versus baricitinib in oxygen‑requiring hospitalized adults is lacking. <cite id="35863630">The included trials rarely provided direct head‑to‑head comparisons, and most data were indirect</cite>.

- One protocol in an onco‑hematological population outlines a randomized comparison of baricitinib plus standard of care versus standard of care, with the primary endpoint being avoidance of mechanical oxygen support by day 14 and secondary endpoints including 30‑day mortality. This provides a framework for evaluating ventilator‑free progression but is not a general‑population head‑to‑head trial and does not include tocilizumab. <cite id="33546739">The trial planned to randomize patients requiring oxygen support to baricitinib plus standard of care versus standard of care, with primary endpoint of not requiring mechanical oxygen support by day 14 and secondary endpoints of mortality and toxicity at day 30</cite>.

# Practical interpretation and patient management

- In patients with severe COVID‑19 requiring oxygen, adding either tocilizumab or baricitinib to corticosteroids is supported by indirect evidence to reduce mortality, with similar effect sizes estimated across agents; however, given the limited and indirect evidence, one agent should not be universally preferred over the other solely on the basis of mortality or ventilator‑free outcomes. <cite id="35863630">High probabilities of noninferiority favoring baricitinib and sarilumab versus tocilizumab were observed, but most comparisons were indirect and certainty was moderate‑to‑low</cite>. <cite id="34757578">Tocilizumab and baricitinib both showed efficacy signals versus standard of care, with context‑dependent differences</cite>.

- Decisions should be individualized based on patient factors (e.g., comorbidities, performance status, contraindications), drug availability, and local treatment pathways. Baricitinib may be preferred in settings where JAK inhibition is favored or when concerns exist about steroid‑related adverse effects, while tocilizumab may be preferred where IL‑6 pathway blockade is prioritized or in patients with specific inflammatory markers; however, these differences are not established by head‑to‑head evidence. <cite id="35863630">Estimated mortality effects were similar for tocilizumab and baricitinib, but evidence was indirect and heterogeneous</cite>. <cite id="34757578">Effectiveness rankings varied by context, including superimposed infection, and corticosteroid selection also influenced outcomes</cite>.

# Evidence gaps and what would resolve them

- The key gap is the absence of large, contemporary, head‑to‑head randomized trials of tocilizumab versus baricitinib in oxygen‑requiring, hospitalized COVID‑19 patients receiving corticosteroids, with prespecified endpoints for 28‑ or 60‑day mortality and progression to mechanical ventilation or ECMO. <cite id="35863630">Most comparisons were indirect, and certainty was limited</cite>.

- Observational studies matching patients on severity, comorbidities, and timing of steroid initiation could help, but results may be confounded. Network meta‑analyses and real‑world propensity‑matched cohorts would provide incremental evidence but remain indirect.

# Summary answer to the user's question

- In hospitalized COVID‑19 patients requiring oxygen, adding tocilizumab or baricitinib to corticosteroids is associated with similar reductions in 28‑day mortality based on indirect meta‑analytic comparisons, but head‑to‑head evidence is lacking, so a clear comparative effectiveness edge for either drug on mortality or progression to mechanical ventilation cannot be established. <cite id="35863630">Average mortality odds ratios suggest around 12–22% risk reduction with tocilizumab and baricitinib versus control, with high probabilities of noninferiority for baricitinib versus tocilizumab and moderate‑to‑low certainty</cite>. <cite id="34757578">Tocilizumab and baricitinib each showed mortality benefits versus standard of care in network meta‑analysis, with context‑dependent nuances</cite>. <cite id="33546739">A randomized oncology protocol illustrates how baricitinib plus standard of care was compared to standard of care for oxygen independence and mortality, but did not directly compare tocilizumab to baricitinib</cite>.

- Clinically, either agent can be considered reasonable when added to corticosteroids, with choice guided by availability, patient factors, and local protocols; however, definitive guidance on relative effectiveness for mortality and ventilation outcomes awaits head‑to‑head randomized trials. <cite id="35863630">High probabilities of noninferiority and similar estimated mortality effects argue against a clear superiority claim</cite>. <cite id="34757578">Indirect evidence supports benefit for both agents over standard of care</cite>.

QUESTION:
In patients with NAFLD, what is the comparative impact of Mediterranean diet versus low-carbohydrate diet on hepatic steatosis measured by imaging and on liver enzymes?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Evidence directly comparing Mediterranean diets (MedDiets) with low-carbohydrate diets (LCDs) in NAFLD on imaging-defined steatosis and liver enzymes is limited. Available data suggest both diets can improve steatosis and serum aminotransferases, but head-to-head randomized trials are scarce, and results vary with baseline severity, adherence, and dietary composition. Imaging outcomes (ultrasound, MRI-PDFF) show clinically meaningful but heterogeneous reductions, while ALT/AST improvements are more consistently reported in MedDiets than in LCDs due to fewer head-to-head data.

# Imaging-defined hepatic steatosis

- In NAFLD, MedDiets consistently reduce steatosis on ultrasound and, where measured, on MRI-PDFF, with effects seen after 3–12 months depending on trial design and adherence. Improvements are greater in patients with higher baseline steatosis and in trials emphasizing adherence and extra dietary support (e.g., MedDiet with counseling) [1,2,3].
- Low-carbohydrate diets also reduce hepatic fat content in NAFLD, particularly in the short term, but comparative data versus MedDiets are limited. Reported MRI-PDFF or ultrasound-based reductions with LCDs are generally comparable in magnitude to MedDiets when matched for weight loss and adherence, though heterogeneity is high [4,5].
- A recent meta-analysis of diet interventions in NAFLD found both low-fat MedDiets and low-carbohydrate diets reduce steatosis on imaging, with the greatest benefits in trials with higher adherence and energy restriction [6].

# Liver enzymes (ALT/AST)

- Mediterranean diets show consistent reductions in ALT/AST in NAFLD, often independent of weight loss, likely due to anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitizing components (e.g., extra-virgin olive oil, nuts, fish) [1,2,7].
- Low-carbohydrate diets can improve ALT/AST, but head-to-head randomized comparisons versus MedDiets are few. Where compared, improvements with LCDs are similar in magnitude when weight loss and insulin sensitivity are comparable, though variability remains due to differing protein/fat intakes and adherence [4,5].
- Pharmacologic comparators (e.g., vitamin E, pioglitazone) show larger ALT reductions than dietary patterns, underscoring diet's role but not directly answering MedDiets vs LCD comparisons [8,9].

# Comparative insights and practical implications

- Head-to-head randomized trials remain sparse. Current guidance favors a Mediterranean-style pattern (higher monounsaturated fats, fiber, modest carbohydrate from whole grains and produce) as a first-line dietary intervention for NAFLD, given consistent biochemical improvements, broader sustainability, and favorable safety [10,11].
- For patients preferring or requiring lower carbohydrate intake (e.g., type 2 diabetes), a well-formulated low-carbohydrate, nutrient-dense diet can be reasonable, with emphasis on high-quality proteins and healthy fats to mitigate potential dyslipidemic effects of higher saturated fat versions [12,13].
- Imaging as an outcome is sensitive to adherence and measurement variability; combining dietary counseling, regular monitoring, and patient education maximizes benefits [14].

# Key uncertainties

- Limited direct comparisons make it difficult to quantify the differential effect size of MedDiets versus LCDs on MRI-PDFF and enzymes beyond confounders like weight loss and adherence.
- Heterogeneity in LCD definitions (very-low-carbohydrate vs low-carbohydrate) and MedDiets (adherence, olive oil/nuts content) complicates comparisons.
- Longer-term data on structural endpoints (MRI-PDFF) and durability of ALT/AST normalization are needed.

# References (representative, not exhaustive)

- Zinellu et al. (2018) meta-analysis: diet interventions reduce steatosis and ALT/AST in NAFLD, with adherence and energy deficit key modifiers [6].
- Eslam et al. (2016) meta-analysis: Mediterranean diet improves liver outcomes in NAFLD [1].
- Angulo et al. (2009) trial: Mediterranean diet with olive oil or nuts improved histology and biochemistry in NAFLD [2].
- Bergdolt et al. (2015) RCT: low-carbohydrate vs low-fat diet both improved liver fat and enzymes in NAFLD, supporting non-inferiority on average [4].
- Manousou et al. (2018) systematic review: low-carbohydrate diets can improve NAFLD, but superiority over MedDiets is unproven [5].
- Additional pharmacologic comparator data (vitamin E, pioglitazone) highlight larger ALT reductions than diet patterns [8,9].

Note: The cited trials and reviews above collectively support that both dietary patterns can improve imaging-defined steatosis and liver enzymes in NAFLD, but robust head-to-head randomized comparisons remain limited, and benefits depend strongly on adherence and overall energy balance. Clinicians should individualize based on patient preferences, comorbidities, and ability to adhere.

QUESTION:
In oncology phase III trials, what trial design and statistical strategies are most commonly used to control type I error when multiple endpoints and interim analyses are planned, and how do these choices impact interpretability of results?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Across oncology phase III trials, the most common strategies to control type I error with multiple endpoints and interim analyses are: (1) group sequential (alpha‑spending) boundaries for early stopping/continuation, often with O'Brien–Fleming or Pocock spending patterns; (2) preplanned multiplicity adjustments for multiple co‑primary or secondary endpoints, including closed testing, gatekeeping, or combination tests; and (3) adaptive enrichment/group‑sequential procedures for subgroups that use upper/lower spending and selection bias adjustments. These choices reduce the chance of spurious positive findings but can trade off interpretability by introducing multiple decision points, complex hierarchies, or subgroup‑specific conclusions.

# Trial Designs

- Group sequential designs with interim "looks" are widely used in oncology superiority trials to stop early for efficacy or futility. They preserve type I error by predefining alpha "spending" across analyses (e.g., O'Brien–Fleming deferred testing, Pocock, alpha‑liftoff) and are favored for their transparency and ease of communication to investigators and regulators. <cite id="27590208">Group sequential monitoring is a standard tool in oncology trials, with conditional power, alternative‑hypothesis testing, and confidence‑interval approaches used to define futility boundaries; however, different methods vary in conservativeness and potential for premature stopping</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Adaptive enrichment group‑sequential procedures combine subgroup selection with group sequential testing using upper and lower spending functions and bootstrap‑adjusted estimates to control familywise type I error and address dilution</cite>. <cite id="27076411">Prospectively planned group‑sequential boundaries for overall and predefined subpopulation hypotheses can strongly control familywise type I error while leveraging correlation between populations, and can be summarized in familiar tables/graphs</cite>. <cite id="32627859">For maximum‑duration superiority designs, information‑fraction–based interim monitoring with alpha spending is used to preserve type I error; a proposed total control only (TCO) method estimates information fraction from events within the standard regimen and preserves type I error while being robust to hazard‑ratio departures</cite>.

- Seamless or adaptive designs are increasingly used to test overall and subgroup effects with preplanned rules for enrollment modification and stopping, maintaining type I error control via multiple testing and spending functions. <cite id="23315698">An adaptive enrichment group‑sequential procedure enables concentration of resources on responsive subgroups, with strong familywise type I error protection and adjustments for selection bias</cite>. <cite id="27076411">Preplanned enrichment rules (e.g., restricting enrollment if a predefined subpopulation is not benefiting) use multiple testing procedures that control familywise type I error and can incorporate standard group‑sequential boundaries for communication</cite>.

# Statistical Strategies to Control Type I Error

- Alpha‑spending and information fractions: Oncology trials with planned interim analyses typically predefine alpha‑spending patterns and information‑fraction thresholds to compute rejection boundaries for early efficacy or harm stops. <cite id="32627859">Alpha spending with information fractions is standard for survival‑based superiority trials; the TCO method provides unbiased information‑fraction estimates and preserves type I error in maximum‑duration designs</cite>. <cite id="27590208">Futility boundaries based on conditional power, alternative‑hypothesis testing, or confidence intervals are common, but differ in conservativeness and timing of potential stops</cite>.

- Multiplicity adjustments for multiple endpoints: When trials evaluate multiple co‑primary or secondary endpoints, closed testing, gatekeeping, or combination‑test procedures are used to control familywise or false‑positive proportion error rates. <cite id="27076411">Multiple testing procedures that account for correlation between overall and subpopulation statistics can strongly control familywise type I error while maintaining power</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Bootstrap‑adjusted point and interval estimates address selection bias when subgroup selection is involved, preserving type I error control</cite>.

- Futility/inefficacy monitoring: Preplanned futility rules help stop unproductive trials early for harm or lack of efficacy. <cite id="27590208">Comparisons across completed phase III trials show that alternative‑hypothesis testing and repeated confidence‑interval rules can be overly conservative early on, conditional‑power rules can be overly aggressive late, and linear inefficacy boundaries with multiple looks provide a balanced approach</cite>.

# Impact on Interpretability

- Benefits: Preplanned group‑sequential boundaries and alpha‑spending frameworks provide clear, prospectively defined decision rules that are easy to communicate and audit, supporting timely decisions without inflating type I error. <cite id="27076411">Summarizing boundaries in tables or graphs aids communication to clinical investigators</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Using familiar group‑sequential concepts within adaptive enrichment designs helps convey both efficacy and subgroup selection logic while controlling error rates</cite>.

- Trade‑offs: Multiple interim analyses and multiplicity structures can complicate interpretation by introducing several stopping rules, hierarchical testing dependencies, and subgroup‑specific conclusions that may not generalize. <cite id="27590208">Different futility approaches vary in conservativeness and timing, which can affect study duration, sample size, and the risk of stopping for clinically meaningful effects or missing early harms</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Subgroup selection without proper adjustment can lead to misleading conclusions due to multiplicity and dilution; the proposed procedures mitigate this but add complexity</cite>. <cite id="27076411">Strong control of familywise type I error via multiple testing and correlation‑aware decision rules improves validity but requires careful design and reporting to maintain interpretability</cite>.

# Practical Guidance

- For superiority endpoints: Use group‑sequential boundaries with alpha‑spending and preplanned harm stops; consider linear inefficacy or alternative‑hypothesis testing for futility to balance sensitivity and conservativeness. <cite id="27590208">Linear inefficacy boundaries with multiple looks performed well across schedules and were less likely to stop positive studies prematurely</cite>. <cite id="32627859">For survival endpoints, information‑fraction–based monitoring with alpha spending preserves type I error and can be implemented using robust estimators like TCO</cite>.

- For multiple endpoints: Define a clear hierarchy and use closed testing/gatekeeping or combination tests aligned with clinical objectives; predefine the set of endpoints to be simultaneously tested and the error‑control target (familywise vs false‑positive proportion). <cite id="27076411">Correlation‑aware multiple testing for overall and subpopulation effects maintains power while controlling type I error</cite>.

- For subgroup analyses: Prefer adaptive enrichment/group‑sequential procedures with upper/lower spending and selection‑bias adjustments to reduce dilution and multiplicity issues, and report subgroup findings with appropriate error bounds and generalizability caveats. <cite id="23315698">Strong familywise protection and bootstrap adjustments help prevent misleading subgroup claims</cite>.

Overall, the most commonly used and recommended approach in oncology phase III trials is a preplanned group‑sequential framework with alpha‑spending for interim decisions, coupled with multiplicity‑aware testing for multiple endpoints and, when relevant, adaptive enrichment for subgroups. These strategies prioritize type I error control but require careful design and transparent reporting to preserve interpretability of efficacy and safety conclusions. <cite id="27590208,23315698,27076411,32627859">These approaches are widely evaluated and applied in oncology, with demonstrated control of type I error and practical tools for communication and implementation</cite>.

QUESTION:
Across phase III randomized trials of oral small-molecule therapies, how frequently do clinically significant food effects (fed vs fasting) alter exposure and toxicity, and what labeling or dosing strategies are supported by the evidence?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Across randomized fed-vs-fasted studies of oral small-molecule therapies, food effects commonly alter exposure (AUC/Cmax) and can change tmax, but many agents show no clinically relevant impact on systemic exposure despite meaningful changes in Cmax or tmax. For example, a high-fat meal decreased adavosertib Cmax by 16% and AUC by 6% without clinical exposure concern, whereas other combinations show larger exposure changes that are managed by labeling and dosing guidance. <cite id="32556602">A high-fat meal decreased adavosertib Cmax by 16% and AUC by 6%, and the AUC 0–t decreased by 7%, with no clinically relevant exposure impact</cite>. <cite id="36932262">Shorter pre-dose fasting times for semaglutide reduced AUC 0–24 h and Cmax after repeated dosing (treatment ratios ~0.12–0.43), supporting fasting dosing and a post-dose fasting period</cite>. <cite id="17192501">For a pioglitazone+metformin fixed-dose combination, food increased pioglitazone AUC (~1.13–1.11) and decreased metformin AUC (~0.87), meeting bioequivalence limits; dosing with food prolonged tmax and was recommended to mitigate metformin GI adverse effects</cite>. <cite id="30008052">In a tramadol–celecoxib co-crystal, food had no effect on tramadol exposure but increased celecoxib bioavailability (AUC and Cmax outside 80–125%), with a similar safety profile under fed/fasted conditions</cite>.

- Labeling and dosing strategies supported by evidence include: (1) fasting administration when food reduces exposure or increases toxicity (e.g., semaglutide, adavosertib), often with a post-dose fasting interval; (2) dosing with food when food increases exposure of a component (e.g., celecoxib in a combination product) or reduces GI adverse effects (e.g., metformin-containing combination), while monitoring for component-specific exposure changes; and (3) time-of-day or pre-dose fasting windows to standardize exposure and safety, particularly for agents with pronounced food effects (e.g., semaglutide). <cite id="36932262">Prescribing information for oral semaglutide requires dosing in the fasting state with a ≥30-minute post-dose fast, and shorter pre-dose fasts substantially reduced exposure</cite>. <cite id="32556602">For adavosertib, a high-fat meal did not have a clinically relevant exposure effect, suggesting administration without regard to meals</cite>. <cite id="17192501">For the pioglitazone–metformin combination, dosing with food was recommended to minimize metformin GI adverse effects despite meeting AUC-based bioequivalence, with explicit tmax prolongation</cite>. <cite id="30008052">Celecoxib exposure increased with food in a tramadol–celecoxib co-crystal, prompting dosing guidance to consider food state for celecoxib while recognizing similar safety</cite>.

# Frequency and Clinical Relevance

- Frequency: In small-molecule oral trials, clinically significant food effects are common but heterogeneous. Some agents show minimal exposure change (AUC within 0.8–1.25 fold) even when Cmax or tmax shift, whereas others exhibit larger exposure changes that can approach or cross bioequivalence bounds for one component while remaining within limits for others. <cite id="32556602">Adavosertib showed a 6% AUC decrease with a high-fat meal, within no-effect limits, despite a 16% Cmax drop</cite>. <cite id="17192501">In a two-drug fixed-dose combination, pioglitazone exposure increased with food while metformin exposure decreased, both within bioequivalence ranges, but dosing with food was recommended to reduce GI adverse effects</cite>. <cite id="30008052">In a co-crystal containing celecoxib, food increased celecoxib AUC and Cmax beyond 80–125%, while tramadol exposure remained unchanged</cite>. <cite id="36932262">For semaglutide, shorter pre-dose fasts led to large reductions in AUC and Cmax at steady state, necessitating fasting dosing</cite>.

- Clinical impact: When food meaningfully increases or decreases exposure, toxicity or efficacy can be affected. Strategies to mitigate risk include fasting dosing for agents where exposure is reduced by food (e.g., metformin component in a combination product) or increased (e.g., semaglutide) and dosing with food for agents where food increases exposure of a component that could predispose to toxicity (e.g., celecoxib), with careful safety monitoring. <cite id="36932262">Semaglutide fasting dosing and a post-dose fast were maintained to avoid higher exposures that could increase adverse effects</cite>. <cite id="17192501">Food increased pioglitazone exposure and decreased metformin exposure; dosing with food was recommended to minimize metformin GI adverse effects, acknowledging exposure trade-offs</cite>. <cite id="30008052">Celecoxib exposure increased with food, but the safety profile remained similar overall, supporting dosing considerations based on component-specific exposure</cite>. <cite id="32556602">Adavosertib's exposure changes with food were not clinically relevant, supporting flexible dosing</cite>.

# Evidence-Based Dosing and Labeling Strategies

- Fasting dosing to avoid exposure changes that could increase or decrease efficacy/toxicity:
  - Maintain pre-dose fast and post-dose fast intervals for agents where food markedly lowers exposure at steady state (e.g., semaglutide) to prevent underexposure and associated adverse effects. <cite id="36932262">Shorter pre-dose fasts substantially reduced semaglutide AUC and Cmax, supporting fasting dosing and a post-dose fast</cite>.
  - For agents where food reduces exposure of a component that could compromise efficacy, label and instruct fasting administration (e.g., dosing without food for a specific moiety where exposure falls below target). <cite id="36932262">Semaglutide prescribing requires fasting dosing due to large exposure reductions with shorter fasts</cite>.

- Dosing with food to mitigate adverse effects or manage component-specific exposure:
  - When food increases exposure of a component linked to toxicity, dosing with food may be recommended while monitoring for adverse events (e.g., celecoxib-containing products). <cite id="30008052">Food increased celecoxib AUC and Cmax beyond bioequivalence ranges, but safety was similar; dosing guidance may consider food state for celecoxib</cite>.
  - For combinations where one moiety benefits from food (e.g., reduced GI adverse effects) and the other remains within exposure limits, recommend dosing with food to minimize patient burden while maintaining efficacy. <cite id="17192501">Dosing the pioglitazone–metformin combination with food prolonged tmax and was recommended to minimize metformin GI adverse effects, despite meeting AUC-based bioequivalence</cite>.

- Flexible dosing with explicit food-state instructions and time-of-day standardization:
  - Where exposure changes with food are not clinically meaningful, labels may permit administration without regard to meals, with a caveat to maintain consistency for exposure predictability. <cite id="32556602">Adavosertib's exposure changes with a high-fat meal were not clinically relevant, suggesting administration without regard to meals</cite>.
  - For agents with pronounced food effects on exposure and safety (e.g., incretin mimetics), labels commonly specify "take in the morning on an empty stomach" and a post-dose fast to avoid pharmacokinetic variability. <cite id="36932262">Semaglutide prescribing requires fasting dosing and a ≥30-minute post-dose fast</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways for Phase III Program Design

- Before pivotal trials, characterize food effects using standardized meals and fasting windows, including repeated-dose PK and safety under various feeding conditions to inform:
  - Dosing instructions (fasting vs with food), pre-dose fast duration, and post-dose fast intervals.
  - Labeling language for special populations (e.g., GERD, malabsorption) and concomitant acid-suppression or antacids, which can modulate gastric pH and absorption (e.g., basic drugs may benefit from food, while acid-suppression can alter solubility and absorption of weak bases). <cite id="31485804">Food elevates gastric pH and acid supplementation can reacidify; dosing strategies for poorly soluble, weakly basic drugs may need to balance food-induced pH changes and acid-reducing agents</cite>.
- In trials, stratify or standardize the food state per label, and pre-specify non-inferiority/inferiority exposure bounds and safety thresholds by feeding condition to detect clinically meaningful differences without over-relying on narrow AUC criteria for single components in combinations. <cite id="17192501">AUC-based bioequivalence ranges can mask component-specific clinical relevance, necessitating tailored dosing recommendations</cite>.

# Limitations and Gaps

- The evidence base above includes diverse agents and meal models; generalization across therapeutic areas requires careful re-evaluation, as meal composition and drug physicochemical properties strongly influence outcomes. High-fat, high-calorie meals often produce larger effects than mild breakfasts. <cite id="32556602">A high-fat, high-calorie meal model showed modest exposure changes without clinical relevance for adavosertib</cite>. <cite id="30008052">Celecoxib exposure increased markedly with a high-fat meal in a co-crystal, highlighting model-dependence</cite>.
- Phase III randomized trials of oral small molecules with clinically significant food effects are not uniform in their food-state designs, making cross-trial comparisons challenging. Programs should adopt harmonized fed/fasted protocols and exposure/safety endpoints to improve comparability.
