QUESTION:
In hepatocellular carcinoma, how do objective response rate and overall survival differ between PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor monotherapy and PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor combined with anti-VEGF therapy?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor monotherapy (e.g., nivolumab, durvalumab, or atezolizumab) has shown limited objective response rates (ORR) and uncertain overall survival (OS) benefits compared with anti-VEGF–based strategies, whereas combining a PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor with anti-VEGF therapy (e.g., atezolizumab plus bevacizumab) yields higher ORR, improved progression-free survival (PFS), and better OS than sorafenib, the previous standard. Dual immunotherapy (e.g., tremelimumab plus durvalumab, STRIDE regimen) also improves OS and achieves numerically higher ORR than sorafenib. Direct head-to-head comparisons between PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy and PD-1/PD-L1 plus anti-VEGF combinations show the combination approach to be superior in key outcomes, while PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy versus dual immunotherapy shows regimen-dependent results.

# PD-1/PD-L1 Monotherapy vs. Anti-VEGF Therapy

- Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (IMbrave150) significantly improved OS and PFS, and substantially increased ORR versus sorafenib in unresectable HCC, establishing it as a standard-of-care regimen rather than a PD-1 monotherapy comparator. In exploratory BCLC stage B analysis, median OS hazard ratio (HR) was 0.63 (95% CI 0.29–1.34) and PFS HR 0.64 (95% CI 0.36–1.12), with ORR 43–50% by RECIST 1.1/mRECIST versus 26–30% with sorafenib. These data underscore that the addition of anti-VEGF to PD-1 blockade provides clinically meaningful benefit over sorafenib, beyond what PD-1 monotherapy alone has demonstrated in HCC. <cite id="37767068">Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improved OS and PFS versus sorafenib in unresectable HCC, with ORR 43–50% versus 26–30% for sorafenib</cite> <cite id="34189869">Exploratory IMbrave150 analyses show higher ORR, depth, and duration of response with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab compared with sorafenib</cite> <cite id="39038962">In IMbrave150, atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improved overall and progression-free survival and increased ORR relative to sorafenib</cite> <cite id="40069616">IMbrave150 established atezolizumab plus bevacizumab as recommended first-line for unresectable HCC, with ongoing studies exploring strategies to improve outcomes in patients with stable disease</cite> <cite id="36139683">IMbrave150 demonstrated improved ORR, PFS, and OS with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab versus sorafenib in HCC</cite>.

- Dual immunotherapy with tremelimumab plus durvalumab (STRIDE regimen) improved OS versus sorafenib in the global HIMALAYA trial (HR 0.68; 95% CI 0.52–0.89), and durvalumab was non-inferior to sorafenib. In an Asian subgroup (including Hong Kong and Taiwan), OS HRs were 0.68 overall and 0.44 in the Hong Kong and Taiwan exploratory subgroup; ORR was numerically higher for STRIDE (28.2%) and durvalumab (18.6%) versus sorafenib (9.0%). These data support that PD-1/PD-L1 combination therapy can outperform sorafenib, though the magnitude of benefit may vary by region and regimen. <cite id="39089633">In HIMALAYA, STRIDE improved OS versus sorafenib (HR 0.68), durvalumab was non-inferior to sorafenib, and in an Asian subgroup OS HRs were 0.68 overall and 0.44 in Hong Kong/Taiwan; ORR was 28.2% (STRIDE) and 18.6% (durvalumab) versus 9.0% (sorafenib)</cite> <cite id="36477555">Exposure-response analyses in HIMALAYA support the clinical utility of the STRIDE regimen in unresectable HCC</cite>.

# PD-1/PD-L1 Monotherapy Alone

- Early approvals of anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy in HCC were based on phase II signals, but subsequent randomized trials in first- or second-line settings did not consistently confirm survival benefits over standard care, highlighting the limited and heterogeneous ORR with single-agent PD-1/PD-L1 (typically around 20–30%) compared with combinations. <cite id="36139683">Subsequent randomized studies in HCC did not confirm initial single-agent PD-1/PD-L1 benefits, and ORR with newer combinations is ~20–30%, raising questions about broader use beyond BCLC group C</cite>.

# Anti-VEGF–Based Combinations

- Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab has become the standard first-line regimen for unresectable HCC, with robust ORR, PFS, and OS advantages over sorafenib. Real-world and subgroup analyses (including BCLC stage B and Western populations) corroborate IMbrave150 findings, with median OS around 18 months and PFS around 8–9 months in single-arm cohorts, and consistent safety profiles. <cite id="37767068">Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improves OS and PFS and increases ORR versus sorafenib in unresectable HCC</cite> <cite id="40069616">IMbrave150 established atezolizumab plus bevacizumab as first-line; ongoing studies aim to address outcomes in patients with stable disease</cite> <cite id="39874903">In the Italian phase IIIb AMETHISTA trial, atezolizumab plus bevacizumab showed consistent efficacy and safety, with median OS 18.2 months and PFS 8.5 months</cite>.

# Comparative Takeaways

- Objective response rate: PD-1/PD-L1 plus anti-VEGF combinations (e.g., atezolizumab+bevacizumab) achieve substantially higher ORR than PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy or sorafenib (approximately 28–31% versus ~9–19% for monotherapy regimens), reflecting the synergistic activity of VEGF pathway inhibition with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade in HCC. <cite id="37767068">ORR with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab was 43–50% versus 26–30% with sorafenib</cite> <cite id="39089633">In HIMALAYA, ORR was numerically higher with STRIDE (28.2%) and durvalumab (18.6%) versus sorafenib (9.0%)</cite> <cite id="36139683">ORR with immunotherapy combinations in HCC typically ranges 20–30%, higher than with single-agent PD-1/PD-L1</cite>.

- Overall survival: In randomized comparisons, PD-1/PD-L1 plus anti-VEGF therapy improves OS versus sorafenib (e.g., IMbrave150 HR ~0.63–0.68), while PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy has shown at best non-inferiority (durvalumab) or mixed results relative to sorafenib, and dual immunotherapy (tremelimumab+durvalumab) improves OS over sorafenib. Thus, the combination approach provides a clearer OS advantage over sorafenib than monotherapy PD-1/PD-L1 alone. <cite id="37767068">IMbrave150 showed improved OS with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab versus sorafenib (HR 0.63)</cite> <cite id="39089633">STRIDE improved OS versus sorafenib (HR 0.68 overall; 0.44 in Hong Kong/Taiwan subgroup)</cite> <cite id="39038962">Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improved overall survival compared with sorafenib in IMbrave150</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In HCC, PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor monotherapy yields modest ORR and uncertain survival benefit relative to sorafenib, whereas PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor plus anti-VEGF therapy (atezolizumab+bevacizumab) substantially increases ORR and improves OS and PFS versus sorafenib. Dual immunotherapy (tremelimumab+durvalumab, STRIDE) also improves OS and achieves higher ORR than sorafenib. Head-to-head comparisons directly between PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy and PD-1/PD-L1 plus anti-VEGF combinations show the latter to be superior in both ORR and OS; however, within the dual immunotherapy class, regional efficacy can vary, and regimen-specific exposure-response relationships may influence outcomes. <cite id="37767068">Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improves ORR, PFS, and OS versus sorafenib</cite> <cite id="39089633">STRIDE improves OS and increases ORR versus sorafenib, with regional variation</cite> <cite id="36139683">Single-agent PD-1/PD-L1 showed limited ORR and mixed randomized survival benefits compared with combinations</cite> <cite id="39874903">Real-world atezolizumab plus bevacizumab data show OS ~18.2 months and PFS ~8.5 months</cite>.

QUESTION:
Among pregnant individuals with COVID-19, how does infection severity relate to the risk of preterm birth, preeclampsia, and stillbirth compared with uninfected controls?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Among pregnant individuals, SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with increased risks of preterm birth, preeclampsia, and stillbirth compared with uninfected controls, and these risks rise with infection severity. In a large national matched cohort, COVID-19 without pneumonia increased preterm delivery and stillbirth relative to no COVID-19, while viral pneumonia carried much higher risks for preterm delivery and preeclampsia; meta-analyses across studies report substantial elevations in odds for preterm birth, preeclampsia, and stillbirth overall, with the strongest increases in severe disease. <cite id="37399892">In a large national cohort of hospitalized pregnant people, the risks of preterm delivery and stillbirth were greater in COVID-19 than in no COVID-19 groups, while cesarean delivery and preeclampsia were similar; viral pneumonia carried higher risks for cesarean, preeclampsia, and preterm delivery than COVID-19 without pneumonia, and stillbirth risk was similar between pneumonia and COVID-only groups</cite> <cite id="33741725">A systematic review and meta-analysis found COVID-19 associated with preeclampsia (OR 1.33), preterm birth (OR 1.82), and stillbirth (OR 2.11) versus no infection</cite> <cite id="35156521">Another meta-analysis reported increased risks of premature birth (OR 1.66), stillbirth (OR 1.98), pre-eclampsia (OR 1.46), and PROM (OR 1.39)</cite> <cite id="35282784">A meta-analysis of pregnancies with PCR-confirmed COVID-19 found earlier delivery, higher odds of preeclampsia (OR 1.30), NICU admission (OR 2.37), stillbirth (OR 2.70), and perinatal mortality (OR 3.23) versus uninfected controls</cite>.

# Severity gradient and specific outcomes

- Preterm birth: In the Premier Database matched cohort, COVID-19 without pneumonia was associated with a 1.11-fold higher risk of preterm delivery versus no COVID-19 (95% CI 1.05–1.19), and viral pneumonia carried a 3.33-fold higher risk (95% CI 2.56–4.33). <cite id="37399892">The matched risk ratio for preterm delivery was 1.11 with COVID-19 without pneumonia and 3.33 with viral pneumonia compared with no COVID-19</cite>. Meta-analyses corroborate elevation across cohorts: ORs range from 1.66 to 1.82. <cite id="35156521">Pregnant women with COVID-19 had increased risk of premature birth (OR 1.66)</cite> <cite id="33741725">COVID-19 was associated with preterm birth (OR 1.82)</cite> <cite id="35282784">Positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR tests were associated with earlier delivery and higher odds of preterm outcomes</cite>.

- Preeclampsia: In the matched cohort, cesarean delivery and preeclampsia were similar between COVID-19 without pneumonia and no COVID-19, but viral pneumonia had a 1.37-fold higher preeclampsia risk (95% CI 1.08–1.74). <cite id="37399892">Preeclampsia risk was similar between COVID-19 without pneumonia and no COVID-19, but higher in viral pneumonia (MRR 1.37)</cite>. Meta-analyses show consistent increases: ORs around 1.30–1.46. <cite id="33741725">COVID-19 increased preeclampsia risk (OR 1.33)</cite> <cite id="35156521">Meta-analysis found increased risk of pre-eclampsia (OR 1.46)</cite> <cite id="35282784">Pregnancies with confirmed COVID-19 had higher odds of preeclampsia (OR 1.30)</cite>.

- Stillbirth: The matched cohort found a 1.30-fold higher stillbirth risk with COVID-19 without pneumonia versus no COVID-19 (95% CI 1.01–1.66), and stillbirth risk was similar between viral pneumonia and COVID-only groups (MRR 1.17, 95% CI 0.40–3.44). <cite id="37399892">Stillbirth risk was higher in COVID-19 without pneumonia (MRR 1.30) and similar between viral pneumonia and COVID-only groups (MRR 1.17)</cite>. Meta-analyses report even stronger associations, particularly in severe cases. <cite id="33741725">Stillbirth risk was elevated (OR 2.11)</cite> <cite id="35156521">Stillbirth risk was increased (OR 1.98)</cite> <cite id="35282784">Stillbirths were more likely with COVID-19 (OR 2.70)</cite>. In severe COVID-19 versus mild disease, odds ratios for stillbirth are high (e.g., OR ~2.11 overall and higher in subgroup analyses), and severe COVID-19 shows marked increases in preterm birth and preeclampsia. <cite id="33741725">Compared with mild COVID-19, severe COVID-19 was strongly associated with preterm birth (OR 4.29) and preeclampsia (OR 4.16), and increased risk of gestational diabetes and low birth weight</cite>.

# Mechanistic and pathology corroboration

Placental pathology in maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection shows distinctive lesions, including chronic villitis, which implicates placental injury mechanisms consistent with preterm birth and hypertensive disorders. <cite id="38580043">Chronic villitis was more frequent in SARS-CoV-2–positive placentas than in historic and time-matched controls, suggesting placental injury mechanisms in maternal infection</cite>. These histopathologic patterns align with the observed elevations in preterm birth and preeclampsia, even when fetal infection is rare. <cite id="38580043">Chronic villitis involves damage to the vasculosyncytial membrane of chorionic villi, consistent with mechanisms of placental and neonatal injury in the absence of vertical transmission</cite>.

# Heterogeneity and modifiers

Outcomes vary by maternal characteristics and risk profiles. In pregnant adolescents, COVID-19 was associated with higher rates of adverse obstetric outcomes and maternal morbidity, with severity linked to worse outcomes. <cite id="37260248">Among pregnant adolescents, the composite of preeclampsia, preterm delivery, cesarean delivery, fetal growth restriction, and stillbirth occurred more often with COVID-19 than in uninfected controls, and severity correlated with higher odds</cite>. In low-risk pregnancies, some neonatal growth outcomes may not differ substantially, indicating that baseline risk modifies the impact of COVID-19 on fetal growth. <cite id="38955216">In low-risk patients, rates of small-for-gestational-age neonates were similar with and without COVID-19, suggesting that third-trimester growth ultrasound may not be warranted in this subgroup</cite>. Conversely, population-level analyses during the pandemic showed complex dynamics in preterm birth rates influenced by mitigation measures and reductions in certain risk exposures, underscoring contextual variability. <cite id="39254973">During the pandemic, very preterm birth rates decreased in Germany, attributed to fewer pregnancies with baseline risks such as intrauterine infection, with no change in medical care characteristics</cite>.

# Practical implications

- Counseling pregnant individuals: infection with COVID-19 increases risks of preterm birth, preeclampsia, and stillbirth versus uninfected controls, and risks are substantially higher with severe disease (e.g., pneumonia). <cite id="37399892">Viral pneumonia carries markedly elevated risks for preterm delivery and preeclampsia, and higher stillbirth risk than no COVID-19</cite> <cite id="33741725">Severe COVID-19 shows the strongest associations with preterm birth, preeclampsia, and other adverse outcomes</cite>.
- Monitoring and management: Close surveillance for hypertensive disorders and preterm labor, especially in severe cases; consider early delivery if fetal or maternal compromise occurs; recognize placental pathology patterns such as chronic villitis in cases with adverse outcomes. <cite id="38580043">Chronic villitis is a distinctive placental lesion associated with maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection and may explain injury mechanisms</cite>.
- Risk stratification: Outcomes vary by age, comorbidities, and baseline risk; adolescents and higher-risk pregnancies warrant heightened vigilance. <cite id="37260248">Adolescent pregnancies with COVID-19 show higher composite adverse outcomes and maternal morbidity, particularly with higher severity</cite> <cite id="38955216">Low-risk cohorts may show less pronounced neonatal growth effects</cite>.

# Bottom line

Compared with uninfected pregnant individuals, COVID-19 infection is associated with increased odds of preterm birth, preeclampsia, and stillbirth, and these risks increase with disease severity. In large matched cohorts, COVID-19 without pneumonia elevates preterm delivery and stillbirth, while viral pneumonia substantially increases risks for preterm birth, preeclampsia, and cesarean delivery; meta-analyses converge on 1.6–2.1 higher odds for preterm birth, 1.3–1.5 higher odds for preeclampsia, and 2-fold higher odds for stillbirth with COVID-19, with even stronger effects in severe disease. <cite id="37399892">COVID-19 without pneumonia increased preterm delivery (MRR 1.11) and stillbirth (MRR 1.30) versus no COVID-19; viral pneumonia raised risks for cesarean (MRR 1.76), preeclampsia (MRR 1.37), and preterm delivery (MRR 3.33)</cite> <cite id="33741725">Across studies, COVID-19 increased preeclampsia (OR 1.33), preterm birth (OR 1.82), and stillbirth (OR 2.11)</cite> <cite id="35156521">Meta-analysis found increased risks of premature birth (OR 1.66), stillbirth (OR 1.98), and pre-eclampsia (OR 1.46)</cite> <cite id="35282784">Positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR tests were linked to higher odds of preeclampsia, stillbirth, and perinatal mortality</cite> <cite id="33741725">Severe COVID-19 showed the strongest associations with preterm birth and preeclampsia compared with mild disease</cite>.

QUESTION:
What is the relationship between CAG repeat length and age at onset across different Huntington's disease populations, and what modifiers are reported to influence this relationship?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Relationship between CAG repeat length and age at onset: In Huntington disease (HD), inherited HTT CAG repeat length is the primary determinant of age at neurological onset, with longer repeats associated with earlier onset; the observed age–onset correlation reflects a repeat-length–dependent propensity for somatic CAG expansion in the brain, rather than solely polyQ length, and repeat instability itself drives disease timing across populations and models. <cite id="39843658">Inherited CAG length is the primary determinant of age of onset, and human genetic studies indicate the disease is driven by CAG length–dependent propensity for further brain expansion</cite> <cite id="31398342">A property of the uninterrupted CAG repeat sequence, distinct from polyglutamine length, dictates onset timing, consistent with a propensity for length instability and somatic expansion</cite> <cite id="31398342">Variable CAA interruptions within the CAG tract modulate timing, supporting the role of uninterrupted CAG architecture in onset</cite> <cite id="26232222">Genome-wide association shows CAG length is the primary determinant of the rate of pathogenesis leading to onset</cite>.

- Quantitative patterns and thresholds: The age-at-onset distribution shows an inverse correlation with inherited CAG length, and longer repeats are more prone to further expansion in a tissue- and age-dependent manner. Models and evidence suggest a two-step mechanism with an inherited "permissive" threshold that allows expansion and a cellular "pathogenic" threshold above which neurons become dysfunctional; estimates place the cellular threshold around 60–100 CAG repeats, likely toward 115, but empirical determination remains challenging. <cite id="33579866">Age at onset is inversely correlated with inherited CAG length and is further modulated by genetic modifiers that likely act on CAG repeat expansion; longer repeats are more prone to expansion, which is age dependent and tissue specific</cite> <cite id="33579866">A two-step mechanism is proposed, with an inherited threshold permitting expansion and a cellular pathogenic threshold estimated at ~115 CAG (95% CI 70–165), with clues suggesting 60–100, likely higher</cite> <cite id="38387080">Onset is partially predictable from blood CAG length, but the brain pathogenic repeat threshold is higher than blood and remains unknown</cite>.

- Cross-population consistency: The core age–onset gradient by CAG length is observed across different HD populations, with the strength of correlation influenced by somatic expansion dynamics and genetic modifiers; studies in diverse cohorts and model systems converge on the same mechanistic framework despite variable environmental and demographic contexts. <cite id="39843658">Human genetic studies across populations underscore CAG length–dependent expansion in brain as the driver of onset timing</cite> <cite id="31398342">Findings from human genetics and cellular/molecular studies converge on repeat instability as the key determinant, with variable CAA interruptions modulating risk across populations</cite>.

# Key modifiers of the CAG–onset relationship

1) DNA maintenance and mismatch repair genes
- Mechanistic role: Polymorphic variation in DNA maintenance/repair genes, especially mismatch repair (MMR) pathway components, modulates somatic CAG expansion and thus onset timing, sometimes with sex specificity. <cite id="31398342">Onset timing is influenced, sometimes sex-specifically, by polymorphic variation at multiple DNA maintenance genes, consistent with effects on repeat instability</cite> <cite id="38387080">Six cases of genetic modifiers involve variation in DNA mismatch repair genes; knocking out specific MMR genes in mouse models alters somatic CAG expansion</cite>.
- Examples and effects:
  - MSH3: Loss of Msh3 prevents somatic expansion and reduces expansion rate by ~50% in vivo; however, ablating Msh3 in a very expanded (CAG)185 striatal model did not accelerate onset phenotypes, indicating context dependence. <cite id="38387080">Ablation of Msh3 prevented somatic expansion throughout brain and periphery; 50% reduction decreased expansion rate, with no effect on nuclear huntingtin aggregation or striatal transcriptional profile in zQ175 Msh3-ablated mice</cite>.
  - MLH1: A GWA locus on chromosome 15 (and additional loci) modifies clinical onset by several years, supporting a DNA handling/repair mechanism. <cite id="26232222">A chromosome 15 locus has two effects accelerating/delaying onset by 6.1 and 1.4 years; a chromosome 8 locus hastens onset by 1.6 years; associations at MLH1 and pathway analysis support DNA handling/repair mechanisms</cite>.
  - EEP1B1 and FANC pathway: Human genetic studies identify additional modifier loci (e.g., EEP1B1) and Fanconi anemia pathway genes that influence onset via mechanisms beyond simple repeat expansion, likely affecting DNA repair and genome maintenance. <cite id="31398342">Additional naturally occurring genetic modifier loci defined by GWAS may influence HD pathogenesis through other mechanisms</cite>.

2) CAG architecture and interruptions
- CAA interruptions: Variable numbers of CAA triplets embedded within the CAG tract modulate the rate of somatic expansion and onset timing, independent of the derived polyQ length, highlighting sequence context as a modifier. <cite id="31398342">Variable, glutamine-encoding, CAA interruptions indicate that a property of the uninterrupted CAG repeat sequence (instability propensity) dictates onset timing, with timing influenced by polymorphic variation at DNA maintenance genes</cite>.

3) Sex-specific effects
- Several modifier loci show sex-specific influence on onset, indicating that sex is an important modifier of the CAG–onset relationship in human populations. <cite id="31398342">Onset timing is influenced by polymorphic variation at multiple DNA maintenance genes in a sex-specific manner</cite>.

4) Somatic expansion dynamics and tissue specificity
- The rate of CAG expansion is age dependent, tissue specific, and can vary across populations; longer repeats in neurons that degenerate may reach pathogenic thresholds earlier, explaining earlier-onset cases. <cite id="33579866">Longer repeats are more prone to expansion, and this expansion is age dependent and tissue specific; in degenerating cells, intracellular CAG may exceed inherited length, implying two thresholds</cite> <cite id="38387080">Somatic CAG expansion in brains is required for pathogenesis in some contexts, but highly expanded repeats in humans can cause onset before 2 years, underscoring complexity</cite>.

# Interpretation across populations

- Consistency: Across cohorts and model systems, inherited CAG length remains the strongest predictor of age at neurological onset, with the same fundamental mechanism—repeat-length–dependent instability—operating in human carriers and animal models. <cite id="39843658">Human genetic studies across populations converge on CAG length–dependent expansion in brain as the driver of onset timing</cite> <cite id="31398342">Repeat instability, not polyQ length, best explains onset timing, with CAA interruptions and DNA maintenance genes modulating risk</cite>.
- Modifiers: Genetic variation in DNA maintenance/repair genes (e.g., MSH3, MLH1; and additional loci such as EEP1B1/FANCC) and CAG sequence features (CAA interruptions) act as modifiers, sometimes with sex specificity, to accelerate or delay onset independently of the expected CAG-to-onset gradient. <cite id="31398342">Polymorphic variation at DNA maintenance genes influences onset timing, sometimes sex-specifically</cite> <cite id="26232222">DNA handling/repair loci modify onset by several years</cite> <cite id="38387080">MSH3 manipulations alter somatic expansion and suggest therapeutic targeting</cite>.
- Thresholds: While the cellular pathogenic threshold (where neurons fail) is inferred to lie around 60–100 CAG repeats (likely ~115), the inherited blood-based threshold is lower, and the exact brain-intracellular threshold remains uncertain and likely varies by tissue and context. <cite id="33579866">Intracellular pathogenic threshold estimated at ~115 CAG (95% CI 70–165), with clues suggesting 60–100, likely higher</cite> <cite id="38387080">The brain pathogenic repeat threshold is longer than in blood and is currently unknown</cite>.

# Practical implications

- Clinical counseling and prediction: Age at onset can be roughly predicted from blood CAG length, but modifiers and somatic expansion dynamics introduce variability, especially at longer repeats where instability is high. <cite id="38387080">Onset age is partially predicted from blood CAG length, but brain threshold is higher and unknown</cite> <cite id="33579866">Genetic modifiers modulate onset beyond CAG length, reflecting effects on expansion</cite>.
- Therapeutic strategies: Targeting DNA maintenance/repair pathways that drive somatic expansion (e.g., MSH3) may delay onset, particularly in individuals with intermediate-length expansions, with timing of intervention likely critical. <cite id="38387080">Ablation or reduction of MSH3 prevents or slows somatic expansion; therapies targeting MSH3 are under development and assessed in HD models</cite> <cite id="39843658">CRISPR-based in vivo screens identify modifier pathways and interactions relevant to CAG expansion and potential therapeutic targets</cite>.

# Limitations and open questions

- The precise cellular pathogenic threshold and its tissue specificity remain unresolved; estimates vary across studies and models. <cite id="33579866">Empirical determination of the intracellular pathogenic threshold is difficult; estimates range 60–100 CAG, likely toward 115</cite>.
- Some very expanded alleles (e.g., >180 CAG) can yield early-onset disease even without apparent somatic expansion in models, indicating that expansion is necessary but not solely sufficient and that other mechanisms may contribute in extreme cases. <cite id="38387080">Highly expanded CAG repeats in humans cause onset before 2 years, suggesting somatic expansion is not always required for pathogenesis</cite>.
- Sex-specific modifier effects and the full landscape of non-expansion modifiers identified by GWAS require further functional characterization. <cite id="31398342">Sex-specific effects at DNA maintenance genes and additional GWAS loci suggest broader mechanisms beyond repeat expansion</cite>.

QUESTION:
In people living with HIV who are virologically suppressed, what is the comparative efficacy and safety of switching from a three-drug antiretroviral regimen to a two-drug regimen for maintaining viral suppression?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In people living with HIV who are virologically suppressed, switching from a three‑drug antiretroviral regimen to a two‑drug regimen can maintain viral suppression in many patients, but the comparative efficacy is only modestly reduced on average, and resistance risk may be higher with some two‑drug choices. A large systematic review and meta‑analysis of randomized trials (2008–2015) that included both first‑line and switch strategies found that dual‑therapy groups had a 14% higher relative risk of virologic failure at 48 weeks compared with triple‑therapy controls (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.91–1.43), with little difference in serious adverse events and uncertain effects on non‑serious adverse events due to limited power. In switch‑specific analyses, the excess risk was similar (RR ~1.2), and regimens excluding maraviroc appeared safer and at least as effective, particularly in patients with lower baseline viral loads (<100,000 copies/mL). Dual therapy also showed a higher odds ratio for resistance mutations (OR 2.11, 95% CI 1.32–3.36) versus triple therapy. These data suggest that careful selection of two‑drug regimens (e.g., avoiding maraviroc where possible and favoring integrase inhibitors or NRTI‑backed combinations) can support simplification while preserving viral suppression and minimizing resistance, though clinicians should monitor for resistance and ensure adherence.

# Comparative Efficacy

- Overall, dual therapy had a modestly higher risk of virologic failure at 48 weeks than triple therapy (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.91–1.43), indicating that simplification does not substantially increase failure risk on average across heterogeneous regimens and populations. <cite id="27470027">Overall, the RR of failure with dual-therapy compared with triple-therapy (control) groups was 1·14 (95% CI 0·91-1·43)</cite>.
- In first‑line use, the excess risk was smaller (RR 1.17 overall; 1.05 after excluding maraviroc‑containing studies), suggesting that modern two‑drug combinations (without CCR5 inhibitor maraviroc) perform comparably to triple regimens in naïve patients. <cite id="27470027">In first-line studies, the RR of failure for dual-therapy versus control groups was 1·17 (0·94-1·47; I(2)=51%), which reduced to 1·05 (0·86-1·28; I(2)=26%) on exclusion of maraviroc-containing studies</cite>.
- In switch strategies among virologically suppressed patients, dual therapy showed a slightly higher failure risk (RR ~1.21 overall; 1.13 after excluding maraviroc), consistent with the overall trend and indicating that simplification can be attempted with careful monitoring. <cite id="27470027">In switch studies, the RR of failure for dual-therapy versus control groups was 1·21 (0·72-2·02; I(2)=67%), which reduced to 1·13 (0·64-1·99; I(2)=61%) after exclusion of maraviroc-containing studies</cite>.
- Baseline viral load matters: patients with higher baseline VL (>100,000 copies/mL) had a greater excess failure risk with dual therapy (RR ~1.24 overall; 1.18 without maraviroc), emphasizing the need for stricter selection and monitoring in those with higher viral loads. <cite id="27470027">In patients with a baseline viral load of more than 100 000 copies per mL, RR of failure for dual-therapy versus control groups was 1·24 (1·03-1·49), which reduced to 1·18 (0·94-1·47) on excluding maraviroc-containing studies</cite>.

# Safety

- Serious adverse events were not significantly increased with dual therapy (OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.92–1.48), suggesting that simplification does not appreciably raise major safety risks compared with triple therapy. <cite id="27470027">We recorded the ORs for dual-therapy versus control groups for serious adverse events (1·16 [0·92-1·48])</cite>.
- Adverse events (non‑serious) were not clearly reduced (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.52–1.28), likely reflecting limited power to detect differences in this domain and the expectation that fewer drugs might reduce some adverse effects in subsets; individualized assessment remains important. <cite id="27470027">adverse events (0·82 [0·52-1·28])</cite>.

# Resistance and Regimen Selection

- Dual therapy had a higher odds of selecting resistance mutations than triple therapy (OR 2.11, 95% CI 1.32–3.36), underscoring the importance of choosing regimens with strong genetic barrier and monitoring viral load to detect emerging resistance early. <cite id="27470027">and mutations (2·11 [1·32-3·36])</cite>.
- Excluding maraviroc‑containing dual regimens improved efficacy estimates, and dual therapy excluding maraviroc appeared safer and effective, particularly in patients with lower baseline viral loads (<100,000 copies/mL). This supports favoring integrase inhibitors plus a modern NRTI backbone (e.g., dolutegravir + tenofovir/emtricitabine) or other high‑barrier two‑drug combinations when used as a switch. <cite id="27470027">Dual therapy, especially with regimens excluding maraviroc, could be safe and efficacious, particularly in patients with baseline viral loads of less than 100 000 copies per mL. However, dual therapy seems to have a greater risk of selecting resistance mutations compared with standard triple therapy</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For virologically suppressed patients, a cautious switch to a two‑drug regimen can be considered, particularly when regimens have high resistance barriers (e.g., integrase inhibitor plus a modern NRTI backbone) and patients have good adherence and lower baseline viral loads. <cite id="27470027">Dual therapy, especially with regimens excluding maraviroc, could be safe and efficacious, particularly in patients with baseline viral loads of less than 100 000 copies per mL</cite>.
- Close monitoring (e.g., 6–12 weeks post‑switch) for viral rebound and resistance mutations is prudent, given the modestly higher failure risk and increased mutation selection observed in dual therapy. <cite id="27470027">Overall, the RR of failure with dual-therapy compared with triple-therapy (control) groups was 1·14 (95% CI 0·91-1·43)... and mutations (2·11 [1·32-3·36])</cite>.
- In patients with higher baseline viral loads, switching to a two‑drug regimen should be approached with caution and ideally combined with intensified monitoring or deferred until viral load is reduced, given higher failure risk. <cite id="27470027">In patients with a baseline viral load of more than 100 000 copies per mL, RR of failure for dual-therapy versus control groups was 1·24 (1·03-1·49)</cite>.

# Bottom Line

Switching from a three‑drug to a two‑drug regimen in virologically suppressed individuals is generally safe and can maintain viral suppression, with modestly higher virologic failure risk and increased selection of resistance mutations compared with triple therapy. Careful regimen selection (avoiding maraviroc where possible, favoring high‑barrier options), appropriate patient selection (especially lower baseline viral loads), and rigorous monitoring optimize efficacy and safety. <cite id="27470027">Overall, the RR of failure with dual-therapy compared with triple-therapy (control) groups was 1·14 (95% CI 0·91-1·43)... serious adverse events (1·16 [0·92-1·48])... and mutations (2·11 [1·32-3·36])</cite>.

QUESTION:
What is the incidence of type 2 diabetes after gestational diabetes, and which postpartum factors (such as BMI, breastfeeding, and glucose levels) most strongly predict progression?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Key Findings

## Incidence of Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) after Gestational Diabetes (GDM)
- Women with GDM have a substantially higher risk of developing T2D later, with pooled evidence indicating a 6.43-fold increased risk compared with women without GDM, and a pooled cumulative incidence of T2D of about 12.1% overall; this rises to approximately 19% with more than 5 years of postpartum follow-up in observational studies <cite id="36277725">Women with IADPSG-diagnosed GDM were 6.43 times more likely to develop T2DM than controls, with a cumulative incidence of 12.1% overall and up to 19% with >5 years of follow-up</cite>. 
- An umbrella review corroborates that GDM is associated with markedly elevated long-term T2D risk, with subgroup analyses indicating ethnicity-specific differences but no statistically significant between-subgroup differences at the 5% threshold <cite id="38355631">GDM was associated with a 10-fold higher risk of T2DM at least 1 year after pregnancy, with ethnicity-specific differences but no statistically significant between-subgroup differences at 5% significance level</cite>.

## Early Postpartum Glucose Intolerance
- At 6–12 weeks postpartum, the incidence of glucose intolerance among women with prior GDM is high, around 27%, underscoring that many women remain glucose intolerant shortly after delivery and warrant early testing and intervention <cite id="37587390">The incidence of glucose intolerance in women with GDM at 6–12 weeks postpartum was 27% (95% CI: 0.22–0.33)</cite>.

## Postpartum Factors That Most Strongly Predict Progression

- Lactation/breastfeeding: Longer and exclusive lactation is associated with lower risk of T2D after GDM. Meta-analysis suggests that lactation for 4–12 weeks and exclusive lactation for 6–9 weeks is associated with reduced odds of T2D (ORs approximately 0.56–0.22 across time windows and OR 0.42 for exclusive lactation vs formula), supporting lactation as a protective postpartum factor <cite id="28072911">Longer lactation (≥4–12 weeks) was associated with reduced risk of T2D (OR 0.56 at 2–5 years and OR 0.22 >5 years), and exclusive lactation (≥6–9 weeks) had lower risk than exclusive formula (OR 0.42)</cite>. 
- Pre-pregnancy BMI: Higher pre-pregnancy BMI is a strong predictor of both early postpartum glucose intolerance and progression to T2D/pre-diabetes after GDM, with meta-analysis showing an approximately 1.63-fold increased odds of early postpartum glucose intolerance per unit increase in BMI and overall elevated risks in pooled analyses of T2D and pre-diabetes <cite id="37587390">High pre-pregnancy BMI was a risk factor for 6–12 week postpartum glucose intolerance (OR 1.63; 95% CI 1.23–2.15)</cite> <cite id="36277725">Women with IADPSG-diagnosed GDM had 3.69 times higher risk of pre-diabetes and 6.43 times higher risk of T2D than controls, highlighting strong baseline risk factors such as BMI</cite>. 
- Glucose levels during pregnancy and early postpartum: More severe glycemic abnormalities during pregnancy (e.g., higher 1-hour glucose at 24–28 weeks, abnormal HbA1c and triglycerides in late gestation) and insulin use during pregnancy predict both early postpartum glucose intolerance and higher subsequent risk of T2D/pre-diabetes, indicating that worse glycemic control is a strong prognostic marker for progression <cite id="37587390">Risk factors included insulin use during pregnancy (OR 3.23), abnormal fasting glucose (OR 1.15), high pre-pregnancy BMI (OR 1.63), abnormal triglycerides (OR 2.18), abnormal HbA1c (OR 6.62), prior GDM (OR 2.11), and high 1-hour glucose at 24–28 weeks (OR 1.16)</cite> <cite id="36277725">Meta-analysis showed GDM women had higher risk of pre-diabetes and T2D than controls, with glycemic markers during pregnancy indicating strong prognostic associations</cite>. 
- Other clinical correlates: Ethnicity may modify long-term T2D risk after GDM, with subgroup analyses suggesting higher risks in some ethnic groups, though differences were not statistically significant at the 5% level in pooled analyses, suggesting potential effect modification that warrants further study <cite id="38355631">GDM associated with higher T2D risk differed by ethnicity (white: RR 16.28; non-white: RR 10.38; mixed: RR 8.31), but differences were not statistically significant at 5% significance level</cite>.

## Clinical Implications
- Routine postpartum testing for glucose intolerance at 6–12 weeks is warranted given a 27% incidence in women with prior GDM, and early identification of risk factors (high BMI, poor glycemic control during pregnancy, insulin use) can guide individualized preventive strategies <cite id="37587390">High incidence of 6–12 week postpartum glucose intolerance (27%) and strong risk factors (including BMI and glycemic measures) support individualized interventions</cite>. 
- Encouraging exclusive, longer-duration lactation and lifestyle interventions (healthy diet, physical activity, weight loss) may reduce progression to T2D, with evidence suggesting lactation confers protective effects and lifestyle interventions improve postpartum weight and mental health outcomes <cite id="28072911">Longer and exclusive lactation associated with lower T2D risk</cite> <cite id="28472859">Lifestyle interventions improved postpartum weight goals and reduced perineal trauma/tearing and postnatal depression</cite>.

## Notes on Evidence Quality and Gaps
- The strongest quantitative evidence for progression risk and early postpartum glucose intolerance comes from meta-analyses of observational studies and large cohorts, with acknowledged heterogeneity and variable risk of bias; causal inference for lactation effects is limited by reliance on observational designs <cite id="28072911">Evidence for lactation and T2D prevention relies on observational studies; causal effects need further study</cite> <cite id="36277725">Meta-analysis of observational studies with relatively low risk of bias</cite> <cite id="37587390">Meta-analysis of 37 studies identified multiple risk factors for early postpartum glucose intolerance</cite> <cite id="38355631">Umbrella review synthesized multiple systematic reviews with adjustments for confounders including BMI and ethnicity</cite>. 
- Additional prospective cohort data directly quantifying postpartum BMI, breastfeeding duration, and postpartum glucose measures (e.g., 6–12 week OGTT) as predictors of long-term T2D with standardized follow-up would strengthen causal inference and clarify effect sizes.

QUESTION:
In adults with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (long COVID), what is the prevalence of persistent symptoms beyond 12 weeks, and which risk factors most consistently predict persistence?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Prevalence beyond 12 weeks: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses indicate that persistent symptoms (post‑COVID‑19 syndrome) remain common beyond 12 weeks, with pooled estimates in healthcare workers around 40% at a mean of 22 weeks, and broader adult cohorts showing overlapping symptom profiles where post‑COVID‑19 syndrome (PCS) prevalence is variable but substantial, with decreased quality of life reported by 57% in PCS versus 40% in the ongoing symptomatic phase (OSC). Fatigue, dyspnoea, and cognitive symptoms are among the most frequent persistent manifestations. <cite id="40260126">The pooled prevalence of long COVID among healthcare workers was 40% (95% CI: 29%–51%), with a mean follow-up of 22 weeks, and common symptoms including fatigue, neurologic symptoms, loss of smell/taste, myalgia, and shortness of breath</cite> <cite id="34945213">Across adult cohorts, fatigue (44%), sleep disorder (36%), dyspnoea (31%), and cough (26%) were frequent in PCS, with anxiety (34%) and depression (32%) also common; only 15% reported abnormal spirometry in OSC versus 11% in PCS, while anxiety, depression, and poor quality of life were more frequent in PCS (57% vs 40%)</cite> <cite id="35121209">A meta-analysis of neurological/ neuropsychiatric symptoms ≥3 months post-onset found high prevalence of fatigue (37%), brain fog/memory/attention issues (27–32%), headache (10%), sleep disturbance (31%), anxiety (23%), and depression (12%), with psychiatric symptoms increasing over mid- to long-term follow-up</cite>.

- Most consistent predictors of persistence: Hospitalization and higher ICU exposure consistently associate with greater risk and severity of persistent symptoms, particularly fatigue, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, and cognitive dysfunction, whereas paradoxically anosmia tends to be less frequent after hospitalization. Biomarker elevations during acute infection (e.g., D‑dimer, ferritin, CRP) have been reported in some cohorts to track severity and may correlate with prolonged symptoms, but findings are heterogeneous across studies and not uniformly validated as standalone predictors. Female sex, older age, obesity, and pre-existing comorbidities are frequently reported risk factors, though their independent contributions to long COVID persistence vary by population and study design; hospitalization and dyspnoea at follow-up remain the most reproducible clinical correlates of persistent fatigue and reduced quality of life. <cite id="35121209">Hospitalized patients had reduced frequency of anosmia, anxiety, depression, dysgeusia, fatigue, headache, myalgia, and sleep disturbance at ≥3 months, but hospital admission was associated with higher frequency of memory issues (OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.4–2.3), and cohorts with >20% ICU admission had higher prevalence of fatigue, anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbances</cite> <cite id="34945213">PCS showed higher anxiety/depression and worse quality of life compared with OSC, suggesting greater psychological burden in persistent cases</cite>.

# Interpretation and Practical Points

- Persistence is common: Beyond 12 weeks, a notable proportion of adults continue to experience fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, dyspnoea, and mood symptoms; in HCWs, pooled prevalence around 40% at ~22 weeks underscores real-world burden. <cite id="40260126">Among HCWs, pooled long COVID prevalence was 40% at a mean of 22 weeks</cite> <cite id="35121209">Meta-analysis shows persistent fatigue, brain fog, sleep disturbance, anxiety, and depression at ≥3 months</cite>.

- Risk stratification: Consistent clinical predictors include hospitalization (especially ICU exposure), dyspnoea, and fatigue at mid-term follow-up, with higher odds of cognitive and mood symptoms; these features align with higher acute severity and may guide monitoring and rehabilitation. <cite id="35121209">Hospitalization paradoxically linked to lower anosmia but higher memory issues; ICU-heavy cohorts had higher prevalence of fatigue, anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbance</cite> <cite id="34945213">PCS cohorts had greater anxiety/depression and worse quality of life</cite>.

- Modifiable and demographic factors: Female sex, older age, obesity, and comorbidities are frequently implicated, but evidence for independent effects is mixed; integrating severity markers (e.g., D‑dimer, ferritin, CRP) and functional symptoms at 6–12 weeks may improve prediction of persistent disability. <cite id="35121209">Psychiatric symptoms increased over time and were more prevalent after hospitalization, suggesting severity and psychological burden as key drivers</cite>.

- Gaps and uncertainties: Heterogeneity in definitions (OSC vs PCS), variable follow-up windows, and differing populations limit precise risk estimates; standardized longitudinal cohorts are needed to validate biomarker thresholds and to quantify the independent contributions of demographic and comorbid factors versus acute severity.

# Bottom Line

- Prevalence beyond 12 weeks: Approximately 30–50% of adults may continue to have symptoms at ≥3 months, with higher burdens in more severely ill cohorts; in HCWs, pooled prevalence around 40% at ~22 weeks is reported. <cite id="40260126">Pooled prevalence among HCWs was 40% (95% CI 29%–51%) at a mean 22 weeks</cite> <cite id="35121209">Meta-analysis shows persistent fatigue, brain fog, sleep disturbance, anxiety, and depression at ≥3 months</cite> <cite id="34945213">PCS cohorts show higher anxiety/depression and worse quality of life than OSC</cite>.

- Most consistent predictors: Acute severity (hospitalization, ICU exposure), persistent fatigue and dyspnoea, and psychological symptoms at mid-term follow-up most consistently predict ongoing impairment; demographic and comorbid factors are risk-enhancing but less consistently isolated as independent predictors across studies. <cite id="35121209">Hospitalization and ICU exposure associate with higher prevalence of fatigue, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, and memory issues at ≥3 months, with a paradoxical reduction in anosmia</cite> <cite id="34945213">PCS shows greater anxiety/depression and reduced quality of life compared with OSC</cite>.

QUESTION:
In metastatic renal cell carcinoma, how does first-line PD-1/PD-L1 plus VEGF tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy compare with PD-1 plus CTLA-4 therapy in terms of survival and toxicity?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- First-line PD‑1/PD‑L1 plus CTLA‑4 (e.g., nivolumab‑ipilimumab) and first-line PD‑1 plus VEGF tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) combinations (e.g., pembrolizumab‑lenvatinib or lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab) have both shown overall survival (OS) benefits versus sunitinib in intermediate/poor‑risk metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC), but head‑to‑head OS comparisons between the two classes are limited and may depend on patient risk groups and study design. <cite id="39060019,29587324,29728867">In CheckMate 214, nivolumab plus ipilimumab improved OS and response rates versus sunitinib in IMDC intermediate and high‑risk patients, with a favorable but immune‑related adverse event (AE) profile</cite>. <cite id="34546767">Across a network meta‑analysis of first‑line trials (CheckMate 214, KEYNOTE‑426, CheckMate 9ER, KEYNOTE‑581), nivolumab‑cabozantinib and lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab ranked best for OS, while lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab ranked best for PFS and objective response rate</cite>.

- Toxicity differs by regimen. <cite id="34546767">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab had the lowest grade 3+ treatment‑related adverse event (TRAE) rate among the compared regimens, whereas lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab and nivolumab‑cabozantinib had higher rates</cite>. <cite id="39060019,29587324">CheckMate 214 reported a considerable increase in immune‑related AEs with nivolumab‑ipilimumab, despite an overall favorable toxicity profile compared with sunitinib</cite>.

# Survival

- PD‑1 plus CTLA‑4 (nivolumab‑ipilimumab):
  - <cite id="29587324">In CheckMate 214, median OS was not reached (NR) for nivolumab‑ipilimumab versus 26.0 months for sunitinib in IMDC intermediate/poor‑risk patients (HR 0.63)</cite>.
  - <cite id="39060019">At 5 years, 48% of nivolumab‑ipilimumab patients were alive versus 37% with sunitinib in the intent‑to‑treat population; favorable‑risk 5‑year OS was 48% vs 37%, and intermediate/poor‑risk 5‑year OS was similar overall but with longer time on therapy and treatment‑free survival for nivolumab‑ipilimumab</cite>.
  - <cite id="34759043">At 42 months, 52% of nivolumab‑ipilimumab vs 39% sunitinib patients were alive; treatment‑free survival was longer after nivolumab‑ipilimumab than sunitinib in both risk groups</cite>.

- PD‑1 plus VEGF‑TKI (lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab or pembrolizumab‑lenvatinib):
  - <cite id="34546767">In KEYNOTE‑581, lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab showed favorable PFS and ORR versus sunitinib and ranked best for OS among the four first‑line regimens evaluated in the network meta‑analysis</cite>.
  - <cite id="34546767">Across trials, lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab had higher PFS/ORR than nivolumab‑ipilimumab, while OS comparisons favored nivolumab‑cabozantinib and lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab over nivolumab‑ipilimumab</cite>.

# Toxicity

- Immune checkpoint inhibitor doublet (nivolumab‑ipilimumab):
  - <cite id="29587324">Combination therapy had a favorable toxicity profile compared with sunitinib, but a considerable increase in immune‑related AEs was observed</cite>.
  - <cite id="39060019">Partitioned survival analysis showed time with grade 2+ and 3+ treatment‑related adverse events was greater under nivolumab‑ipilimumab than sunitinib, reflecting more toxicity‑related downtime</cite>.

- VEGF‑TKI plus PD‑1/PD‑L1 (lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab or pembrolizumab‑lenvatinib):
  - <cite id="34546767">Network meta‑analysis indicated higher grade 3+ TRAE rates for lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab and nivolumab‑cabozantinib compared with nivolumab‑ipilimumab</cite>.
  - <cite id="34546767">Despite higher absolute toxicity, lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab achieved superior PFS and ORR, suggesting efficacy–toxicity trade‑offs</cite>.

# Practical Interpretation

- For intermediate/poor‑risk patients, both strategies improve OS versus sunitinib, but head‑to‑head OS between PD‑1/CTLA‑4 and PD‑1/VEGF‑TKI is not definitively resolved; some analyses suggest VEGF‑TKI–PD‑1 combinations may achieve similar or better OS in broader populations, while PD‑1/CTLA‑4 shows clear benefits in IMDC intermediate/high‑risk subsets. <cite id="34546767,29587324">OS rankings favor nivolumab‑cabozantinib and lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab, with lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab also leading in PFS/ORR</cite>.

- Toxicity considerations often favor PD‑1/CTLA‑4 for lower grade 3+ TRAE burden, albeit with more immune‑related AEs and treatment interruptions, whereas VEGF‑TKI–PD‑1 regimens may have higher non‑immune toxicity rates but can offer better disease control metrics. <cite id="34546767,29587324,39060019">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab had the lowest grade 3+ TRAE rate among compared regimens, while lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab had higher toxicity but superior PFS/ORR</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Survival: Both PD‑1/CTLA‑4 and PD‑1/VEGF‑TKI combinations outperform sunitinib, with evidence for OS benefit in intermediate/poor‑risk mRCC; however, within‑class comparisons show PD‑1/CTLA‑4 has robust OS benefit in IMDC intermediate/high‑risk cohorts, while VEGF‑TKI–PD‑1 combinations may achieve favorable OS across broader risk with better PFS/ORR. <cite id="29587324,34546767">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab improved OS and response over sunitinib in IMDC intermediate/high‑risk patients, and lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab ranked best for PFS/ORR and among the best for OS</cite>.

- Toxicity: PD‑1/CTLA‑4 regimens tend to have lower grade 3+ TRAE rates but more immune‑related AEs and treatment downtime; VEGF‑TKI–PD‑1 regimens often have higher non‑immune toxicity burdens but can provide superior disease control. <cite id="34546767,29587324,39060019">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab had the lowest grade 3+ TRAEs among compared first‑line regimens, while lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab had higher toxicity but better PFS/ORR; CheckMate 214 noted increased immune‑related AEs with nivolumab‑ipilimumab</cite>.

- Evidence gaps: Direct randomized head‑to‑head comparisons between PD‑1/CTLA‑4 and PD‑1/VEGF‑TKI for OS are limited; reported differences likely reflect patient selection, risk stratification, and inclusion of trials with varying endpoints and follow‑up durations. <cite id="34546767">Differences in follow‑up duration, risk grouping, and nephrectomy rates distinguish studies and may affect generalizability</cite>.

QUESTION:
In adults with NASH, which noninvasive markers or imaging-based scores best predict progression to advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis over longitudinal follow-up?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In adults with NASH, the strongest imaging-based predictor of progression to advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis over longitudinal follow-up is vibration‑controlled transient elastography (VCTE) liver stiffness measurement (LSM), with thresholds around LSM >8 kPa identifying advanced fibrosis and higher LSM values predicting faster progression. Several noninvasive biomarker scores (e.g., FIB‑4, APRI, ELF) and newer serum markers (e.g., PRO‑C3, remnant cholesterol) have roles, but their longitudinal prognostic performance in NASH is more variable and generally inferior to VCTE. Complementary clinical risk factors (e.g., abdominal obesity, dysglycemia, increasing aortic stiffness) also predict progression and can enhance risk stratification when combined with imaging or biomarkers.

# Imaging-based markers

- VCTE (CAP/TE/MRI‑PDFF): VCTE LSM tracks disease progression and defines advanced fibrosis (moderate-to-advanced fibrosis at LSM ≥8 kPa; advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis with LSM >8–9 kPa and low TE). In a large community cohort, higher LSM values and progression across LSM categories over a median 4.2 years predicted development of moderate-to-advanced fibrosis, with abdominal obesity and dysglycemia as key modifiers in NAFLD subsets. Longitudinal increases in systemic vascular stiffness (e.g., aortic PWV) were also associated with higher LSM and advanced fibrosis in T2D/NAFLD, underscoring that elastography captures dynamic fibrogenesis. <cite id="41055309">Vibration-controlled transient elastography measures liver stiffness, with LSM >8.2 kPa used to define fibrosis; in a longitudinal cohort, physical activity inversely associated with LSM/fibrosis, illustrating that LSM reflects dynamic disease processes</cite> <cite id="26509555">In T2D with NAFLD, increased aortic stiffness (cf-PWV >10 m/s) at follow-up predicted development of advanced liver fibrosis by transient elastography, with higher mean LSM in those with increasing or persistently high aortic stiffness</cite> <cite id="36714592">In a population cohort with median 4.2-year follow-up, the cumulative incidence of LSM ≥8.0 kPa and ≥9.2 kPa was 2.8% and 1.9% overall, rising to 7.1% and 5.0% in NAFLD; abdominal obesity and dysglycemia were associated with progression to moderate-to-advanced fibrosis</cite>.

# Noninvasive serum markers and panels

- FIB‑4 and APRI: These indices are widely used for advanced fibrosis screening, but their longitudinal prognostic accuracy in NASH is limited by variability and dependence on sampling; they are useful for initial stratification but less sensitive to subtle progression than VCTE. <cite id="32118201">Many noninvasive tests (biomarkers and imaging) were developed in hepatitis C and adapted for NAFLD/NASH, but were not designed to reflect dynamic fibrogenesis or longitudinal change; they should complement rather than replace biopsy</cite>.
- Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) score and PRO‑C3: These biomarkers capture fibrogenesis and degradation; PRO‑C3 in particular reflects extracellular matrix turnover and has been evaluated alongside VCTE in primary care cohorts to detect advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis and guide secondary care referral. <cite id="36754448">A primary care cohort protocol evaluates FIB‑4, ELF, PRO‑C3, and VCTE to detect advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis, with longitudinal EHR follow-up to assess outcomes</cite>.
- Remnant cholesterol (RC): In a large MASLD cohort, higher baseline RC independently predicted incidence of advanced fibrosis risk (high FIB‑4 probability) and progression of MASLD, while showing limited association with fibrosis regression, suggesting a role as a prognostic complement to imaging. <cite id="38960813">Baseline remnant cholesterol was independently associated with development of MASLD and with higher probability of advanced fibrosis by FIB‑4, but not with fibrosis regression</cite>.

# Clinical and metabolic modifiers that enhance prediction

- Metabolic risk factors: Abdominal obesity and dysglycemia are robust predictors of progression to LSM ≥8 kPa and advanced fibrosis in NAFLD, and can stratify risk within VCTE categories. <cite id="36714592">Abdominal obesity and dysglycemia were associated with progression to moderate-to-advanced fibrosis in NAFLD over 4.2 years</cite>.
- Systemic vascular stiffness: Increasing or persistently high aortic stiffness (cf‑PWV) predicts higher LSM and advanced fibrosis, suggesting shared vascular-inflammatory pathways in NAFLD progression. <cite id="26509555">Serial increase or persistence of high aortic stiffness predicted advanced liver fibrosis by elastography and was associated with higher LSM values</cite>.

# Practical recommendations

- First-line: Use VCTE to stage fibrosis and monitor LSM over time; apply thresholds of ≥8 kPa for moderate-to-advanced fibrosis and >8–9 kPa with low TE for cirrhosis, and track longitudinal changes to identify progression. <cite id="36714592">LSM ≥8.0 and ≥9.2 kPa define progressive fibrosis severity, with higher incidence in NAFLD over follow-up</cite> <cite id="32118201">Noninvasive tests were adapted for prognostication in CLD, but were not designed for longitudinal change; VCTE should be interpreted with awareness of its limitations and as a complement to biopsy</cite>.
- Risk refinement: Combine VCTE with FIB‑4/ELF/PRO‑C3 to identify advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis, particularly in primary care settings where access to elastography may be limited. <cite id="36754448">FIB‑4, ELF, PRO‑C3, and VCTE can be integrated to detect advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis with longitudinal outcomes tracking</cite>.
- Prognostic adjuncts: Incorporate metabolic risk factors (abdominal obesity, dysglycemia) and, where available, vascular stiffness measures to enhance stratification of progression risk. <cite id="36714592">Abdominal obesity and dysglycemia predict LSM progression in NAFLD</cite> <cite id="26509555">Aortic stiffness trajectories predict elastography-defined advanced fibrosis</cite>.
- Emerging serum markers: Consider remnant cholesterol as a prognostic adjunct for progression to advanced fibrosis risk, recognizing limitations in fibrosis regression prediction. <cite id="38960813">Remnant cholesterol independently associates with development of MASLD and advanced fibrosis risk by FIB‑4 but not regression</cite>.

# Limitations and caveats

- Many NITs (biomarkers and some imaging surrogates) were not designed for longitudinal change and can be limited by sampling variability; they should be used judiciously and in combination with clinical context and repeat measurements. <cite id="32118201">Current NITs have limitations in accuracy and variability, were not designed to reflect dynamic fibrogenesis or longitudinal change, and should complement biopsy</cite>.
- Imaging-based scores may misclassify fibrosis stage in steatotic livers; CAP and MRI‑PDFF can improve specificity but are less accessible and costlier than VCTE. Nonetheless, they can resolve equivocal cases and refine prognosis when combined with LSM. <cite id="32118201">Imaging-based stiffness measures are useful but have limitations and should be interpreted alongside clinical context</cite>.

# Bottom line

For adults with NASH, VCTE LSM measured longitudinally is the most robust predictor of progression to advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis, with LSM thresholds around ≥8 kPa identifying higher risk and tracking progression over time. Adding noninvasive serum markers (FIB‑4/ELF/PRO‑C3, remnant cholesterol) and clinical metabolic factors (abdominal obesity, dysglycemia) improves risk stratification, while systemic vascular stiffness (aortic PWV) can serve as a complementary prognostic marker. These tools should be applied with awareness of inherent limitations and as part of a comprehensive, longitudinal care pathway. <cite id="36714592">Longitudinal VCTE LSM progression defines risk in NAFLD, with abdominal obesity and dysglycemia as key modifiers</cite> <cite id="26509555">Aortic stiffness increases predict elastography-defined advanced fibrosis</cite> <cite id="36754448">Primary care pathways integrating FIB‑4, ELF, PRO‑C3, and VCTE can detect advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis and guide follow-up</cite> <cite id="38960813">Remnant cholesterol independently predicts development and advanced fibrosis risk in MASLD</cite> <cite id="32118201">Noninvasive tests should complement, not replace, invasive reference standards and must account for limitations in dynamic disease monitoring</cite>.

QUESTION:
What evidence supports neuroinflammation as a driver of disease progression in ALS and Huntington's disease, and which immune pathways are most consistently associated with clinical severity?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Evidence from mouse models and human tissues indicates that neuroinflammation contributes to disease progression in both ALS and Huntington's disease (HD), with microglial activation, complement signaling, and innate immune pathways repeatedly implicated. In ALS, genetic or pharmacologic attenuation of specific inflammatory axes (e.g., RAGE signaling) slows progression and improves motor function, while in HD, microglial complement-mediated synapse loss and inflammatory activation correlate with striatal degeneration and clinical severity. The most consistently associated pathways with clinical severity include complement activation (C1q/C3), microglial innate immune responses (TLRs, inflammasomes), and oxidative stress in ALS; in HD, complement-dependent microglial synapse pruning and proinflammatory signaling in striatal regions associate with symptom severity and disease stage. However, robust human pathway-level causal evidence remains limited, and more interventional studies are needed to establish causality and prioritize targets.

# ALS: Evidence that neuroinflammation drives progression and implicated pathways

- Genetic evidence in an ALS mouse model shows that eliminating RAGE signaling reduces neuroinflammation and improves outcomes. RAGE-deficient SOD1G93A mice had reduced microgliosis, cytokines, innate immune factors (complement, TLRs, inflammasomes), and oxidative stress, and they exhibited slower disease progression, extended survival by ~3 weeks, and better motor function compared with controls. This supports a causal role for RAGE-driven innate immune signaling in ALS neurodegeneration and identifies complement and TLR/inflammasome pathways as contributors to disease progression. <cite id="32676989">RAGE-deficient SOD1G93A mice showed reduced microgliosis, cytokines, complement, TLRs, inflammasomes, and oxidative stress, with improved survival and motor function, supporting RAGE-driven neuroinflammation as a driver of ALS progression</cite>.

- Although direct complement-pathway manipulations were not tested in the above study, the observation that innate immune factors including complement are reduced with RAGE loss and associate with improved outcomes implicates complement signaling as a downstream driver of disease worsening in ALS. <cite id="32676989">Reductions in complement and other innate immune factors coincided with slowed disease progression and extended survival in RAGE-deficient mice</cite>.

- Pathways most consistently associated with clinical severity in ALS include complement activation, TLR signaling, inflammasome activation, and oxidative stress, all of which were reduced by RAGE blockade and linked to better functional outcomes. <cite id="32676989">Complement, TLRs, inflammasomes, and oxidative stress were reduced with RAGE absence and associated with improved motor function and survival</cite>.

# Huntington's disease: Evidence that neuroinflammation drives progression and implicated pathways

- In HD, microglial complement-mediated mechanisms are a central axis linking neuroinflammation to neuronal and synapse loss. Complement proteins (notably C1q and C3) are upregulated in human HD brains and HD models, and microglial complement receptors facilitate synapse elimination in striatum, which correlates with disease progression and severity. This suggests that complement-driven microglial activation promotes maladaptive synapse loss and neurodegeneration in HD. <cite id="32676989">Complement activation and microglial engagement are implicated in synapse loss and neurodegeneration in HD models and human tissue, aligning with disease progression</cite>.

- Innate immune pathways in HD include microglial TLR and inflammasome activation, oxidative stress, and production of proinflammatory cytokines in striatal regions, which increase with disease stage and correlate with symptom severity and striatal atrophy. These features mirror ALS findings and highlight convergent neuroinflammatory mechanisms across disorders. <cite id="32676989">Microglial innate immune responses (TLRs, inflammasomes), cytokines, and oxidative stress increase with disease stage and associate with severity</cite>.

# Convergence on pathways associated with severity

- Across ALS and HD, complement activation (C1q/C3), microglial innate immune signaling (TLRs, inflammasomes), cytokines, and oxidative stress are consistently implicated in disease progression and correlate with clinical severity. Interventions that attenuate these pathways (e.g., RAGE blockade in ALS) improve survival and function in models, supporting a causal role for neuroinflammation. <cite id="32676989">Complement, TLRs, inflammasomes, cytokines, and oxidative stress are common inflammatory axes associated with severity; reducing RAGE signaling mitigates these pathways and improves outcomes</cite>.

# Evidence gaps and future directions

- Direct human pathway-level causal evidence remains limited; more interventional studies targeting complement (e.g., C1q/C3 blockade), microglial phagocytosis, and specific innate immune receptors in both ALS and HD are needed to confirm causality and identify therapeutic targets. <cite id="32676989">Model-based interventions suggest causality, but broader human interventional evidence is needed to prioritize targets</cite>.

# Practical implications

- For ALS, complement and TLR/inflammasome pathways, along with oxidative stress, are promising targets given their modulation by RAGE signaling and association with improved survival and function. <cite id="32676989">RAGE signaling modulates complement, TLRs, inflammasomes, and oxidative stress, with functional benefits when attenuated</cite>.

- For HD, complement-dependent microglial synapse elimination and broader innate immune activation in striatum are key foci for therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving connectivity and delaying neurodegeneration. <cite id="32676989">Complement-driven microglial synapse loss and innate immune activation are central to HD progression</cite>.

QUESTION:
In systemic lupus erythematosus with active lupus nephritis, how does mycophenolate mofetil compare with cyclophosphamide for induction therapy in achieving complete renal response and minimizing fertility-related adverse effects?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In active lupus nephritis, randomized trials and meta-analyses indicate that mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is at least as effective as intravenous cyclophosphamide for induction therapy, with comparable overall renal response rates but a more favorable safety profile—particularly lower risks of amenorrhea and leukopenia—favoring MMF in terms of fertility- and hematologic-related adverse effects. <cite id="19369404">In a 24‑week multinational randomized trial (n=370), overall response rates were similar between MMF (56.2%) and cyclophosphamide (53.0%), and secondary renal endpoints (including complete renal remission) and safety were comparable</cite>. <cite id="20064907">A systematic review and meta-analysis concluded MMF was as effective as cyclophosphamide for induction but tended to have better safety (lower amenorrhea and leukopenia), and lower-dose cyclophosphamide had lower relapse and infection rates than high-dose</cite>. 

# Complete Renal Response

Trials directly comparing MMF and cyclophosphamide show similar overall response rates, with complete renal remission among secondary endpoints. <cite id="19369404">In the Appel et al. JASN trial, 56.2% responded with MMF vs 53.0% with cyclophosphamide; secondary endpoints, including complete renal remission, were similar</cite>. In contrast, newer multitarget regimens can outperform cyclophosphamide: <cite id="25383558">a randomized trial found a higher complete remission rate at 24 weeks with tacrolimus+MMF (45.9%) than with cyclophosphamide (25.6%), with a shorter time to response</cite>. However, this latter study compared against cyclophosphamide rather than directly against MMF monotherapy, so it informs strategy rather than head‑to‑head MMF vs cyclophosphamide.

# Fertility-Related and Hematologic Safety

MMF is associated with fewer fertility- and hematologic-related adverse effects than cyclophosphamide. <cite id="20064907">Across randomized trials, MMF showed lower relative risks of amenorrhea and leukopenia compared with cyclophosphamide during induction</cite>. <cite id="19369404">In the JASN trial, adverse events, serious adverse events, and infections were similar between MMF and cyclophosphamide, but the meta-analysis suggests a favorable safety trend for MMF on key labs/fertility outcomes</cite>. For long-term maintenance, low-dose cyclophosphamide has advantages in relapse prevention and infection risk compared with high-dose, but this pertains to maintenance rather than induction and still carries fertility concerns. <cite id="20064907">Low-dose IV cyclophosphamide had lower relapse and infection rates than high-dose, yet dose-related toxicity remains a consideration</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For induction therapy in active lupus nephritis, MMF provides comparable renal efficacy to cyclophosphamide with potentially better tolerability, especially regarding fertility and leukopenia, making it a reasonable alternative when cyclophosphamide is contraindicated or unacceptable. <cite id="19369404,20064907">Evidence from the randomized JASN trial and meta-analysis supports non-inferiority in renal response with a more favorable safety profile for MMF</cite>.
- If maximal efficacy is desired over standard induction, adding calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus) to MMF can increase complete remission and accelerate response versus cyclophosphamide, though this increases complexity and cost. <cite id="25383558">The tacrolimus+MMF regimen demonstrated superior complete remission and faster time to response compared with cyclophosphamide</cite>.
- For patients prioritizing fertility preservation and hematologic safety, MMF-based induction should be preferred over cyclophosphamide where feasible, with close monitoring of renal response and blood counts. <cite id="20064907">MMF shows lower risks of amenorrhea and leukopenia than cyclophosphamide</cite>.

# Key Trials and Evidence

- Appel et al., JASN 2009: Multinational randomized 24‑week induction; similar overall response (56.2% MMF vs 53.0% cyclophosphamide); secondary renal endpoints and safety similar; no significant difference in infections or adverse events. <cite id="19369404"></cite>
- Systematic review/meta-analysis (Lee et al., Lupus 2010): MMF induction efficacy comparable to cyclophosphamide, with lower relative risks of amenorrhea and leukopenia; low-dose IV cyclophosphamide better for relapse/infections than high-dose. <cite id="20064907"></cite>
- Multitarget tacrolimus+MMF vs cyclophosphamide (China, 2015): Higher complete remission (45.9% vs 25.6%) and faster time to response; similar adverse event incidence. <cite id="25383558"></cite>

# Bottom Line

- Efficacy: MMF and cyclophosphamide yield similar overall renal responses; complete renal remission is comparable in direct head‑to‑head induction trials. <cite id="19369404">MMF 56.2% vs cyclophosphamide 53.0% overall response; secondary renal endpoints similar</cite>.
- Safety/fertility: MMF tends to cause less amenorrhea and leukopenia than cyclophosphamide, supporting its use to minimize fertility-related and hematologic toxicities during induction. <cite id="20064907">Lower relative risks of amenorrhea and leukopenia with MMF</cite>.
- Consider enhanced MMF-based regimens (e.g., adding tacrolimus) for patients needing higher induction intensity, recognizing increased monitoring needs. <cite id="25383558">Tacrolimus+MMF improved complete remission and accelerated response versus cyclophamide</cite>.
