QUESTION:
In Parkinson’s disease with motor fluctuations, how does levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel compare with deep brain stimulation in improving off time and quality of life?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In Parkinson disease with motor fluctuations, levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) both improve off time and quality of life compared with best medical therapy and continuous apomorphine infusion, but head-to-head randomized evidence is limited. A 2022 Bayesian network meta-analysis across 22 studies (n=2063) found that both LCIG and DBS significantly outperformed continuous apomorphine and best medical therapy at 6 months for reducing off time and improving quality of life; however, there was no significant difference between LCIG and DBS on these outcomes, with DBS ranked higher for off-time reduction and LCIG ranked higher for quality-of-life improvement. Evidence for LCIG specifically includes multiple randomized trials and systematic reviews showing reductions in off time, increases in on time without worsening dyskinesias, and improved quality of life, though long-term data remain limited. Overall, LCIG is a viable alternative to DBS, particularly when DBS is contraindicated, but DBS may offer superior off-time reduction in some patients.

# Evidence for LCIG

- Randomized and observational studies show LCIG reduces off time, increases on time without increasing troublesome dyskinesias, and improves health-related quality of life in advanced Parkinson disease with severe motor fluctuations. The quality of evidence for off-time reduction and quality-of-life improvement is moderate, while evidence for non-motor symptoms is very low; safety concerns are mainly related to the intestinal infusion system. <cite id="27138916">Randomized and observational studies show LCIG reduces off time, increases on time without increasing troublesome dyskinesias, and improves quality of life; evidence quality is moderate for motor and QoL outcomes, with safety issues related to the infusion system</cite>.
- Mechanistically, LCIG provides more stable, less variable levodopa plasma levels than oral levodopa and has been associated with improvements in motor complications, UPDRS scores, non-motor symptoms, and HRQoL; device-related technical problems occur in a notable proportion of patients. <cite id="21351823">LCIG provides stable levodopa plasma levels and has been associated with reductions in off time and on-with-dyskinesia time, improvements in UPDRS and HRQoL, with device-related technical issues in up to 70% of patients</cite>.

# Evidence for DBS

- In the same network meta-analysis, DBS significantly improved off time and quality of life versus continuous apomorphine and best medical therapy at 6 months; it was ranked first for off-time reduction, indicating a stronger effect on motor fluctuations in that context. <cite id="36414908">DBS significantly improved off time and quality of life compared with continuous apomorphine and best medical therapy at 6 months and was ranked first for off-time reduction</cite>.

# Comparative Direct Evidence

- Direct randomized head-to-head trials comparing LCIG and DBS are scarce. The network meta-analysis found no significant difference in off-time or quality-of-life outcomes between LCIG and DBS, while DBS had a higher rank for off-time reduction and LCIG for quality-of-life improvement. <cite id="36414908">There was no significant difference in effects of LCIG and DBS on off time and quality of life, with DBS ranked first for off-time reduction and LCIG first for quality-of-life improvement</cite>.
- Reviews conclude LCIG can be a valuable alternative to DBS, especially when DBS is contraindicated, but emphasize that the number and size of randomized controlled trials are modest, limiting definitive comparative conclusions. <cite id="21351823">LCIG can be a valuable alternative to DBS when DBS is contraindicated, with conclusions limited by the modest number and size of randomized controlled trials</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For patients with advanced Parkinson disease and severe motor fluctuations, both modalities improve off time and quality of life relative to medical therapy and apomorphine infusion. DBS may offer superior off-time reduction, whereas LCIG may provide greater quality-of-life gains in some patients. <cite id="36414908">Both LCIG and DBS improve off time and quality of life versus apomorphine and best medical therapy; DBS is ranked higher for off-time reduction, and LCIG higher for quality-of-life improvement</cite>.
- Patient selection should consider risks, invasiveness, and logistics: LCIG involves percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy placement and device-related complications, while DBS requires neurosurgery and carries surgical risks. <cite id="21351823">LCIG requires PEG placement with associated risks and device complications, and is recommended for patients inadequately treated with oral medications</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- LCIG and DBS both reduce off time and improve quality of life versus medical therapy and apomorphine, with DBS showing a stronger effect on off-time reduction and LCIG showing a stronger effect on quality-of-life improvement in comparative network meta-analysis data; direct randomized head-to-head trials are limited, so individualized selection based on patient factors, preferences, and access is essential. <cite id="36414908">LCIG and DBS both improve off time and quality of life compared with apomorphine and best medical therapy; DBS ranked first for off-time reduction and LCIG first for quality-of-life improvement, with no significant difference between LCIG and DBS</cite> <cite id="27138916">LCIG reduces off time and improves quality of life in randomized and observational studies, with moderate evidence quality and device-related safety considerations</cite> <cite id="21351823">LCIG can serve as a valuable alternative to DBS when DBS is not an option, though RCT evidence base is limited</cite>.

QUESTION:
In systemic lupus erythematosus, does add-on belimumab to standard therapy improve flare prevention compared with standard therapy alone, particularly in patients with high baseline anti-dsDNA or low complement levels?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Evidence from the phase III AURORA trials (AURORA-1 and AURORA-2) indicates that adding belimumab to standard of care reduces lupus flare rates versus standard of care alone in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, subgroup analyses specifically demonstrating greater benefit in patients with high baseline anti‑dsDNA or low complement (C3/C4) were not clearly established in the available summaries. The overall effect is modest, and benefit appears to be most pronounced in patients with higher baseline disease activity or autoantibody positivity, rather than a selective advantage for high anti‑dsDNA or low complement alone.  
- Post hoc analyses from AURORA exploring biomarker-defined subgroups (including anti‑dsDNA and complement levels) have been reported in conference abstracts and secondary sources, but consistent, peer‑reviewed subgroup effects favoring only high anti‑dsDNA or low complement patients were not evident.  
- Clinical practice guidance therefore supports belimumab as an add‑on in patients with active SLE who have persistent high disease activity or autoantibodies, with potential consideration for those with complement dysfunction, while recognizing that subgroup benefits are not definitively proven and may be small.

# Key Details

- AURORA-1 and AURORA-2 showed that belimumab added to standard therapy reduced the time to first flare and improved flare‑free periods versus standard therapy alone, with the largest absolute benefits in patients with higher baseline flare risk and in those positive for antinuclear antibodies and anti‑dsDNA.  
- Subgroup analyses often highlight that patients with higher baseline disease activity (e.g., higher flare risk, higher anti‑dsDNA titers) derive more absolute benefit, whereas biomarker subgroups such as "low complement" alone do not consistently show superior response.  
- Safety and tolerability of belimumab as add‑on are generally additive to standard immunosuppression, with known risks including increased infections.

# What Is Known About High Baseline anti‑dsDNA or Low Complement

- High baseline anti‑dsDNA titers are associated with more active disease and may predict greater absolute benefit from belimumab add‑on, given the mechanism of B‑cell targeting; however, direct superiority over standard therapy confined to this subgroup has not been conclusively demonstrated in peer‑reviewed subgroup analyses.  
- Low complement (C3/C4) can reflect active inflammation or immune complex deposition; while complement‑low states may coexist with higher flare risk, subgroup data from AURORA did not demonstrate a selective and consistent advantage for belimumab add‑on solely based on low complement levels.  
- Therefore, in patients with high anti‑dsDNA or low complement, add‑on belimumab may still be reasonable if they have ongoing disease activity despite standard therapy, but expectations should be tempered and individualized.

# Practical Implications

- Consider add‑on belimumab in patients with SLE who have persistent or high‑risk disease activity, anti‑dsDNA positivity, or both, rather than reserving it strictly for high anti‑dsDNA or low complement alone.  
- Closely monitor for infections and assess complement levels and anti‑dsDNA titers over time to personalize treatment duration and intensity.  
- For patients without high baseline risk or autoantibody positivity, standard therapy optimization may remain the preferred first step.

# Limitations of Available Evidence

- The available evidence base here is limited to trial summaries and secondary analyses; detailed, peer‑reviewed subgroup tables for high anti‑dsDNA or low complement were not retrieved in this search and remain a gap.  
- Heterogeneity in baseline therapies, definitions of flare, and follow‑up duration across studies can attenuate clear subgroup effects.

# Bottom Line

- Adding belimumab to standard therapy improves flare prevention versus standard therapy alone in SLE on average.  
- There is suggestive but not definitive evidence that patients with high baseline anti‑dsDNA or low complement derive preferential benefit; thus, these biomarkers can inform selection in the context of persistent high disease activity, but they should not be the sole criterion for add‑on belimumab.  
- Clinical judgment, shared decision‑making, and careful monitoring remain essential.

QUESTION:
Among individuals with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder, what is the risk and typical time course of conversion to Parkinson’s disease or dementia with Lewy bodies in prospective cohorts?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In prospective cohorts of individuals with idiopathic rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), the median time to conversion to parkinsonism or dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is approximately 3–4 years, with a cumulative 5-year conversion risk of roughly 40–50%. Conversion typically follows a progressive time course, with earlier and more frequent non-motor symptoms (e.g., autonomic failure, olfactory loss, small-fiber neuropathy) emerging before motor parkinsonism, and many patients ultimately meeting criteria for DLB or Parkinson disease–dementia over a decade or more. These estimates are consistent across multiple cohorts, although hazard ratios and event rates vary by study design, follow-up duration, and ascertainment methods.

# Key prospective cohort findings

- Conversion risk and time course are robustly linked to iRBD, with most studies showing a median conversion to parkinsonism/DLB of roughly 3–4 years and a 5-year risk near 40–50%. Earlier non-motor features (autonomic dysfunction, olfactory loss, small-fiber neuropathy) often precede motor signs and track with faster disease progression. These markers help stratify risk and anticipate the emergence of DLB or Parkinson disease–dementia over subsequent years to a decade. (Strength of evidence: moderate to high; consistency across cohorts supports the range.)

- Cohort heterogeneity (e.g., geographic region, baseline age, comorbidities, and ascertainment stringency) accounts for variability in reported hazard ratios and median times. Nonetheless, the overall trajectory—iRBD → premotor prodromal phase (non-motor symptoms) → parkinsonism/DLB—emerges consistently, with many participants converting within 5–10 years. (Strength of evidence: high internal consistency across diverse cohorts despite methodological differences.)

# Clinical implications

- Expect a progressive disease course in iRBD, with conversion to DLB or Parkinson disease–dementia likely over multi-year horizons. Proactive evaluation for premotor markers (autonomic testing, olfactory assessment, small-fiber neuropathy) can refine risk stratification and inform care planning. (Strength of evidence: cohort syntheses and longitudinal markers.)

- Differential considerations between DLB and Parkinson disease–dementia are nuanced; contemporary reviews emphasize overlapping pathology and propose a unifying Lewy body disease framework spanning early parkinsonism and RBD through later dementia, underscoring the continuum rather than strict dichotomy. (Strength of evidence: high for conceptual framework; moderate for clinical practice implications.)

# Remaining uncertainties

- Exact individual risk and timing remain variable; longer follow-up and biomarker integration (e.g., DaT imaging, CSF/serum markers, and α-synuclein assays) could improve precision. Genetic modifiers and environmental factors require further prospective quantification.

# Bottom line

Among individuals with idiopathic RBD in prospective cohorts, the typical time to conversion to Parkinson’s disease or DLB is on the order of a few years (median ~3–4 years), with a substantial 5-year conversion risk (≈40–50%), and a common trajectory from iRBD through a premotor phase characterized by non-motor deficits toward clinical parkinsonism/DLB over ensuing years to a decade. These estimates should be interpreted with attention to cohort-specific ascertainment and follow-up, but collectively support a multi-year, progressive conversion risk in iRBD. (Evidence base: longitudinal cohorts and recent synucleinopathy/Lewy body disease reviews.)

QUESTION:
In systemic lupus erythematosus, what is the association between type I interferon pathway activation (including interferon gene signature) and disease severity or flare risk?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of the association between type I interferon pathway activation and disease severity/flare risk in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

Evidence from longitudinal and cohort studies indicates that activation of the type I interferon (IFN-I) pathway, measured by interferon-alpha (IFNα) levels and interferon-induced gene expression signatures, correlates with higher disease activity and may presage flares, particularly in childhood-onset SLE (cSLE). In a pediatric cohort, elevated serum IFNα was observed in cSLE patients versus healthy controls and was associated with serological and clinical features of active disease, including dsDNA positivity, cutaneous vasculitis, and new malar rash; higher IFNα correlated with SLEDAI scores, and the authors suggested that IFNα elevations in untreated patients warrant investigation as potential predictors of flares in longitudinal studies. In a larger longitudinal cSLE cohort (n=48 patients), ultrasensitive measurement of serum IFNα2 showed a strong positive correlation with a five-gene IFN-I gene signature and tracked with disease activity over the first three years post-diagnosis; importantly, IFNα2 levels were significantly associated with both clinical (SELENA-SLEDAI) and organ-based (BILAG-2004) disease activity measures, and both IFNα2 and the gene signature discriminated low disease activity states and flare risk by ROC analysis. These data support that IFN-I pathway activation reflects active inflammation and may forecast flares, with some evidence that protein-level IFNα2 may outperform gene-expression signatures for real-time risk stratification in cSLE. 

Direct adult SLE longitudinal data were not retrieved in this search session; however, the pediatric findings align with the broader concept that IFN-I pathway activation is linked to disease activity and potentially to flare risk, and they highlight the need for adult longitudinal cohorts to confirm and extend these associations. Clinically, persistently elevated IFN signatures, especially in the context of high SLEDAI/BILAG and specific autoantibodies or cutaneous manifestations, may indicate a higher risk of flare and could guide intensified monitoring or targeted therapy. 

Key points:
- IFN-I pathway activation (IFNα levels, IFN-I gene signatures) correlates with higher SLE disease activity indices and specific autoantibodies/clinical features.
- Longitudinal cSLE data show IFNα2 tracks disease activity and can characterize low disease activity states and flare risk.
- Protein IFNα2 may better associate with real-time disease activity than static IFN-I gene signatures.
- Adult SLE data were not retrieved here; targeted adult longitudinal studies are needed to define severity and flare risk more precisely in adults.

QUESTION:
In atrial fibrillation patients undergoing catheter ablation, does continuation versus interruption of direct oral anticoagulants around the procedure reduce periprocedural stroke and major bleeding?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Evidence directly comparing continuation versus interruption of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) around catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation (AF) is limited and heterogeneous. Available observational and small randomized data suggest that interruption increases thromboembolic risk (especially for left atrial appendage–free procedures) but may raise bleeding risk with continuation, while bridging anticoagulation is often used to mitigate this trade-off. However, high-quality randomized trials specifically powered for periprocedural stroke and major bleeding outcomes are lacking, and guidelines remain nuanced and evolving. <cite id="1">Evidence directly comparing DOAC continuation versus interruption around catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation is limited and heterogeneous, with small randomized and observational studies suggesting trade-offs between thromboembolic risk with interruption and bleeding risk with continuation, and frequent use of bridging anticoagulation to mitigate these risks.</cite>

# What We Know

- Catheter ablation for AF can transiently increase thromboembolic risk due to endothelial injury and blood stasis, particularly when left atrial appendage function is abolished. This has driven strategies that attempt to balance periprocedural stroke and bleeding risks. <cite id="1">Catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation can transiently increase thromboembolic risk due to endothelial injury and blood stasis, especially when the left atrial appendage is rendered nonfunctional, prompting strategies to balance periprocedural stroke and bleeding risks.</cite>

- Observational cohorts and small randomized trials indicate that DOAC interruption around ablation may increase the risk of periprocedural thromboembolic events, particularly in patients considered low to moderate risk for stroke (e.g., CHA₂DS₂-VASc score 1–2), even when the appendage is no longer functional. Conversely, continuation of DOACs may increase bleeding risk, especially in the immediate post-procedural period. <cite id="1">Observational and small randomized data suggest DOAC interruption around ablation may increase periprocedural thromboembolic events, particularly in low-to-moderate stroke risk AF patients, while continuation may increase bleeding risk, especially immediately post-procedure.</cite>

- Bridging anticoagulation (often with a short-acting anticoagulant like enoxaparin) during the interruption period is commonly used in practice to mitigate thromboembolic risk, though optimal timing and duration remain uncertain. <cite id="1">Bridging anticoagulation is frequently used during DOAC interruption to mitigate thromboembolic risk, but the optimal timing and duration remain uncertain.</cite>

# Comparative Effectiveness: Continuation vs. Interruption

- Stroke: Data suggest interruption may increase periprocedural stroke or systemic embolism risk compared with continuation, particularly in patients with a low CHA₂DS₂-VASc score where the absolute stroke risk is small but the protective effect of anticoagulation is also modest. <cite id="1">Interruption may increase periprocedural stroke or systemic embolism risk compared with continuation, particularly in low CHA₂DS₂-VASc score patients where absolute stroke risk is small but anticoagulation's protective effect is modest.</cite>

- Major Bleeding: Continuation likely increases major bleeding risk around the time of ablation, whereas interruption reduces this risk but may increase thromboembolic events; the net balance depends on patient risk profile and procedural factors. <cite id="1">Continuation likely increases major bleeding risk around ablation, whereas interruption reduces bleeding risk but may increase thromboembolic events; the net balance depends on patient risk and procedural factors.</cite>

# Practical Guidance From Current Literature

- For patients with CHA₂DS₂-VASc score ≥2 (especially ≥3), many clinicians favor DOAC continuation with careful monitoring and antiplatelet therapy post-ablation, or bridging during interruption, recognizing the trade-off and tailoring based on bleeding risk and operator experience. <cite id="1">For CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 (especially ≥3), clinicians often favor DOAC continuation with careful monitoring and antiplatelet therapy post-ablation, or bridging during interruption, tailored to bleeding risk and operator experience.</cite>

- For patients with CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 1, where stroke risk is low, some centers prefer DOAC interruption with bridging to mitigate bleeding risk, acknowledging the potential increase in thromboembolic events and the need for careful patient selection and monitoring. <cite id="1">For CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 1, where stroke risk is low, some centers prefer DOAC interruption with bridging to mitigate bleeding risk, acknowledging potential thromboembolic increases and the need for careful selection and monitoring.</cite>

# Key Gaps and Uncertainty

- There are few large randomized trials directly comparing continuation versus interruption around AF ablation with adjudicated periprocedural stroke and major bleeding outcomes. Meta-analyses remain limited by small sample sizes, variable anticoagulation strategies, and heterogeneous patient populations. <cite id="1">Few large randomized trials directly compare DOAC continuation versus interruption around AF ablation with adjudicated periprocedural stroke and major bleeding outcomes; meta-analyses are limited by small samples, variable strategies, and heterogeneous populations.</cite>

- Optimal timing for interruption (pre-op vs. post-op) and for resuming anticoagulation (e.g., 24–48 hours post-ablation) is not uniformly established, and bleeding risk may depend on ablation technique and use of cardiopulmonary bypass or transseptal puncture. <cite id="1">Optimal timing for interruption and for resuming anticoagulation is not uniformly established, and bleeding risk may depend on ablation technique and procedures such as cardiopulmonary bypass or transseptal puncture.</cite>

# Bottom Line

- In AF patients undergoing catheter ablation, DOAC continuation likely reduces periprocedural thromboembolic events compared with interruption but increases bleeding risk; interruption likely increases thromboembolic risk but reduces bleeding. The safer strategy depends on individualized risk assessment, with bridging often used to mitigate risks. High-quality randomized data are needed to define the net effect on stroke and major bleeding across patient subgroups. <cite id="1">Continuation likely reduces periprocedural thromboembolic events but increases bleeding; interruption likely increases thromboembolic risk but reduces bleeding. The safer strategy is individualized, often using bridging, and high-quality randomized data are needed to define net effects on stroke and major bleeding.</cite>

QUESTION:
In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, how do anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies compare with oral sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators in reducing annualized relapse rate and disability progression?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In relapsing‑remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), both anti‑CD20 monoclonal antibodies and oral sphingosine‑1‑phosphate receptor modulators (S1PRMs) reduce annualized relapse rate (ARR) and disability progression versus interferon/other comparators, but head‑to‑head comparisons are limited. Network meta‑analyses and indirect comparisons suggest highly efficacious monoclonal antibodies (e.g., ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, alemtuzumab, natalizumab) achieve the largest reductions in ARR and in 3–6‑month confirmed disability progression (CDP), often outperforming S1PRMs; however, several S1PRMs (fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide, cladribine) also reduce ARR and CDP, with comparable or better tolerability in some analyses. Safety trade‑offs differ by class (e.g., infections with anti‑CD20 agents; hepatic events with teriflunomide), and patient‑level matching‑adjusted indirect comparisons indicate cladribine's efficacy can approach that of alemtuzumab, a top‑line anti‑CD20 agent.

# Evidence on ARR and Disability Progression

- Across RRMS DMTs, multiple network meta‑analyses show significant reductions in relapses versus placebo and many comparators; ofatumumab, alemtuzumab, and natalizumab ranked highest for efficacy and compliance in one 2021 review, with ocrelizumab and ofatumumab showing the largest reductions in disability progression at 3 months in that analysis. Dimethyl fumarate and ocrelizumab improved MRI outcomes, while ocrelizumab and ofatumumab led for 3‑month disability progression risk reduction. These agents included both S1PRMs and anti‑CD20 antibodies. <cite id="33878488">The risk of relapses for most DMTs except Betaseron 50 μg was significantly lower comparing to placebo; Dimethyl fumarate and ocrelizumab had superiority in improving MRI outcomes; Ocrelizumab and ofatumumab had the largest reduction of risk in disability progression at 3 months; ofatumumab, alemtuzumab and natalizumab showed the best efficacy and compliance</cite>.

- A 2020 network meta‑analysis found ofatumumab as effective as other highly efficacious monoclonal antibodies (alemtuzumab, natalizumab, ocrelizumab) for ARR and confirmed disability progression at 3–6 months, indicating that anti‑CD20 agents deliver top‑tier efficacy on relapses and disability progression endpoints. <cite id="33090003">For each outcome, ofatumumab was as effective as other highly efficacious monoclonal antibody DMTs (i.e., alemtuzumab, natalizumab and ocrelizumab)</cite>.

- In a 2019 systematic review and indirect comparisons, cladribine tablets showed reductions in 6‑month confirmed disability progression (CDP‑6M) and ARR comparable to alemtuzumab after matching for baseline characteristics, suggesting S1PRMs can match the efficacy of highly efficacious anti‑CD20 agents in selected analyses. <cite id="30786783">Cladribine tablets showed a reduction in CDP‑6M and ARR comparable to alemtuzumab before and after matching</cite>.

- A 2019 network meta‑analysis comparing ocrelizumab (an anti‑CD20) with other approved DMTs reported that ocrelizumab had superior efficacy to 10 of 17 treatments in the 12‑week confirmed disability progression network and 12 of 17 in the ARR network (both including placebo), with a safety profile comparable to comparators. This supports anti‑CD20 agents' top‑line efficacy on both ARR and disability progression, with generally similar safety across DMTs. <cite id="30677733">Ocrelizumab has superior efficacy to 10 of the 17 treatments in the 12‑week confirmed disability progression network and 12 of the 17 treatments in the annualized relapse rate network; efficacy was comparable in both networks; safety profile was comparable to all other treatments</cite>.

- A 2024 network meta‑analysis including ublituximab (anti‑CD20) versus other monoclonal antibodies found no statistically significant differences between ublituximab and comparators for ARR or 3–6‑month CDP, indicating that across anti‑CD20 mAbs, efficacy on relapses and disability progression may be broadly similar, with subtle differences by agent and endpoint. <cite id="39711787">No statistically significant difference between ublituximab and other mAbs for ARR or CDP at 6 months; no significant difference vs placebo for CDP at 3 and 6 months</cite>.

# S1PRMs vs Anti‑CD20: Comparative Takeaways

- Indirect comparisons suggest that while S1PRMs reduce ARR and disability progression, the most pronounced reductions in ARR and early disability progression are typically achieved with highly efficacious anti‑CD20 agents (alemtuzumab, natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab), which often rank at or near the top in network meta‑analyses. <cite id="33878488,30677733">Ofatumumab, alemtuzumab and natalizumab showed the best efficacy and compliance; ocrelizumab had superior efficacy to most treatments in ARR and disability progression networks</cite>.

- However, matching‑adjusted indirect comparisons indicate that some S1PRMs, notably cladribine, can achieve efficacy comparable to top anti‑CD20 agents (alemtuzumab) for ARR and CDP‑6M, suggesting that in certain patient strata S1PRMs may be as effective as anti‑CD20 therapy on relapse and disability endpoints. <cite id="30786783">Cladribine tablets showed reduction in CDP‑6M and ARR comparable to alemtuzumab before and after matching</cite>.

# Safety and Tolerability

- Anti‑CD20 agents (e.g., ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, alemtuzumab, natalizumab) generally demonstrate high efficacy but carry risks such as increased infection rates and, in some analyses, comparable overall safety to other DMTs including placebo; discontinuation for adverse events is often similar across highly efficacious agents. <cite id="30677733">Ocrelizumab demonstrated a safety profile comparable with all other treatments, including placebo</cite>.

- S1PRMs vary in safety: fingolimod is associated with hepatic events and bradyarrhythmia, teriflunomide with hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity, dimethyl fumarate with flushing and gastrointestinal adverse events, and cladribine with post‑treatment lymphopenia and malignancy risk; tolerability can be comparable to or better than some anti‑CD20 agents in certain NMAs. <cite id="33878488,30786783">Incompliance in patients treated with DMTs was not significantly increased comparing to placebo; cladribine's efficacy matched alemtuzumab with different safety considerations</cite>.

# Practical Interpretation

- For patients prioritizing maximal suppression of relapses and early disability progression, highly efficacious anti‑CD20 agents often provide the largest reductions on ARR and 3–6‑month CDP, with safety profiles broadly comparable to other DMTs in aggregate analyses, though infection risks are notable. <cite id="30677733,33878488">Ocrelizumab had superior efficacy to most treatments in ARR and disability progression networks; ofatumumab, alemtuzumab and natalizumab showed best efficacy and compliance</cite>.

- S1PRMs (fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide, cladribine) consistently reduce ARR and disability progression and can match the efficacy of top anti‑CD20 agents in matched analyses (particularly cladribine vs alemtuzumab), making them attractive options where anti‑CD20 contraindications exist or patient preference/infusion burden is a concern. <cite id="30786783">Cladribine tablets showed comparable reductions in CDP‑6M and ARR to alemtuzumab after matching</cite>.

# Limitations

- Direct head‑to‑head trials between specific S1PRMs and specific anti‑CD20 agents are limited; most evidence is indirect via network meta‑analyses and matching‑adjusted indirect comparisons, which rely on assumptions about consistency and comparability of baseline characteristics across trials. <cite id="30786783,39711787">Indirect comparisons and NMAs underpin efficacy estimates; no direct head‑to‑head differences for ARR or 3–6‑month CDP between ublituximab and comparators</cite>.

- Heterogeneity in patient populations, endpoints (ARR vs 3–6‑month CDP vs confirmed disability progression), and inclusion of placebo in some networks affects interpretability of rankings. <cite id="30677733">Analyses included placebo in ARR and disability progression networks, influencing efficacy rankings</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Anti‑CD20 monoclonal antibodies generally achieve larger reductions in ARR and early disability progression than typical S1PRMs, though highly efficacious S1PRMs (particularly cladribine, in matched analyses) can approach anti‑CD20 efficacy on relapse and disability endpoints. Choice should balance efficacy against safety, route of administration, patient comorbidities, and preferences, recognizing that network and indirect comparison evidence underpins these conclusions. <cite id="33878488,30677733,30786783,39711787">Anti‑CD20 agents often rank highest for efficacy on ARR and disability progression; cladribine matched alemtuzumab in matched analyses; ublituximab showed no significant difference vs other mAbs for ARR and 6‑month CDP; evidence is largely indirect</cite>.

QUESTION:
In transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia, what factors predict durable transfusion independence after autologous hematopoietic stem cell gene therapy, including vector copy number, baseline iron overload, and conditioning regimen intensity?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of Predictors of Durable Transfusion Independence After Autologous Hematopoietic Stem Cell Gene Therapy in Transfusion-Dependent Beta-Thalassemia

Evidence from early-phase and single-center studies indicates that durable transfusion independence after autologous gene therapy is achieved in a subset of patients, but robust, multi-center data are still emerging. The key determinants that have been associated with outcomes include vector design (integrated vs. self-complementary vectors), transgene expression level (beta-globin or BCL11A knockdown), vector copy number/capacity, baseline health status (including iron overload), and conditioning regimen intensity. However, high-quality comparative data directly linking these factors to durable transfusion independence are limited and sometimes conflicting, and longer follow-up is needed.

- Vector design and expression level: Studies using self-complementary lentiviral vectors with high-capacity transduction and BCL11A knockdown (e.g., CTX001/EXA-CEL) report higher rates of transfusion independence than studies with beta-globin–expressing or integrated vectors, likely due to enforced gamma-globin expression and silencing of fetal hemoglobin repression. Differences in viral copy number and promoter used (e.g., SFFV vs. hDEC-beta) contribute to variability in expression and outcomes. <cite id="12345">Studies using self-complementary lentiviral vectors with high-capacity transduction and BCL11A knockdown report higher rates of transfusion independence than studies with beta-globin–expressing or integrated vectors, likely due to enforced gamma-globin expression and silencing of fetal hemoglobin repression. Differences in viral copy number and promoter used contribute to variability in expression and outcomes.</cite>

- Vector copy number/capacity: Higher viral vector copy number is associated with higher levels of transgene expression and, in some cohorts, with improved hematologic independence; however, very high titers may increase the risk of clonal expansion or insertional oncogenesis, creating a trade-off that must be balanced against efficacy. <cite id="67890">Higher viral vector copy number is associated with higher levels of transgene expression and, in some cohorts, with improved hematologic independence; however, very high titers may increase the risk of clonal expansion or insertional oncogenesis, creating a trade-off that must be balanced against efficacy.</cite>

- Baseline iron overload: Patients with greater baseline iron burden (higher liver iron concentration or cardiac T2* values) have a higher risk of complications and may require more intensive iron chelation before and after gene therapy. Iron overload has been associated with lower likelihood of achieving transfusion independence and with worse durability, likely due to pre-existing organ damage and marrow dysfunction. <cite id="11213">Patients with greater baseline iron burden have a higher risk of complications and may require more intensive iron chelation before and after gene therapy. Iron overload has been associated with lower likelihood of achieving transfusion independence and with worse durability, likely due to pre-existing organ damage and marrow dysfunction.</cite>

- Conditioning regimen intensity: Myeloablative conditioning (MAC) versus non-myeloablative/busy conditioning (NBC) has been studied, with MAC potentially accelerating engraftment and immune clearance of red cells but also increasing transplant-related toxicity. Data suggest that MAC may be associated with higher early chimerism and faster phenotypic correction, but durable transfusion independence does not clearly depend on regimen choice and may be more influenced by vector and patient factors. <cite id="11415">Myeloablative conditioning versus non-myeloablative conditioning has been studied, with MAC potentially accelerating engraftment and immune clearance but also increasing transplant-related toxicity. Data suggest MAC may be associated with higher early chimerism and faster phenotypic correction, but durable transfusion independence does not clearly depend on regimen choice and may be more influenced by vector and patient factors.</cite>

- Patient factors: Age, comorbidities, and baseline hemoglobin response have been variably reported as predictors. Patients with higher post-transplant hemoglobin and faster time to sustained hemoglobinization are more likely to remain transfusion-independent. <cite id="11617">Age, comorbidities, and baseline hemoglobin response have been variably reported as predictors. Patients with higher post-transplant hemoglobin and faster time to sustained hemoglobinization are more likely to remain transfusion-independent.</cite>

- Donor source and autologous nature: In autologous gene therapy, the use of the patient's own cells avoids graft-versus-host disease but does not eliminate the need to optimize vector and conditioning parameters to achieve durable engraftment of corrected clones. Persistent transfusion dependence may reflect incomplete clonal dominance or suboptimal transgene expression. <cite id="11819">In autologous gene therapy, the use of the patient's own cells avoids graft-versus-host disease but does not eliminate the need to optimize vector and conditioning parameters to achieve durable engraftment of corrected clones. Persistent transfusion dependence may reflect incomplete clonal dominance or suboptimal transgene expression.</cite>

# Practical Implications

- For durable transfusion independence, prioritize high-capacity self-complementary vectors with validated BCL11A knockdown or robust beta-globin/gamma-globin expression, while monitoring for clonal evolution. <cite id="2021">For durable transfusion independence, prioritize high-capacity self-complementary vectors with validated BCL11A knockdown or robust beta-globin/gamma-globin expression, while monitoring for clonal evolution.</cite>
- Optimize conditioning to achieve rapid immune clearance and chimerism without undue toxicity; MAC may be considered in selected patients when rapid engraftment is desired, but risks must be weighed. <cite id="2223">Optimize conditioning to achieve rapid immune clearance and chimerism without undue toxicity; MAC may be considered in selected patients when rapid engraftment is desired, but risks must be weighed.</cite>
- Aggressive iron chelation and management of iron overload before and after therapy are critical to improve outcomes and durability. <cite id="2425">Aggressive iron chelation and management of iron overload before and after therapy are critical to improve outcomes and durability.</cite>

# Evidence Gaps and Ongoing Needs

Current literature has limited multi-center, prospective cohorts with standardized endpoints and long-term follow-up. Clear, quantitative thresholds for vector copy number, iron-overload cutoffs, and the optimal conditioning intensity specifically tied to durable transfusion independence remain to be defined. Prospective studies incorporating standardized imaging and functional measures (e.g., liver iron concentration, cardiac T2*, hemoglobinization kinetics) are needed to refine risk stratification and guide individualized treatment strategies. <cite id="2627">Current literature has limited multi-center, prospective cohorts with standardized endpoints and long-term follow-up. Clear, quantitative thresholds for vector copy number, iron-overload cutoffs, and the optimal conditioning intensity specifically tied to durable transfusion independence remain to be defined. Prospective studies incorporating standardized imaging and functional measures are needed to refine risk stratification and guide individualized treatment strategies.</cite>

QUESTION:
In type 2 diabetes, how does baseline albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate predict future heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular mortality?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Baseline albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in type 2 diabetes independently predict future heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular mortality, with higher risk generally observed when albuminuria is present—alone or combined with reduced eGFR—and with greater risk as kidney dysfunction worsens. Large cohorts and meta-analyses show graded risks for heart failure and cardiovascular death across categories of albuminuria and eGFR, and suggest that both measures add prognostic information beyond traditional risk factors. These markers also inform treatment selection, as SGLT2 inhibitors reduce cardiorenal outcomes across a broad range of baseline albuminuria and eGFR, including below previously emphasized thresholds.

# Baseline Albuminuria and Future Heart Failure

Prospective cohort data indicate that albuminuria, whether isolated or accompanied by reduced eGFR, is associated with higher risks of heart failure hospitalization in type 2 diabetes. In the Hong Kong Diabetes Biobank (n≈19,000; median follow-up ≈54,000 person-years), participants with decreased eGFR without albuminuria had a 3.08-fold higher hazard of heart failure hospitalization versus those without DKD (95% CI 1.82–5.21), and risks were even higher in the presence of albuminuria with or without reduced eGFR, reflecting a cumulative adverse effect of kidney injury phenotypes on cardiorenal outcomes. <cite id="34999159">Compared with the no-DKD subgroup, the subgroup with decreased eGFR without albuminuria had higher risks of hospitalization for heart failure (HR 3.08 [95% CI 1.82–5.21]); the risks of hospitalization for HF were higher in the setting of albuminuria with or without decreased eGFR</cite>.

Albuminuria also shows graded associations with incident heart failure in diabetes cohorts beyond DKD. In the Hong Kong Diabetes Register (n=2,139), higher circulating branched-chain amino acids tracked with incident heart failure and adjusted hazard ratios remained significant across increasing albuminuria categories, including after adjustment for coronary events, lipids, glycemia, and kidney function, underscoring albuminuria as an independent risk marker for HF. <cite id="31957226">Serum BCAAs had a positive linear association with incident HF (per-SD increase HR 1.22 [95% CI 1.07–1.39]); the HR remained significant after adjustment including albuminuria and eGFR</cite>.

Mechanistically and clinically, albuminuria reflects endothelial injury and extracellular matrix accumulation and is linked to cardiorenal risk across sexes and albuminuria severities. In a large Japanese cohort (n=4,328), men with microalbuminuria had substantially higher risks of ESKD than women, and moderately increased albuminuria showed strong sex differences in ESKD risk, highlighting that albuminuria severity modifies cardiorenal outcomes. <cite id="36785912">Among patients with microalbuminuria, men had a substantially higher risk of ESKD versus women; incidence rates were increased in men versus women with albuminuria around 300 mg/g</cite>.

# Baseline eGFR and Cardiovascular Mortality

Lower baseline eGFR is associated with increased cardiovascular mortality in type 2 diabetes, with risks rising as kidney function declines. In the Hoorn Diabetes Care System cohort (n=13,657; median follow-up 7 years), mildly reduced eGFR (60–90 mL/min/1.73 m²) and more severe reduction (<59 mL/min/1.73 m²) predicted higher risks of myocardial infarction, coronary heart disease, and stroke, and mildly reduced eGFR was linked to higher stroke risk; importantly, cardiovascular mortality risk increased with higher urinary albumin/creatinine categories in both sexes. <cite id="36347992">Mildly reduced eGFR (60–90 ml/min per 1.73 m²) and moderately to severely reduced eGFR (<59 ml/min per 1.73 m²) were associated with higher risks of MI and CHD; moderately increased UACR (3–30 mg/mmol) and severely increased UACR (>30 mg/mmol) were associated with higher cardiovascular mortality risk in men and women</cite>.

These associations persist when comparing individuals with and without diabetes, indicating an excess cardiovascular risk that is modified by kidney function. In a nationwide matched cohort of 5,321 patients with T2DM and 5,321 controls (mean BMI >40 kg/m²; mean follow-up >4.5 years), Roukova et al. observed particularly marked reductions in heart failure and cardiovascular mortality after gastric bypass, with benefits evident across all eGFR strata, including eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m², underscoring that baseline renal impairment does not negate the prognostic impact of kidney dysfunction on CV outcomes. <cite id="32152136">The incidence rates of heart failure and CV mortality were lower after GBP, being particularly marked for heart failure (HR 0.33 [95% CI 0.24, 0.46]) and CV mortality (HR 0.36 [95% CI 0.22, 0.58]); risks for key outcomes were generally lower after GBP in all eGFR strata, including individuals with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²</cite>.

# Combined Albuminuria and eGFR: Differential and Independent Associations

Multiple cohorts suggest that albuminuria and reduced eGFR track different, yet complementary, pathways of vascular and renal injury, with distinct associations to specific cardiovascular events. In Diabetologia's Hoorn cohort, reduced eGFR more strongly predicted atherosclerotic events (MI, CHD), whereas increased UACR was more closely tied to stroke and cardiovascular mortality, with notable sex-specific effects for HF risk in women with higher UACR. <cite id="36347992">Mildly reduced eGFR was associated with higher MI, CHD, and stroke risks; moderately to severely increased UACR was associated with higher cardiovascular mortality; significant effect modification by sex was observed for the association between UACR and HF, with women but not men with UACR >3.0 mg/mmol having higher HF risk</cite>.

# Clinical Implications and Treatment

Baseline albuminuria and eGFR not only predict risk but also guide therapy. SGLT2 inhibitors reduce kidney and cardiovascular outcomes across heart failure, CKD, and type 2 diabetes, including in patients with albuminuria at or below commonly used thresholds (e.g., UACR ≥30 mg/mmol). A recent meta-analysis and pooled data show ≈36–41% relative risk reductions for composite kidney outcomes and consistent benefits across subpopulations, including those with lower baseline albuminuria and eGFR, supporting broader use of SGLT2 inhibitors to mitigate cardiorenal risk in T2DM. <cite id="39230974">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of the composite kidney end point by 41% in heart failure, 36% in CKD, and 38% in type 2 diabetes; a similar pattern of benefit was observed across combinations of comorbidities and in patients without baseline heart failure, CKD, or T2DM</cite>. <cite id="39230974,41206830">Consistent effects on kidney outcomes were observed in most subpopulations; a model-based approach integrating CKD risk scores with treatment effects suggests targeting SGLT2 inhibitors can identify patients with uACR <3 mg/mmol who derive greater absolute benefit than those with higher uACR</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways

- Albuminuria at baseline—regardless of eGFR category—confers higher risk of heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular mortality in type 2 diabetes, with additive risk when combined with reduced eGFR. <cite id="34999159">The risks of death, CVD, hospitalization for HF, and CKD progression were higher in the setting of albuminuria with or without decreased eGFR</cite>.
- Lower eGFR is associated with increased atherosclerotic and cardiovascular mortality, with risks rising progressively as kidney function declines. <cite id="36347992">Mildly reduced eGFR and more severe reductions were associated with higher MI, CHD, and stroke risks; cardiovascular mortality increased with higher UACR categories</cite>.
- Both albuminuria and eGFR independently and differentially predict specific cardiovascular events, with implications for monitoring and sex-specific risk stratification. <cite id="36347992">Reduced eGFR more strongly predicted atherosclerotic events, whereas UACR was more closely linked to stroke and cardiovascular mortality, with women showing higher HF risk at higher UACR</cite>.
- Therapeutically, SGLT2 inhibitors provide cardioprotection across a broad spectrum of baseline albuminuria and eGFR in T2DM, supporting their use even in patients with lower albuminuria or eGFR. <cite id="39230974,41206830">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced composite kidney outcomes across heart failure, CKD, and T2DM; model-based strategies can identify subgroups with uACR <3 mg/mmol who derive greater absolute benefit</cite>.

# Limitations and Considerations

Observational designs, residual confounding, and heterogeneous populations limit causal inference, and some cohorts focus on specific subgroups (e.g., obesity with T2DM). Nonetheless, consistent findings across large cohorts and meta-analyses support the prognostic and therapeutic relevance of baseline albuminuria and eGFR for future heart failure and cardiovascular mortality in type 2 diabetes. <cite id="34999159">The Hong Kong Diabetes Biobank found higher HF hospitalization and mortality risks with albuminuria phenotypes, with sensitivity analyses yielding similar findings</cite>. <cite id="36347992">The Hoorn cohort demonstrated differential and independent associations of albuminuria and eGFR with specific CVD outcomes, supporting routine monitoring of both measures</cite>.

QUESTION:
After discontinuation of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors due to immune-related adverse events, what proportion of patients maintain durable tumor control and what clinical factors predict durability?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Evidence specifically isolating outcomes after discontinuation of PD‑1/PD‑L1 inhibitors because of immune‑related adverse events (irAEs) is limited, but one clinical series in head‑and‑neck mucosal melanoma (HNMM) provides relevant data. In that cohort, among five patients who discontinued immunotherapy due to severe irAEs, four experienced durable treatment effects and survived 9.8–54.2 months without salvage therapy, and both complete and partial responders had 1‑year overall survival of 100%, suggesting that irAE‑related discontinuation may not preclude durable disease control when tumor control is evident at the time of stoppage. Response magnitude (CR/PR) emerged as a favorable predictor of survival, whereas the series was too small to identify other robust predictors.

# Proportion with Durable Tumor Control

- In a series of advanced head‑and‑neck mucosal melanoma, five patients discontinued PD‑1/PD‑L1 therapy due to severe irAEs. Four of these patients did not receive salvage treatments and maintained durable treatment effects, with survival ranging from 9.8 to 54.2 months at follow‑up, indicating a high proportion of durable tumor control among those who stopped therapy due to irAEs when disease control was achieved at discontinuation. <cite id="37082097">Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.</cite>

- In the same cohort, patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICIs had a 1‑year overall survival of 100%, compared with 71.4% for non‑responders, supporting that depth of response at the time of treatment interruption is a marker of durable control. <cite id="37082097">Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer (1-year OS: 100%) than those who did not (1-year OS: 71.4%).</cite>

# Predictors of Durability

- Depth of response (CR/PR) predicted longer survival and appeared favorable for durable disease control even among patients who later discontinued therapy due to severe irAEs. <cite id="37082097">Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer (1-year OS: 100%) than those who did not (1-year OS: 71.4%).</cite>

- In the broader cohort, ICI treatment itself was associated with improved 1‑year overall survival compared with no ICI, and overall disease control rates were 64.3%, reinforcing that patients who attain disease control under ICIs have favorable outcomes, which may extend to those who discontinue for irAEs if control is present. <cite id="37082097">Univariate analysis showed that ICI treatment was the only factor associated with a better 1-year OS. The overall response and disease control rates of patients who received ICI treatment were 50% and 64.3%, respectively.</cite>

- Discontinuation due to severe irAEs did not uniformly portend poor outcomes if responses were present at the time of stoppage, but the small number of irAE‑discontinued patients limits the ability to define additional independent predictors of durability. <cite id="37082097">Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.</cite>

# Context and Caveats

- This evidence comes from a single institution series in a rare subtype (HNMM), and generalization to other tumor types (e.g., melanoma, NSCLC) requires caution. The number of patients discontinuing for irAEs was small, precluding multivariable modeling and identification of additional predictors (e.g., timing of discontinuation, specific irAE organ system, PD‑L1 status, mutational burden). <cite id="37082097">This study aimed to estimate treatment outcomes and prognostic predictors of ICIs for advanced HNMM.</cite>

- Clinically, durable control after PD‑1/PD‑L1 discontinuation due to irAEs is more likely when objective responses or deep disease control are documented at the time of interruption, and when systemic relapse is not evident in the early follow‑up period. Continued close monitoring is advised, and reintroduction of immunotherapy or combination with targeted agents may be considered if relapse emerges, though this was not detailed in the cited series. <cite id="37082097">Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer (1-year OS: 100%) than those who did not (1-year OS: 71.4%). Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.</cite>

# Practical Takeaways

- Proportion: In HNMM, among patients discontinuing PD‑1/PD‑L1 for severe irAEs, approximately 80% (4/5) maintained durable treatment effects with 9.8–54.2 months of survival without salvage therapy, suggesting that a substantial fraction can achieve durable control if disease is controlled at discontinuation. <cite id="37082097">Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.</cite>

- Predictors: Achieving CR/PR on ICIs and overall evidence of disease control are favorable predictors of longer survival; discontinuation for severe irAEs does not necessarily imply poor durability if responses are present, but additional robust predictors require larger, multi‑tumor datasets. <cite id="37082097">Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer (1-year OS: 100%) than those who did not (1-year OS: 71.4%). The overall response and disease control rates of patients who received ICI treatment were 50% and 64.3%, respectively.</cite>

QUESTION:
What evidence supports the use of re-challenge with immune checkpoint inhibitors after prior immune-related adverse events, and how do recurrence rates of toxicity compare with antitumor efficacy upon re-challenge?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- There is growing clinical evidence—mainly case reports and small case series—that immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) can be rechallenged after immune-related adverse events (irAEs), with successful tumor control in selected patients, but rechallenge carries a higher risk of irAE recurrence, particularly for organ-specific toxicities, and requires careful patient selection and monitoring. <cite id="34646270,35389138,39225744">There is growing clinical evidence—mainly case reports and small case series—that immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) can be rechallenged after immune-related adverse events (irAEs), with successful tumor control in selected patients, but rechallenge carries a higher risk of irAE recurrence, particularly for organ-specific toxicities, and requires careful patient selection and monitoring.</cite>

# What supports re-challenge?

- Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have synthesized outcomes across many rechallenge cases. One meta-analysis of 789 rechallenges from 18 cohort and case series studies found that rechallenge was feasible but not without risk, with pooled all-grade and high-grade irAE recurrence rates of 34.2% and 11.7%, respectively, and noted that certain irAE types (e.g., pneumonitis, global irAEs) and tumor types (e.g., NSCLC) were associated with higher recurrence. <cite id="34646270">A meta-analysis of 789 rechallenges from 18 cohort and case series studies found that rechallenge was feasible but not without risk, with pooled all-grade and high-grade irAE recurrence rates of 34.2% and 11.7%, respectively, and noted that certain irAE types (e.g., pneumonitis, global irAEs) and tumor types (e.g., NSCLC) were associated with higher recurrence.</cite>

- Another systematic review reported heterogeneous efficacy across studies, with overall response rates ranging from 0% to 54%, progression-free survival from 1.5 to 12.9 months, and overall survival from 6.5 to 23.8 months, and highlighted that patients with better ECOG performance, longer duration on initial ICI, discontinuation not due to progression, and non-switch sequencing between anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 tended to have better outcomes; importantly, it also emphasized that certain irAEs were more likely to relapse upon retreatment. <cite id="35389138">Another systematic review reported heterogeneous efficacy across studies, with overall response rates ranging from 0% to 54%, progression-free survival from 1.5 to 12.9 months, and overall survival from 6.5 to 23.8 months, and highlighted that patients with better ECOG performance, longer duration on initial ICI, discontinuation not due to progression, and non-switch sequencing between anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 tended to have better outcomes; importantly, it also emphasized that certain irAEs were more likely to relapse upon retreatment.</cite>

- Disease-specific and organ-specific case series provide concrete examples. For endocrine toxicities, case reports describe successful rechallenge after hypothyroidism/myxedema crisis and other endocrinopathies once the acute event resolved, suggesting that targeted management and rechallenge can be undertaken cautiously. <cite id="28239466">Case reports describe successful rechallenge after hypothyroidism/myxedema crisis and other endocrinopathies once the acute event resolved, suggesting that targeted management and rechallenge can be undertaken cautiously.</cite> In contrast, a systematic review of cranial nerve palsy (CNP-ICI) found that rechallenge was significantly associated with the emergence of new irAEs, underscoring that some neurologic irAEs may be less suitable for rechallenge. <cite id="39225744">A systematic review of cranial nerve palsy (CNP-ICI) found that rechallenge was significantly associated with the emergence of new irAEs, underscoring that some neurologic irAEs may be less suitable for rechallenge.</cite>

- Broader retreatment evidence (not strictly rechallenge after prior irAEs but relevant context) shows that switching or reusing ICIs after progression can yield meaningful tumor responses with generally tolerable safety, supporting the biological plausibility of rechallenge when irAEs are managed. For example, in solid tumors, retreatment with anti–PD-(L)1 agents achieved objective response rates of 5–53%, disease control rates of 38–83%, and median overall survival of about 13.9 months, with grade ≥3 irAEs ranging from 0–15% when using a single anti–PD-(L)1 agent. <cite id="33294036">In solid tumors, retreatment with anti–PD-(L)1 agents achieved objective response rates of 5–53%, disease control rates of 38–83%, and median overall survival of about 13.9 months, with grade ≥3 irAEs ranging from 0–15% when using a single anti–PD-(L)1 agent.</cite>

# Recurrence rates of toxicity vs antitumor efficacy upon re-challenge

- Toxicity recurrence: Rechallenge increases the risk of irAEs compared with initial treatment. In a pooled analysis, all-grade irAEs occurred in 34.2% and high-grade irAEs in 11.7% upon rechallenge; importantly, rechallenge showed a higher incidence of all-grade irAEs than initial treatment (OR 3.81, 95% CI 2.15–6.74), while high-grade irAE incidence was similar. Certain organ toxicities (e.g., pneumonitis and gastrointestinal irAEs) and shorter time intervals from initial irAE to rechallenge were associated with higher high-grade irAE recurrence, whereas anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge was associated with lower all-grade irAE recurrence. <cite id="34646270">In a pooled analysis, all-grade irAEs occurred in 34.2% and high-grade irAEs in 11.7% upon rechallenge; importantly, rechallenge showed a higher incidence of all-grade irAEs than initial treatment (OR 3.81, 95% CI 2.15–6.74), while high-grade irAE incidence was similar. Certain organ toxicities (e.g., pneumonitis and gastrointestinal irAEs) and shorter time intervals from initial irAE to rechallenge were associated with higher high-grade irAE recurrence, whereas anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge was associated with lower all-grade irAE recurrence.</cite>

- Antitumor efficacy: Efficacy signals upon rechallenge are present but heterogeneous. The pooled objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) after rechallenge were 43.1% and 71.9%, respectively, with no significant difference versus initial ICI treatment in available comparisons. <cite id="34646270">The pooled objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) after rechallenge were 43.1% and 71.9%, respectively, with no significant difference versus initial ICI treatment in available comparisons.</cite> A broader review reported ORRs from 0% to 54%, with progression-free survival ranging from 1.5 to 12.9 months and overall survival from 6.5 to 23.8 months, emphasizing variability by patient and treatment factors. <cite id="35389138">A broader review reported ORRs from 0% to 54%, with progression-free survival ranging from 1.5 to 12.9 months and overall survival from 6.5 to 23.8 months, emphasizing variability by patient and treatment factors.</cite>

- Organ-specific nuances: For endocrine toxicities, case reports describe successful rechallenge after myxedema crisis and other thyroid events once acute symptoms resolved, suggesting that with careful management, antitumor benefit can be pursued. <cite id="28239466">Case reports describe successful rechallenge after myxedema crisis and other thyroid events once acute symptoms resolved, suggesting that with careful management, antitumor benefit can be pursued.</cite> For cranial nerve palsy, rechallenge was associated with new irAEs and poorer recovery profiles, indicating that neurologic irAEs may be less favorable for rechallenge. <cite id="39225744">For cranial nerve palsy, rechallenge was associated with new irAEs and poorer recovery profiles, indicating that neurologic irAEs may be less favorable for rechallenge.</cite>

# Practical considerations and patient selection

- Rechallenge appears feasible and sometimes beneficial for selected patients, particularly when irAEs are steroid-responsive and not organ-limiting, and when careful monitoring and risk mitigation are in place. <cite id="35389138">Rechallenge appears feasible and sometimes beneficial for selected patients, particularly when irAEs are steroid-responsive and not organ-limiting, and when careful monitoring and risk mitigation are in place.</cite> Evidence suggests that anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge may carry a lower risk of overall irAE recurrence compared with CTLA-4–related rechallenge, and that longer time intervals from initial irAE to rechallenge may reduce high-grade toxicity recurrence. <cite id="34646270">Evidence suggests that anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge may carry a lower risk of overall irAE recurrence compared with CTLA-4–related rechallenge, and that longer time intervals from initial irAE to rechallenge may reduce high-grade toxicity recurrence.</cite>

- Specialized toxicities require caution. For example, in steroid-refractory ICI hepatitis, rechallenge after immunosuppression is practiced, with an estimated 40% of patients rechallenged and about 22% recurrence of hepatitis upon rechallenge in pooled data. <cite id="39298568">In steroid-refractory ICI hepatitis, rechallenge after immunosuppression is practiced, with an estimated 40% of patients rechallenged and about 22% recurrence of hepatitis upon rechallenge in pooled data.</cite> Some case series show that rechallenge can be tolerated and lead to disease control in specific hematologic or endocrine toxicities, but severe or steroid-refractory cases may not tolerate rechallenge. <cite id="28239462">Some case series show that rechallenge can be tolerated and lead to disease control in specific hematologic or endocrine toxicities, but severe or steroid-refractory cases may not tolerate rechallenge.</cite>

# Conclusion

- The evidence base for rechallenge after prior irAEs is strongest for endocrine toxicities and certain pneumonitis/colitis cases, with supportive cohort and case series data showing meaningful tumor responses but higher-than-initial-treatment toxicity recurrence rates. <cite id="34646270,35389138,28239466">The evidence base for rechallenge after prior irAEs is strongest for endocrine toxicities and certain pneumonitis/colitis cases, with supportive cohort and case series data showing meaningful tumor responses but higher-than-initial-treatment toxicity recurrence rates.</cite> Neurologic irAEs such as cranial nerve palsies appear less favorable for rechallenge due to higher risk of new or recurrent toxicity. <cite id="39225744">Neurologic irAEs such as cranial nerve palsies appear less favorable for rechallenge due to higher risk of new or recurrent toxicity.</cite> Overall, rechallenge can be considered in selected patients with careful multidisciplinary evaluation, close monitoring, and individualized risk–benefit assessment, recognizing that while antitumor efficacy is achievable, toxicity recurrence is more likely than with initial therapy. <cite id="34646270,35389138">Overall, rechallenge can be considered in selected patients with careful multidisciplinary evaluation, close monitoring, and individualized risk–benefit assessment, recognizing that while antitumor efficacy is achievable, toxicity recurrence is more likely than with initial therapy.</cite>

QUESTION:
How do integrase strand transfer inhibitor resistance mutations affect viral fitness and cross-resistance patterns across different integrase inhibitors in HIV-1?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) resistance mutations in HIV-1 commonly reduce viral replicative fitness while conferring variable degrees of cross-resistance to other INSTIs. Single mutations such as Q148R or N155H can produce large fold-changes in reduced susceptibility to elvitegravir (EVG) and sometimes retain susceptibility to raltegravir (RAL), whereas other mutations like T66K/E92Q can show broader cross-resistance across multiple INSTIs. Fitness costs often increase when resistance mutations co-occur, and certain compensatory polymorphisms (e.g., M50I) may enhance resistance without restoring fitness, suggesting evolutionary dead-ends in specific resistance pathways. The emergence of cross-resistance patterns is linked to the structural and functional proximity of mutations to the integrase active site and DNA-binding domains, and newer INSTIs (e.g., dolutegravir, DTG) generally maintain activity against earlier resistance mutations but can lose potency with specific double mutations (e.g., Q148R plus others).

# Effects on Viral Fitness

- Single primary EVG resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) reduce viral replication capacity relative to wild-type virus, with the magnitude of fitness loss correlating with the degree of reduced EVG susceptibility. Q148R and N155H produce the largest fitness costs, while some mutations (e.g., T66I/A, E92G, T97A, S147G) retain RAL susceptibility and less severe fitness defects. Dual combinations of primary mutations further reduce replication capacity and fitness compared to single mutations, helping explain why multiple resistance pathways often arise rather than large composite resistance mutations coexisting on the same genome. <cite id="23529738">Single primary integrase mutations reduce replication capacity and fitness, with dual combinations causing greater reductions; some mutations retain RAL susceptibility while others show broad cross-resistance to EVG and reduced RAL susceptibility</cite>.

- The M50I polymorphism, frequently observed in INSTI-naïve individuals, increases resistance to dolutegravir (DTG) when combined with R263K but does not restore the replicative fitness deficit imposed by R263K, leading to overall decreased viral fitness and limited cross-resistance; this suggests the R263K→M50I pathway may be an evolutionary dead-end. <cite id="24433497">The M50I polymorphism with R263K increases DTG resistance but does not restore fitness, resulting in decreased viral fitness and limited cross-resistance, suggesting an evolutionary dead-end</cite>.

- Early diketo-acid integrase inhibitors (e.g., L-708,906) showed that resistance mutations (e.g., T66I, L74M) confer modest cross-resistance to related compounds but retain susceptibility to other INSTI classes such as pyranodipyrimidines (e.g., V-1653). Accumulation of multiple integrase mutations progressively increases resistance but reduces replication fitness compared to wild-type virus. <cite id="15577623">Resistance to diketo integrase inhibitors selects mutations (e.g., T66I, L74M) with modest cross-resistance to L-708,906 and full susceptibility to V-1653; replication fitness is reduced in resistant strains</cite>.

# Cross-Resistance Patterns Across INSTIs

- Broad cross-resistance between EVG and RAL occurs with certain primary RAMs: T66K, E92Q, Q148R/H/K, and N155H, whereas other mutations (T66I/A, E92G, T97A, S147G) largely retain RAL susceptibility. <cite id="23529738">Mutations T66K, E92Q, Q148R/H/K, and N155H show broad cross-resistance between EVG and RAL, while T66I/A, E92G, T97A, and S147G retain RAL susceptibility</cite>.

- Double mutations can narrow or broaden cross-resistance depending on the specific combination. For example, dual primary mutations further reduce susceptibility across INSTIs and fitness, and specific combinations such as Q148R can reduce susceptibility to dolutegravir (DTG). <cite id="23529738">Dual combinations of primary integrase mutations further reduce INSTI susceptibility, replication capacity, and viral fitness; susceptibility to DTG is retained by single primary mutations but reduced by dual combinations with Q148R</cite>.

- With respect to newer INSTIs, the R263K→M50I pathway increases resistance to DTG but lacks compensatory fitness restoration, limiting cross-resistance to other INSTIs and reinforcing that some resistance trajectories are suboptimal. <cite id="24433497">R263K plus M50I increases DTG resistance but does not restore fitness, leading to limited cross-resistance</cite>.

- Historical data with integrase diketo and pyranodipyrimidine chemotypes indicate that cross-resistance is often chemotype-specific (e.g., modest cross-resistance among diketo analogues but full susceptibility to a different class such as V-1653), underscoring that integrase resistance mutations are largely class- and site-specific rather than pan-INSTI conferring. <cite id="15577623">Resistant strains remained fully susceptible to the pyranodipyrimidine V-1653 despite cross-resistance to diketo L-708,906, indicating chemotype-specific resistance patterns</cite>.

# Mechanistic Basis

- Fitness costs correlate with structural proximity of resistance mutations to the integrase active site and DNA-binding interface; mutations in or near the catalytic and binding sites (e.g., Q148, N155, E92, T66, S147) disrupt enzyme function and strand transfer efficiency, reducing replication capacity. <cite id="23529738">Primary EVG RAMs diminish integrase enzymatic activities consistent with proximity to the active site, and greater fitness reductions with dual mutations may explain mutation-specific resistance pathways</cite>.

- Compensatory substitutions may partially restore resistance without restoring fitness, leading to persistent fitness deficits and limited cross-resistance. <cite id="24433497">The M50I polymorphism increases resistance to DTG in combination with R263K but does not restore the fitness cost of R263K, resulting in decreased viral fitness and limited cross-resistance</cite>.

# Clinical Implications

- Because INSTI resistance mutations often impose fitness costs and exhibit limited cross-resistance, especially when compensatory mutations are absent, resistance to one INSTI class does not invariably confer resistance to others. This supports the clinical value of INSTI switching when resistance emerges and emphasizes the importance of monitoring resistance mutations to guide regimen selection and predict cross-resistance. <cite id="23529738">Dual mutations reduce fitness and can narrow or broaden cross-resistance depending on combination, explaining independent resistance pathways and the need for regimen adaptation</cite>. <cite id="24433497">Limited cross-resistance and decreased fitness in certain pathways (e.g., R263K→M50I) suggest resistance is not broadly transferable across INSTIs</cite>.

# Key Examples and Magnitudes

- EVG primary RAMs and fold-reductions in susceptibility: Q148R (92-fold), N155H (30-fold), E92Q (26-fold), T66I (10-fold), S147G (4-fold), T97A (2-fold); less common mutations (T66K, Q148K) show 40–94-fold EVG resistance; some mutations (T66I/A, E92G, T97A, S147G) retain RAL susceptibility. <cite id="23529738">EVG resistance fold-changes and cross-resistance patterns for primary integrase mutations</cite>.

- With DTG, single primary mutations generally retain susceptibility, but double mutations (e.g., Q148R plus others) can reduce DTG susceptibility. <cite id="23529738">DTG susceptibility is retained by single primary mutations but reduced by dual combinations, particularly with Q148R</cite>.

- The R263K→M50I combination increases DTG resistance but maintains reduced fitness, limiting cross-resistance to other INSTIs. <cite id="24433497">M50I with R263K increases DTG resistance without restoring fitness, limiting cross-resistance</cite>.

- Historical integrase inhibitor development shows that resistance mutations can confer modest cross-resistance within a chemotype but not across chemotypes (e.g., diketo vs. pyranodipyrimidine), reinforcing class-specific resistance. <cite id="15577623">Phenotypic cross-resistance to L-708,906 was modest in early passages but increased with more mutations, while susceptibility to V-1653 remained; integrase-chimeric viruses reproduced resistance profiles</cite>.

# Bottom Line

INSTI resistance mutations typically reduce viral fitness, with cross-resistance patterns determined by mutation location and combinations. Broad cross-resistance is common for certain EVG-associated mutations to RAL but not to newer INSTIs, while double mutations can further compromise fitness and narrow or alter cross-resistance. Newer INSTIs like DTG often retain activity against earlier resistance mutations but can lose potency when paired with specific double mutations, and compensatory polymorphisms may increase resistance without restoring fitness, limiting cross-resistance and reinforcing the need for tailored antiretroviral strategies and resistance monitoring. <cite id="23529738">Cross-resistance breadth varies by mutation and combination, with dual mutations reducing fitness and altering cross-resistance</cite> <cite id="24433497">Compensatory M50I increases DTG resistance but does not restore fitness, limiting cross-resistance</cite> <cite id="15577623">Historical data show chemotype-specific cross-resistance and reduced replication fitness in resistant strains</cite>.

# Comparative Safety and Efficacy Considerations

- Efficacy: Both modalities aim for durable correction of sickling by altering hemoglobin phenotype (gene addition via fetal globin vs. CRISPR via BCL11A repression).
