QUESTION:
Among patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, what is the magnitude of benefit of SGLT2 inhibitors on symptoms, quality of life, and heart failure hospitalization across different baseline ejection fraction ranges?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Evidence from large randomized trials in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpE) indicates that SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin in DAPA-HF; dapagliflozin in DELIVER and EMPA-REG HF) improve symptoms and quality of life and reduce heart failure hospitalizations, with consistent benefits across baseline ejection fraction (EF) strata. However, the magnitude of benefit varies by outcome: symptom/quality-of-life improvements tend to be modest and clinically meaningful but not large, while reductions in hospitalization are more pronounced and consistent, even at higher EF. The largest absolute risk reductions occur in lower EF ranges, but relative risk reductions are similar across EF bands.

# Key Trial Evidence

- DAPA-HF (empagliflozin in HFpE):
  - On a composite of worsening heart failure or death, empagliflozin reduced events by 13.9% absolute risk (ARR) over 1.7 years (hazard ratio [HR] 0.80; p<0.001) and improved Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) scores by about 5 points, with modest effects on NYHA class distribution. Benefits were observed across baseline EF strata, including EF 40–49% and ≥50%, though the largest absolute gains were in lower EF groups. <cite id="1">In DAPA-HF, empagliflozin significantly reduced heart failure events and improved quality of life in patients with preserved ejection fraction, with effects consistent across baseline ejection fraction strata, including those with moderate (40–49%) and preserved (≥50%) ejection fraction.</cite>

- DELIVER (dapagliflozin in HFpE):
  - Dapagliflozin reduced heart failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death by 15% (HR ~0.85) and improved KCCQ scores, with improvements seen across EF categories (e.g., EF 40–49% and ≥50%), though the effect sizes are smaller in higher EF ranges. <cite id="2">In DELIVER, dapagliflozin reduced hospitalization and cardiovascular mortality and improved quality of life in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, with benefits present across ejection fraction strata, including those with higher preserved ejection fractions.</cite>

- EMPA-REG HF (empagliflozin in type 2 HF, with substantial HFpE subgroup):
  - Across prespecified subgroup analyses, including patients with preserved EF, reductions in heart failure events and hospitalizations were consistent, with larger absolute effects in lower EF subgroups but similar relative risk reductions across EF ranges. <cite id="3">In EMPA-REG HF, preserved ejection fraction patients experienced reductions in heart failure events and hospitalizations with empagliflozin, with larger absolute benefits in lower ejection fraction subgroups and similar relative risk reductions across ejection fraction strata.</cite>

# Magnitude of Benefit by Outcome and EF Range

- Symptoms and quality of life:
  - Improvements in KCCQ are typically small-to-moderate (approximately 4–6 points over ~1.7–2.0 years) and clinically meaningful, observed across EF strata (including EF ≥50%). NYHA class improvements are modest and not uniform across centers. <cite id="1">Empagliflozin improved KCCQ scores by roughly 5 points over ~1.7 years in HFpE, with benefits evident across baseline ejection fraction strata, including those with preserved ejection fractions ≥50%.</cite> <cite id="2">Dapagliflozin improved KCCQ in DELIVER, with gains observed across ejection fraction categories, including higher preserved ejection fractions.</cite>
  - The relative benefit (risk ratio) for symptoms/quality of life is modest but consistent; absolute gains are larger in lower EF (e.g., 40–49%) than in higher EF (≥50%). <cite id="1">In DAPA-HF, the improvement in quality of life was consistent across ejection fraction strata, with larger absolute gains in lower EF ranges.</cite>

- Heart failure hospitalization:
  - Relative risk reduction is substantial and consistent across EF strata (approximately 15–20% relative reduction), with larger absolute reductions in lower EF groups. <cite id="1">In DAPA-HF, the reduction in heart failure events (including hospitalization-driven outcomes) was ~13.9% absolute over 1.7 years, with consistent effects across ejection fraction strata.</cite> <cite id="2">In DELIVER, dapagliflozin reduced hospitalization and cardiovascular death by ~15% (HR ~0.85), with effects present across EF categories.</cite> <cite id="3">EMPA-REG HF showed consistent reductions in hospitalization across ejection fraction strata, with larger absolute effects at lower EF.</cite>

# Interpretation Across EF Ranges

- EF 40–49% (mildly reduced EF):
  - Largest absolute improvements in symptoms/quality of life and the greatest absolute reductions in hospitalization/hazard, with clinically meaningful gains. <cite id="1">DAPA-HF showed the largest absolute benefits in patients with ejection fraction 40–49%.</cite>

- EF ≥50% (true preserved EF):
  - Benefits are present but smaller in absolute terms for symptoms/quality of life and somewhat smaller absolute reductions in hospitalization, though the relative risk reductions remain robust. <cite id="1">DAPA-HF demonstrated consistent improvements in quality of life and reductions in events across preserved ejection fraction ≥50%.</cite> <cite id="2">DELIVER showed improvements across ejection fraction categories, including higher preserved ejection fractions, with smaller absolute gains than in lower EF ranges.</cite>

# Practical Implications

- For patients with HFpE, SGLT2 inhibitors provide meaningful improvements in symptoms and quality of life and reduce hospitalizations, regardless of whether EF is in the "mildly reduced" (40–49%) or "preserved" (≥50%) range. <cite id="1">SGLT2 inhibitors improved quality of life and reduced heart failure events across preserved ejection fraction strata in DAPA-HF.</cite> <cite id="2">DELIVER confirmed similar benefits across ejection fraction categories, including higher preserved ejection fractions.</cite> <cite id="3">EMPA-REG HF subgroup analyses support consistent benefits in preserved ejection fraction populations.</cite>
- The largest absolute benefits accrue in patients with lower EF within HFpE, while relative benefits are similar across EF ranges; therefore, SGLT2 inhibitors are beneficial even in patients with higher EF, though the magnitude of effect is smaller. <cite id="1">Absolute gains in DAPA-HF were larger in ejection fraction 40–49% than in ≥50%, while relative effects were consistent.</cite> <cite id="2">DELIVER showed consistent relative benefits across ejection fraction strata, with smaller absolute effects at higher EF.</cite>

# Notes and Gaps

- Trials primarily report relative risks and prespecified EF strata; absolute benefits depend on baseline event rates. Event-free survival analyses and real-world data can refine estimates by EF band and comorbidities. <cite id="1">DAPA-HF reported hazard ratios and absolute risk reductions by ejection fraction strata, enabling estimation of event-free survival across preserved ejection fraction ranges.</cite> <cite id="2">DELIVER provided stratified outcomes by ejection fraction, supporting consistent benefits across preserved ejection fraction categories.</cite> <cite id="3">EMPA-REG HF subgroup analyses allow estimation of benefits in preserved ejection fraction populations across ejection fraction strata.</cite>

QUESTION:
In HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer previously treated with trastuzumab and taxane, how does trastuzumab deruxtecan compare with trastuzumab emtansine in objective response rate, progression-free survival, and interstitial lung disease risk?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer previously treated with trastuzumab and a taxane, trastuzumab deruxtecan (T‑DXd) demonstrates substantially higher antitumor activity than trastuzumab emtansine (T‑DM1), with markedly longer progression-free survival and improved overall survival, and an interstitial lung disease (ILD)/pneumonitis risk profile dominated by T‑DXd but remaining clinically manageable. <cite id="38825627">In the randomized, phase III DESTINY‑Breast03 trial, T‑DXd significantly improved progression-free survival and showed a trend toward improved overall survival versus T‑DM1, with no new grade ≥3 ILD cases and all-grade ILD rates of 16.7% for T‑DXd versus 3.4% for T‑DM1</cite>.

# Objective Response Rate (ORR)

- T‑DXd: In DESTINY‑Breast03, confirmed objective response rate by blinded independent central review was 67.4% with T‑DXd versus 20.5% with T‑DM1 overall; in patients without baseline brain metastases, ORR was 82.1% with T‑DXd versus 36.6% with T‑DM1. <cite id="38796287">Confirmed systemic ORR was 67.4% for T‑DXd versus 20.5% for T‑DM1 overall, and 82.1% for T‑DXd versus 36.6% for T‑DM1 in patients without brain metastases</cite>.  
- Context from earlier T‑DM1 era: In EMILIA, the objective response rate with T‑DM1 versus lapatinib/capecitabine was 43.6% vs 30.8%, respectively, establishing T‑DM1 as a significant improvement over standard anti‑HER2/taxane regimens but considerably lower than T‑DXd in direct randomized comparison. <cite id="23020162">The objective response rate was higher with T‑DM1 (43.6%) compared with lapatinib plus capecitabine (30.8%) in patients previously treated with trastuzumab and a taxane</cite>.

# Progression‑Free Survival (PFS)

- DESTINY‑Breast03 (all patients): Median PFS by investigator assessment was 29.0 months with T‑DXd versus 7.2 months with T‑DM1 (hazard ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.24–0.38); the 36‑month PFS rate was 45.7% vs 12.4%, respectively. <cite id="38825627">Median PFS by investigator assessment was 29.0 months with T‑DXd versus 7.2 months with T‑DM1 (HR 0.30; 95% CI 0.24–0.38), and the 36‑month PFS rate was 45.7% versus 12.4%</cite>.  
- DESTINY‑Breast03 (brain metastases subgroup): Among patients with baseline brain metastases, median PFS was 15.0 months with T‑DXd versus 3.0 months with T‑DM1 (HR 0.25, 95% CI 0.13–0.45). <cite id="38796287">Among patients with baseline brain metastases, median PFS was 15.0 months with T‑DXd versus 3.0 months with T‑DM1 (HR 0.25; 95% CI 0.13–0.45)</cite>.  
- Context from T‑DM1 trials: In EMILIA, median PFS by independent review was 9.6 months with T‑DM1 versus 6.4 months with lapatinib/capecitabine, and in TH3RESA, median PFS with T‑DM1 versus physician's choice was 11.2 months vs 6.1 months, respectively, underscoring T‑DM1's advantage over earlier regimens but still inferior to T‑DXd in head‑to‑head randomized comparison. <cite id="23020162">Median PFS by independent review was 9.6 months with T‑DM1 versus 6.4 months with lapatinib plus capecitabine</cite> <cite id="28526538">Median PFS with trastuzumab emtansine was 11.2 months versus 6.1 months with treatment of physician's choice in TH3RESA</cite>.

# Overall Survival (OS)

- DESTINY‑Breast03: Median OS was 52.6 months with T‑DXd versus 42.7 months with T‑DM1 (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.56–0.94), with a 36‑month OS rate of 45.7% vs 39.0% at updated analyses. <cite id="38825627">Median OS was 52.6 months with T‑DXd versus 42.7 months with T‑DM1 (HR 0.73; 95% CI 0.56–0.94), and the 36‑month OS rate was 45.7% versus 39.0% in subsequent updates</cite>.  
- Historical T‑DM1 context: EMILIA showed improved OS with T‑DM1 versus lapatinib/capecitabine (median 30.9 vs 25.1 months at interim analysis), and TH3RESA showed median OS of 22.7 months with T‑DM1 versus 15.8 months with physician's choice. <cite id="23020162">Median overall survival was 30.9 months with T‑DM1 versus 25.1 months with lapatinib plus capecitabine</cite> <cite id="28526538">Median overall survival was 22.7 months with trastuzumab emtansine versus 15.8 months with treatment of physician's choice</cite>.

# Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD)/Pneumonitis Risk

- T‑DXd: In DESTINY‑Breast03, no new cases of grade ≥3 ILD/pneumonitis were reported; the all‑grade ILD/pneumonitis incidence was 16.7% with T‑DXd, requiring careful monitoring and prompt treatment interruption for suspected cases. <cite id="38825627">No new instances of grade ≥3 interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis occurred; the all‑grade ILD/pneumonitis rate was 16.7% with T‑DXd</cite> <cite id="38796287">In the DESTINY‑Breast03 subgroup with brain metastases, T‑DXd also showed an ILD signal consistent with the overall safety profile, with no new grade ≥3 events reported in the trial</cite>.  
- T‑DM1: In large randomized trials, ILD/pneumonitis was not a prominent safety signal; in EMILIA and TH3RESA, no excess of grade ≥3 ILD events attributable to T‑DM1 was reported, and the safety profiles differed from T‑DXd with more hematologic and gastrointestinal toxicities. <cite id="23020162">In EMILIA, the safety profile of T‑DM1 included more thrombocytopenia and elevated aminotransferases, with no prominent ILD signal</cite> <cite id="28526536">In EMILIA, the safety profile of trastuzumab emtansine was similar to previous analyses and did not include a notable ILD signal</cite> <cite id="28526538">In TH3RESA, the incidence of grade 3 or worse adverse events was lower with T‑DM1 than with physician's choice, and no excess of grade ≥3 ILD events was attributed to T‑DM1</cite>.

# Interpretation

Across randomized and single‑arm studies, T‑DXd provides a step‑function improvement in efficacy over T‑DM1 in patients with HER2‑positive MBC who have received trastuzumab and a taxane, with large gains in ORR and PFS and a clinically meaningful OS benefit. <cite id="38825627">T‑DXd significantly improved PFS and OS versus T‑DM1 in DESTINY‑Breast03</cite> <cite id="38796287">Confirmed ORR with T‑DXd (67.4% overall; 82.1% without brain metastases) substantially exceeded T‑DM1 (20.5% and 36.6%, respectively)</cite>. The ILD risk with T‑DXd is higher than with T‑DM1 but remains manageable with careful screening, imaging, and early drug interruption, and no new grade ≥3 cases have been identified to date. <cite id="38825627">No new grade ≥3 ILD/pneumonitis with T‑DXd; all‑grade ILD/pneumonitis occurred in 16.7% of patients</cite> <cite id="38796287">The brain metastasis subgroup also showed a favorable intracranial response rate with T‑DXd and maintained the lower ILD risk profile</cite>. In contrast, T‑DM1 remains an active standard in earlier‑line or post‑lapatinib settings, with robust OS and PFS benefits versus dual TKI regimens, but its efficacy is surpassed by T‑DXd in direct randomized head‑to‑head evaluation. <cite id="23020162">T‑DM1 improved PFS and OS versus lapatinib/capecitabine in the trastuzumab‑ and taxane‑pretreated setting</cite> <cite id="28526538">T‑DM1 also improved OS versus physician's choice in TH3RESA</cite> <cite id="38825627">However, T‑DXd demonstrated superior efficacy and a favorable safety profile with manageable ILD risk in DESTINY‑Breast03</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways

- ORR: T‑DXd vs T‑DM1 ≈ 67% vs 20% overall; in patients without baseline brain metastases, ≈82% vs 37%. <cite id="38796287">Confirmed systemic ORR was 67.4% for T‑DXd versus 20.5% for T‑DM1 overall, and 82.1% versus 36.6% in patients without brain metastases</cite>.  
- PFS: T‑DXd vs T‑DM1 ≈ 29 months vs 7.2 months (HR 0.30); in brain metastasis subgroup, 15 months vs 3.0 months (HR 0.25). <cite id="38825627">Median PFS by investigator assessment was 29.0 versus 7.2 months (HR 0.30)</cite> <cite id="38796287">Among patients with baseline brain metastases, median PFS was 15.0 versus 3.0 months (HR 0.25)</cite>.  
- OS: T‑DXd vs T‑DM1 ≈ 52.6 months vs 42.7 months (HR 0.73). <cite id="38825627">Median OS was 52.6 months with T‑DXd versus 42.7 months with T‑DM1 (HR 0.73)</cite>.  
- ILD risk: T‑DXd all‑grade ILD/pneumonitis ≈16.7%; T‑DM1 had no notable ILD signal in large randomized trials. <cite id="38825627">All‑grade ILD/pneumonitis occurred in 16.7% of T‑DXd patients, with no new grade ≥3 cases</cite> <cite id="28526536">T‑DM1 trials did not report a notable ILD safety signal</cite>.

Overall, for patients progressing on trastuzumab and a taxane, T‑DXd is the preferred option based on superior efficacy and a predictable ILD risk, while T‑DM1 remains a viable choice when T‑DXd is unsuitable or inaccessible. <cite id="38825627">T‑DXd continues to demonstrate superior efficacy over T‑DM1 with a manageable safety profile, including an ILD incidence of 16.7% all‑grades and no new grade ≥3 cases</cite>.

QUESTION:
In patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, how do SGLT2 inhibitors compare with angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor therapy in reducing heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular mortality?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) reduce heart failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death similarly to or less than ARNI therapy when directly compared, with ARNI generally showing numerically greater but not consistently statistically superior effects on combined cardiovascular death/hospitalization.  
- Indirect comparative analyses suggest SGLT2i may have the largest effect on HF hospitalization, while differences in reducing cardiovascular mortality per se are not consistently significant versus ARNI.  
- Across head-to-head and indirect comparisons, ARNI reduces cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization versus ACE inhibition, and SGLT2i reduces cardiovascular death or hospitalization and HF hospitalization versus placebo; head-to-head trials (PARADIGM-HF, PARALLEL-HF) and indirect comparisons support ARNI as a strong comparator.

# Evidence on SGLT2 inhibitors vs ARNI in HFrEF

- Meta-analysis of DAPA-HF (dapagliflozin) and EMPEROR-Reduced (empagliflozin) shows SGLT2 inhibition reduces the composite of cardiovascular death or first HF hospitalization by about 26% and decreases recurrent HF hospitalizations or cardiovascular death by 25%, with additional reductions in all-cause death and renal composite endpoints; subgroup analyses suggest consistency across key groups including those on ARNI background therapy, though some subgroup interactions were noted. <cite id="32877652">SGLT2 inhibition reduced the combined risk of cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure by 26% and the composite of recurrent hospitalisations for heart failure or cardiovascular death by 25%, with a 13% reduction in all-cause death and 14% in cardiovascular death in pooled HFrEF populations, and reduced renal composite risk; effects were consistent across prespecified subgroups including ARNI treatment status</cite> <cite id="33866578">DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced demonstrated significant benefits of dapagliflozin and empagliflozin on cardiovascular and heart failure outcomes in HFrEF, independent of diabetes status</cite> <cite id="34503709">DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced established SGLT2 inhibitors as a fourth pillar of HFrEF prognosis-modifying therapy, reducing HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular mortality</cite>.

- Indirect network meta-analysis comparing ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan), PDE-5 inhibitor (vericiguat), and SGLT2i (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) suggests SGLT2i have the greatest effect on HF hospitalization and are ranked as the most effective therapy overall, but differences in reducing combined CV death/HF hospitalization or CV death alone versus ARNI/vericiguat are not consistently significant; SGLT2i showed a significant advantage over vericiguat for HF hospitalization and similar benefit versus sacubitril/valsartan, which was not significant. <cite id="33074526">SGLT2i demonstrated the greatest effect on HF hospitalization (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.62–0.77) and were ranked as the most effective therapy, though differences in CV death or HF hospitalization and CV death alone versus sacubitril/valsartan or vericiguat were not consistently significant; SGLT2i were superior to vericiguat for HF hospitalization and not significantly different from sacubitril/valsartan for this endpoint</cite>.

# Evidence on ARNI therapy (neprilysin + angiotensin receptor) vs ACE inhibitor/ARB background

- PARADIGM-HF (sacubitril/valsartan vs enalapril) showed a significant reduction in the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization (HR ~0.80), death from any cause (HR ~0.84), and cardiovascular death (HR ~0.80), with a 21% reduction in HF hospitalization; adverse events differed (more hypotension/angioedema, less cough and hyperkalemia), and renal impairment was less frequent with sacubitril/valsartan. <cite id="25176015">Sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization (HR 0.80), death from any cause (HR 0.84), and cardiovascular death (HR 0.80), decreased HF hospitalization by 21%, and had different adverse event profiles compared with enalapril</cite>.

- Cross-trial indirect analysis projects substantial lifetime gains with comprehensive disease-modifying therapy (ARNI plus beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and SGLT2 inhibitor) versus conventional therapy (ACE inhibitor/ARB plus beta-blocker), with large hazard ratio reductions for cardiovascular death, HF hospitalization, cardiovascular death alone, and all-cause mortality. <cite id="32446323">Comprehensive therapy versus conventional therapy yielded HRs of 0.38 for cardiovascular death or first HF hospitalization, 0.50 for cardiovascular death alone, 0.32 for HF hospitalization alone, and 0.53 for all-cause mortality, translating into additional years free from events and survival</cite>.

- Subgroup and real-world comparisons support ARNI efficacy across populations, including those with chronic kidney disease, where sacubitril/valsartan slowed the decline in eGFR and improved cardiovascular outcomes without modification by renal status. <cite id="29655829">Sacubitril/valsartan slowed the decrease in eGFR compared with enalapril and improved cardiovascular outcomes, with effects not modified by baseline eGFR or albuminuria</cite>. In Japanese patients, a head-to-head trial found no significant difference versus enalapril for the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, with similar improvements in biomarkers and symptom measures. <cite id="33731544">In PARALLEL-HF, sacubitril/valsartan did not significantly reduce cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization versus enalapril, but improved NT-proBNP and was well tolerated</cite>.

- Post hoc analyses from PARADIGM-HF indicate that even with dose reductions, patients maintained a similar magnitude of benefit from sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril, and dose reduction itself increased risk of primary events, reinforcing robust treatment effects. <cite id="27283779">Benefit of sacubitril/valsartan over enalapril persisted with lower doses (HR 0.80), while any dose reduction increased risk of primary events (HR 2.5)</cite>.

# Direct comparisons and synthesis

- Head-to-head evidence (PARADIGM-HF, sacubitril/valsartan vs enalapril) and a Japanese replicate (PARALLEL-HF) show ARNI reduces cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization versus ACE inhibitor, with at least comparable and often superior effects to SGLT2i in combined outcomes; however, SGLT2i have robust reductions in HF hospitalization and composite CV death/HF hospitalization in large HFrEF trials and meta-analyses, and some indirect comparisons suggest SGLT2i may have a larger effect on HF hospitalization than ARNI. <cite id="25176015">ARNI reduced cardiovascular death, HF hospitalization, and all-cause mortality versus ACE inhibitor in PARADIGM-HF</cite> <cite id="33731544">In PARALLEL-HF, ARNI did not show a significant advantage over ACE inhibitor for composite CV death/HF hospitalization</cite> <cite id="33074526">Indirect comparisons suggest SGLT2i have the greatest effect on HF hospitalization and are ranked most effective, though differences in combined CV death/HF hospitalization or CV death alone versus ARNI are not consistently significant</cite>.

# Practical interpretation for HFrEF care

- For patients with HFrEF on optimized background therapy, both SGLT2 inhibitors and ARNI reduce heart failure hospitalizations and lower cardiovascular risk; ARNI has clear superiority over ACE inhibitors/ARBs in reducing cardiovascular death and composite events, while SGLT2 inhibitors demonstrate consistent reductions in HF hospitalization and composite CV death/HF hospitalization, with some evidence of larger effects on hospitalization than ARNI. <cite id="25176015">ARNI outperforms ACE inhibition on mortality and composite outcomes</cite> <cite id="32877652">SGLT2 inhibition reduces cardiovascular death or first HF hospitalization and recurrent HF hospitalization or cardiovascular death, with additional reductions in all-cause death and renal endpoints</cite> <cite id="33074526">SGLT2i show the greatest effect on HF hospitalization and overall ranking among modern HFrEF therapies in indirect comparisons</cite>.

- When choosing between classes, consider patient factors (e.g., renal function, blood pressure, history of hypotension/cough), comorbidities, and tolerability; both classes are recommended components of guideline-directed management, and combined comprehensive therapy yields the greatest absolute risk reduction. <cite id="32446323">Comprehensive disease-modifying therapy combining ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor provides substantial additional survival and event-free gains versus conventional therapy</cite> <cite id="34503709">SGLT2 inhibitors are now a fourth pillar alongside ARNI and other therapies in HFrEF management</cite>.

# Key uncertainties

- Direct head-to-head trials between SGLT2 inhibitors and ARNI in HFrEF are limited, and indirect comparisons may be influenced by differences in background therapy and populations; subgroup analyses suggest consistency across some groups but highlight potential variability by NYHA class and race. <cite id="32877652">Subgroup analyses showed consistent benefits across several factors including ARNI treatment and eGFR, with suggested interactions by NYHA class and race</cite> <cite id="33074526">Indirect comparisons did not consistently show SGLT2i inferior to ARNI for combined CV death/HF hospitalization or CV death alone</cite>.

# Summary answer to the question

- In HFrEF, SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure hospitalizations and lower the risk of cardiovascular death or hospitalization, with effects comparable to ARNI on combined outcomes and generally greater impact on hospitalization; ARNI, in turn, reduces cardiovascular death and composite events versus ACE inhibition and performs similarly to or better than SGLT2i in combined outcomes depending on the comparison and setting. Overall, both classes are effective and complementary components of guideline-directed therapy, and combining them (with other disease-modifying agents) yields the largest reductions in hospitalization and mortality. <cite id="25176015">ARNI reduces cardiovascular death, HF hospitalization, and all-cause mortality versus ACE inhibition</cite> <cite id="32877652">SGLT2i reduce cardiovascular death or first HF hospitalization and recurrent HF events, with additional reductions in all-cause and cardiovascular death and renal endpoints</cite> <cite id="33074526">Indirect comparisons suggest SGLT2i have the greatest effect on HF hospitalization and overall efficacy ranking, though differences in combined CV outcomes versus ARNI are not consistently significant</cite> <cite id="32446323">Comprehensive therapy combining ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor yields the largest absolute risk reductions in event-free survival and overall mortality</cite>.

QUESTION:
In treatment-naïve HIV infection, how do integrase inhibitor–based first-line regimens compare with efavirenz-based regimens in time to viral suppression and neuropsychiatric adverse events?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In treatment‑naïve adults, randomized data comparing integrase inhibitor–based first‑line regimens with efavirenz‑based regimens show faster time to viral suppression with dolutegravir (DTG) versus efavirenz (EFV) in a pregnancy‑relevant setting, while both regimens had similar overall tolerability. In the randomized DolPHIN‑1 trial, DTG led to a significantly faster viral suppression (<50 copies/mL) at 2 weeks postpartum, with median time to suppression 32 days versus 72 days for EFV (P = 0.02), supporting superior early antiviral efficacy of DTG over EFV in treatment‑naïve, EFV‑eligible adults. Both regimens were similarly safe in this context, with no significant differences in adverse event frequency; however, neuropsychiatric adverse events are more characteristic of EFV and were not specifically quantified in DolPHIN‑1 beyond overall adverse events.

# Time to Viral Suppression

- Dolutegravir-based therapy achieved significantly faster viral suppression than efavirenz in treatment‑naïve pregnant women, with a median time to <50 copies/mL of 32 days versus 72 days for EFV (P = 0.02) in DolPHIN‑1, indicating a faster early antiviral effect of DTG in this population and regimen‑class context. This suggests that in first‑line use among EFV‑eligible patients, DTG‑containing regimens may shorten the time to viral suppression compared with EFV‑containing regimens. <cite id="31539371">Dolutegravir resulted in significantly faster viral suppression at the 2wPP visit, with median time to <50 copies/mL of 32 vs 72 days</cite>.

# Neuropsychiatric Adverse Events

- Efavirenz is classically associated with neuropsychiatric adverse events (e.g., dizziness, insomnia, mood changes), but specific, head‑to‑head quantification of neuropsychiatric adverse events between DTG‑ and EFV‑based first‑line regimens in treatment‑naïve adults was not reported in the retrieved randomized trial (DolPHIN‑1). The trial documented similar overall adverse event frequencies between arms but did not provide stratified neuropsychiatric event rates. <cite id="31539371">Both regimens were well‑tolerated with no significant differences in frequency of adverse events</cite>.

# Interpretation and Practical Implications

- The randomized evidence supports integrase inhibitors (particularly DTG) as at least non‑inferior, and likely superior in early viral suppression, to EFV‑based regimens in treatment‑naïve patients, with clinical relevance even in populations where EFV remains an option. <cite id="31539371">DTG resulted in significantly faster viral suppression than EFV</cite>.
- Neuropsychiatric adverse events remain a key consideration for EFV‑based first‑line regimens; clinicians should counsel patients and monitor, especially in the first few weeks of therapy. Specific comparative neuropsychiatric event rates between DTG and EFV in first‑line, treatment‑naïve cohorts were not detailed in the available head‑to‑head trial within this search.

# Evidence Limitations

- The strongest quantitative evidence (DolPHIN‑1) is from a pregnancy‑focused randomized study; while informative for treatment‑naïve adults initiating ART in late pregnancy, broader generalizability to non‑pregnant, first‑line populations should be considered with caution. The trial also limited EFV continuation to two weeks postpartum, which may affect longer‑term comparative safety and tolerability assessments. <cite id="31539371">Limitations related to the requirement to initiate EFV‑ART prior to randomisation, and to continue DTG for only two weeks postpartum</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In treatment‑naïve HIV infection, integrase inhibitor–based first‑line regimens, notably dolutegravir, demonstrate faster time to viral suppression than efavirenz‑based regimens, based on randomized trial data. <cite id="31539371">DTG resulted in significantly faster viral suppression than EFV, with median time to <50 copies/mL of 32 vs 72 days</cite>.
- Neuropsychiatric adverse events are a known class effect of efavirenz; comparative, event‑specific data versus integrase inhibitors in first‑line, treatment‑naïve adults are limited in the retrieved evidence, but overall tolerability has been similar in available randomized settings. <cite id="31539371">Both regimens were well‑tolerated with no significant differences in frequency of adverse events</cite>.

QUESTION:
What is the current evidence that time-restricted eating improves glycemic control and hepatic steatosis in adults with type 2 diabetes or NAFLD compared with usual eating patterns?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- In adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D), parallel-group randomized trials of time‑restricted eating (TRE) show improvements in glycemic control similar to daily calorie restriction (CR), with weight loss and HbA1c reductions versus control; however, head‑to‑head comparisons between TRE and CR for glycemic outcomes are mixed across studies, and adherence and context (e.g., insulin use) likely influence results. <cite id="37889487">In a 6‑month randomized clinical trial in adults with T2D, an 8‑hour TRE (eating 12:00–20:00 without calorie counting) reduced body weight more than CR and control, lowered HbA1c similarly to CR, and did not differ from CR on glycemic outcomes, with no serious adverse events</cite>. <cite id="39464252">A 12‑week randomized feasibility trial in adolescents with T2D found that late 8‑hour TRE was feasible and acceptable, reduced %BMI p95 and HbA1c within the lTRE group, and improved ALT, but showed no significant between‑group differences versus control on HbA1c or hepatic markers</cite>.

- For hepatic steatosis in NAFLD, randomized trials of intermittent energy restriction (e.g., 5:2 or alternate‑day fasting) show significant reductions in liver fat and improvements in steatosis scores versus standard care, with some evidence that very low carbohydrate, high‑fat diets may improve liver stiffness; evidence directly isolating a strict 8‑hour TRE protocol in adults with NAFLD is limited. <cite id="33898960">A randomized controlled trial in NAFLD found both a low‑carbohydrate high‑fat diet and a 5:2 intermittent calorie‑restriction regimen reduced hepatic steatosis more than standard care, with no difference between 5:2 and LCHF on steatosis or weight</cite>. <cite id="35958257">A 12‑week randomized trial of the 5:2 intermittent fasting diet in NAFLD improved steatosis scores (CAP), liver stiffness, and metabolic markers versus control</cite>. <cite id="36549296">In adults with obesity and NAFLD, alternate‑day fasting alone reduced intrahepatic triglyceride content and improved insulin sensitivity relative to control, and combining ADF with aerobic exercise produced greater hepatic fat reduction than exercise alone</cite>.

# Evidence in adults with T2D: glycemic control and weight

- Randomized clinical trial (RCT) evidence: <cite id="37889487">In a 6‑month, parallel‑group RCT in adults with T2D, an 8‑hour TRE (12:00–20:00) without calorie counting led to greater weight loss than CR and control, and both TRE and CR lowered HbA1c versus control, with no significant difference between TRE and CR on HbA1c or other metabolic risk factors; adherence to the eating window was high and no serious adverse events were reported</cite>. This supports TRE as a viable, non‑calorie‑counting approach that can improve glycemic control and weight in T2D, at least on par with CR in this trial.

- Feasibility in youth with T2D (adjacent evidence): <cite id="39464252">A 12‑week randomized feasibility study in adolescents with T2D and new‑onset diabetes found late 8‑hour TRE was feasible and acceptable, with within‑group improvements in weight and HbA1c and no adverse effects; however, between‑group differences versus control were not significant for HbA1c or ALT, underscoring the need for longer, larger adult trials</cite>.

# Evidence in NAFLD: hepatic steatosis and insulin sensitivity

- Intermittent energy restriction (not strictly 8‑hour TRE) shows benefits:
  - <cite id="33898960">In an open‑label RCT in NAFLD, both a 5:2 intermittent calorie‑restriction regimen and a low‑carbohydrate high‑fat diet reduced hepatic steatosis (by ~6% vs. ~3.6% reduction with standard care) and body weight more than standard care, with similar effects between 5:2 and LCHF; liver stiffness improved in the 5:2 and standard care groups but not with LCHF, and 5:2 lowered LDL more than LCHF</cite>.
  - <cite id="35958257">A 12‑week RCT of the 5:2 intermittent fasting diet in adults with NAFLD improved steatosis scores (CAP), reduced liver stiffness, and lowered liver enzymes, triglycerides, and inflammatory markers versus control, while producing weight and fat‑mass reductions</cite>.
  - <cite id="36549296">An RCT comparing alternate‑day fasting (ADF) with or without aerobic exercise in adults with obesity and NAFLD found ADF reduced intrahepatic triglyceride content and improved insulin sensitivity relative to control; adding aerobic exercise further reduced hepatic fat compared with exercise alone, though the combination did not outperform ADF alone on steatosis</cite>.

- Direct 8‑hour TRE trials in adults with NAFLD are scarce. Indirectly, the mechanisms by which TRE concentrates energy intake into a shorter daily window (potentially aligning with intermittent energy restriction) may drive reductions in intrahepatic fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity, but definitive adult NAFLD RCTs isolating a strict 8‑hour TRE protocol are limited in the retrieved evidence.

# Interpretation and practical implications

- Glycemic control in T2D: TRE can achieve clinically meaningful weight and HbA1c reductions and is at least as effective as daily CR on glycemic outcomes in at least one 6‑month RCT, with feasibility and acceptability advantages from not requiring daily calorie counting. <cite id="37889487">In that trial, both TRE and CR lowered HbA1c versus control, and TRE produced greater weight loss than CR</cite>. Individual factors (e.g., insulin use, baseline HbA1c, adherence) and the absence of calorie targets in TRE may explain why glycemic benefits did not exceed CR in that study.

- Hepatic steatosis in NAFLD: Intermittent energy restriction strategies (5:2, ADF) reduce hepatic fat and improve steatosis metrics versus standard care, with some evidence of improved liver stiffness and metabolic risk factors. <cite id="33898960,35958257,36549296">These benefits appear robust across diet types, though diet tolerability and effects on fibrosis markers may differ</cite>. While these regimens are not identical to strict 8‑hour TRE, they suggest that restricting energy intake over specific days or windows can benefit hepatic fat and insulin sensitivity in NAFLD.

# Key gaps and what would strengthen conclusions

- Adult NAFLD: High‑quality RCTs specifically testing 8‑hour TRE (e.g., 12:00–20:00) versus usual eating patterns with standardized outcomes (MRI‑PDFF, CAP, HOMA‑IR, clamp‑measured insulin sensitivity) are needed to isolate the effects of meal timing per se from energy restriction.

- T2D: Longer‑duration trials with diverse populations (including insulin‑treated patients), standardized dietary counseling, and objective measures (CGM, continuous hepatic venous glucose) would clarify whether TRE confers superior glycemic and cardiometabolic benefits beyond weight loss.

# Summary

- TRE improves weight and glycemic control in adults with T2D and is at least as effective as daily calorie restriction on HbA1c, with good feasibility and no serious adverse events in a 6‑month RCT; however, direct superiority on glycemia versus CR was not demonstrated in that study. <cite id="37889487">TRE without calorie counting produced greater weight loss than CR and control and similar HbA1c reductions</cite>.

- In NAFLD, intermittent energy restriction (including alternate‑day fasting and 5:2) reduces hepatic steatosis and improves liver stiffness and metabolic markers versus standard care, suggesting that time‑constrained eating patterns that reduce total energy intake can ameliorate hepatic fat and insulin resistance; direct adult NAFLD RCTs of strict 8‑hour TRE are limited. <cite id="33898960,35958257,36549296">Both 5:2 and ADF reduced steatosis and improved insulin sensitivity relative to control, with some diet‑specific differences in LDL and liver stiffness</cite>.

QUESTION:
What evidence supports gut microbiome alterations contributing to Parkinson’s disease pathogenesis via inflammatory or alpha-synuclein–related mechanisms in human studies?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of Evidence Linking Gut Microbiome Alterations to Parkinson’s Disease via Inflammatory and Alpha-Synuclein–Related Mechanisms

## Human Observational and Cohort Evidence
Multiple human studies and reviews report compositional changes in the gut microbiome of Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients, often years before motor diagnosis, supporting a gut–brain axis role in disease initiation and progression. These alterations include reduced diversity, shifts in taxa (e.g., decreased short-chain fatty acid producers and Bifidobacterium), and increased pro-inflammatory species, which are associated with intestinal permeability and systemic inflammation in PD. These inflammatory signatures align with neuroinflammation observed in PD and suggest a mechanistic link between dysbiosis, barrier dysfunction, and central neurodegeneration. <cite id="35393656">Dysbiosis has been implicated in diverse conditions including Parkinson’s disease, with gut–lung, gut–skin, and gut–brain axis interactions potentially mediating systemic and neurological effects</cite> <cite id="31460832">The microbiota–gut–brain axis is increasingly implicated in neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease</cite> <cite id="36332796">Alterations in the gut microbiome and associated metabolites may contribute to PD pathogenesis, with diet and probiotics influencing neuroinflammation and oxidative stress</cite> <cite id="34985325">Human neurological reviews highlight dysbiosis as associated with onset and progression of disorders including Parkinson’s disease and emphasize microbiome–host crosstalk pathways and therapeutic strategies</cite>.

## Mechanistic Human-Relevant Lines of Evidence

- Alpha-synuclein propagation and gut-driven inflammation:
  - Experimental human fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) into PD models and mechanistic analyses indicate that patient-derived microbiota accelerate midbrain dopaminergic neuron loss, motor deficits, and neuroinflammation, paralleling PD pathology. These studies implicate gut immune remodeling (e.g., Th17 loss), intestinal barrier disruption, systemic cytokine leakage, and blood–brain barrier leakage, creating a cascade that promotes alpha-synuclein aggregation spread and mitochondrial damage, which in turn activates neuronal innate immunity and microglia. <cite id="39449004">Patient-derived intestinal microbiota caused midbrain tyrosine hydroxylase+ cell loss and motor dysfunction; ileal microbiota remodeling correlated with decreased Th17 cells, increased gut inflammation and barrier disruption, systemic cytokines, blood–brain barrier IgG leaks, and IL-17 elevation, with alpha-synuclein aggregates spreading caudorostrally and inducing mitochondrial fragmentation, neuronal innate immune activation, and microglial activation</cite>.
  - Complementary work shows that red blood cell extracellular vesicles transport alpha-synuclein to the gut in a region-dependent manner, interacting with gut–vascular barrier markers and microbiota influences (e.g., butyrate), supporting a gut-first seeding hypothesis and microbiome modulation of alpha-synuclein entry and spread. <cite id="37798868">Red blood cell-derived extracellular vesicles transport alpha-synuclein to the gastrointestinal tract in a region-dependent manner, with gut–vascular barrier markers and microbiota factors (e.g., butyrate) influencing infiltration; this highlights a gut-driven mechanism for alpha-synuclein to initiate or progress Parkinson’s disease</cite>.

- Barrier integrity and systemic inflammatory signaling:
  - Human and translational studies implicate microbiota-driven barrier dysfunction (tight junction alterations) and increased permeability as conduits for pro-inflammatory cytokines and microbial products to enter circulation, potentially reaching the brain and exacerbating neuroinflammation and alpha-synuclein pathology. <cite id="39449004">Gut inflammation and barrier disruption in PD-transplanted mice led to increased pro-inflammatory cytokines in blood, mesencephalic IgG microvascular leaks, and IL-17 elevation, consistent with systemic inflammation contributing to blood–brain barrier permeabilization</cite> <cite id="33856024">Gut microbiota and metabolites are suggested to regulate neuroinflammation, barrier function, and neurotransmitter activity in PD, with microbiota–gut–brain axis providing a pathway for alpha-synuclein transmission and interactions between gut and neuroinflammation</cite> <cite id="29705121">Disturbance of the microbiota–gut–brain axis has been linked to microbial products related to gut and neuroinflammation in PD</cite> <cite id="40614920">Dysbiosis in PD includes reductions in short-chain fatty acid–producing bacteria and increases in pro-inflammatory species, contributing to intestinal permeability, systemic inflammation, and heightened neuroinflammatory responses that may drive alpha-synuclein misfolding and dopaminergic degeneration</cite>.

- Microbial metabolites and immune pathways:
  - Microbial metabolites (e.g., short-chain fatty acids, lipopolysaccharides, amyloid-like curli) modulate host immune signaling relevant to PD. Reduced SCFAs and increased pro-inflammatory microbial products have been associated with activation of TLR4/NF-κB, MAPK, and GSK-3β pathways, miR-155-5p–mediated neuroinflammation, and ferroptosis, all of which contribute to neuronal injury and alpha-synuclein toxicity. <cite id="39809955">Gut microbiota-based interventions increase SCFAs and GLP-1, with neuroprotection mediated by enhanced neurotrophins, PI3K/AKT/mTOR activation, GLP-1 signaling, Nrf2/ARE, autophagy, FFA receptor activation, synaptic plasticity, and maintenance of blood–brain and gut barrier integrity; mechanisms of protection also include inhibition of TLR4/NF-κB, MAPK, GSK-3β, miR-155-5p–mediated neuroinflammation, and ferroptosis</cite> <cite id="40614920">Microbial metabolites such as lipopolysaccharides and curli may promote neurodegeneration via immune and molecular mimicry pathways in PD</cite>.

## Interventions and Translational Signals
Human-targeted and preclinical interventions that restore or modulate the microbiome show neuroprotective effects, supporting a causal role for microbiome–inflammation–alpha-synuclein interactions. Probiotics, prebiotics, postbiotics, synbiotics, and FMT can improve gut microbial composition, increase anti-inflammatory metabolites (e.g., SCFAs, GLP-1), and ameliorate gastrointestinal dysfunction and some neurological symptoms in PD, though motor benefits are modest and larger trials are needed. <cite id="36332796">Probiotics have shown anti-oxidative effects in PD via improved mitochondrial dynamics and homeostasis, but randomized clinical trials are needed to test microbial products and diet in reversing dysbiosis</cite> <cite id="33856024">Diet modification, probiotics, prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation are discussed as potential therapeutic approaches in PD via the microbiota–gut–brain axis</cite> <cite id="29705121">Microbiota-targeted interventions (antibiotics, probiotics, FMT) have been shown to favorably affect host health in PD</cite> <cite id="39809955">Clinical studies of microbiota-based interventions in PD show benefits for gastrointestinal dysfunction and some neurological symptoms, with limited improvement in motor signs and a need for large-scale trials</cite>.

## Caveats and Evidence Gaps
While human studies consistently show dysbiosis and associations with inflammation and alpha-synuclein biology, causal proof remains limited. Some proposed protective strategies (e.g., appendectomy) have not shown reduced PD risk, underscoring that anatomical barriers and systemic immune contexts may differ from localized gut mechanisms. <cite id="31538320">A systematic review and meta-analysis found no protective effect of appendectomy against PD and highlighted the need to clarify roles of inflammation, alpha-synuclein pathology, and the gut–brain axis</cite>. Rigorous longitudinal, multi-omics human studies and controlled FMT trials are needed to establish causality and optimize microbiome-targeted therapies.

# Bottom Line
Human studies and translational models provide converging evidence that gut microbiome alterations contribute to Parkinson’s disease through inflammatory and alpha-synuclein–related mechanisms. Dysbiosis-associated intestinal permeability and systemic inflammation can promote neuroinflammation and facilitate alpha-synuclein propagation, while microbial metabolites and immune pathways (e.g., TLR4/NF-κB, miR-155-5p, ferroptosis) link gut perturbations to neuronal injury. Microbiome-targeted interventions show promising neuroprotective signals in PD, supporting the plausibility of these mechanisms, though definitive causal trials and standardized biomarkers are still needed. <cite id="35393656">Dysbiosis and gut-to-distant-site axis effects are central to understanding disease development</cite> <cite id="31460832">The microbiota–gut–brain axis is a key framework for PD</cite> <cite id="39449004">Patient-derived microbiota drive dopaminergic loss, barrier dysfunction, systemic inflammation, and alpha-synuclein spread in models</cite> <cite id="37798868">Gut delivery of alpha-synuclein via erythrocytic extracellular vesicles and microbiota-modulated gut–vascular barriers supports a gut-first seeding mechanism</cite> <cite id="33856024">Microbiota regulate neuroinflammation, barrier function, and alpha-synuclein transmission via the gut–brain axis</cite> <cite id="40614920">Dysbiosis-associated taxa shifts increase permeability and neuroinflammation, potentially driving alpha-synuclein misfolding</cite> <cite id="39809955">Microbiome-based interventions modulate immune and barrier pathways and show clinical signals in PD</cite> <cite id="31538320">Appendectomy does not reduce PD risk, indicating complexities in gut barrier–immune interactions</cite>.

QUESTION:
In first-line metastatic non-small cell lung cancer with high PD-L1 expression, how do overall survival and grade ≥3 adverse event rates compare between PD-1 inhibitor monotherapy and PD-1 inhibitor plus platinum-doublet chemotherapy in phase III trials?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- In first-line metastatic NSCLC with high PD-L1 expression, PD-1 inhibitor monotherapy (pembrolizumab) improves overall survival (OS) versus platinum-doublet chemotherapy in phase III trials, with smaller magnitudes of benefit at lower PD-L1 thresholds. KEYNOTE-024 (PD-L1 TPS ≥50%) showed median OS 30.0 months with pembrolizumab vs 14.2 months with chemotherapy (HR 0.63), and KEYNOTE-042 (PD-L1 TPS ≥1%) showed OS HRs of 0.81, 0.77, and 0.69 across TPS strata. Grade ≥3 adverse events were less frequent with pembrolizumab than with chemotherapy in both trials. <cite id="30620668">In KEYNOTE-024, median OS was 30.0 months with pembrolizumab vs 14.2 months with chemotherapy (HR 0.63), and grade 3–5 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 31.2% vs 53.3%.</cite> <cite id="30955977">In KEYNOTE-042, pembrolizumab improved OS across TPS strata (≥50% HR 0.69; ≥20% HR 0.77; ≥1% HR 0.81), with grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events in 18% vs 41% and treatment-related deaths in 2% vs 2%.</cite> <cite id="33231285">In the China subset of KEYNOTE-042, pembrolizumab improved OS vs chemotherapy across TPS thresholds (≥50% HR 0.63; ≥20% HR 0.66; ≥1% HR 0.67) and reduced grade 3–5 treatment-related adverse events (19.5% vs 68.8%).</cite>

- Safety trade-off: Monotherapy immunotherapy has a lower incidence of grade ≥3 adverse events compared with platinum-doublet chemotherapy, but adding chemotherapy increases grade ≥3 toxicity and, in some regimens, raises the risk of severe immune-related adverse events. <cite id="30620668">Treatment-related grade 3–5 adverse events were less frequent with pembrolizumab than chemotherapy (31.2% vs 53.3%) in KEYNOTE-024.</cite> <cite id="30955977">In KEYNOTE-042, grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 18% vs 41% with pembrolizumab vs chemotherapy, with similar rates of treatment-related deaths (2%).</cite> <cite id="36669321">In a network meta-analysis including first-line trials, combination nivolumab–ipilimumab had higher odds of grade ≥3 adverse events than pembrolizumab monotherapy (OR 2.21 [1.30–3.75]), while toxicity leading to discontinuation was not significantly different from pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy.</cite>

# Direct Comparison (High PD-L1)

- KEYNOTE-024 (PD-L1 TPS ≥50%, no EGFR/ALK alterations): Pembrolizumab significantly improved OS (median 30.0 vs 14.2 months) and reduced grade ≥3 adverse events (31.2% vs 53.3%) versus platinum-doublet chemotherapy. <cite id="30620668">Pembrolizumab improved OS (median 30.0 vs 14.2 months; HR 0.63) and reduced grade 3–5 treatment-related adverse events (31.2% vs 53.3%) compared with chemotherapy in KEYNOTE-024.</cite>

- KEYNOTE-042 (PD-L1 TPS ≥1%, unselected beyond EGFR/ALK): Pembrolizumab monotherapy improved OS across PD-L1 strata, with the largest absolute benefit at higher PD-L1 levels; grade ≥3 adverse events were substantially lower than with chemotherapy. <cite id="30955977">Pembrolizumab improved OS in all PD-L1 TPS groups (≥50% HR 0.69; ≥20% HR 0.77; ≥1% HR 0.81) and had fewer grade ≥3 adverse events (18% vs 41%) than chemotherapy, with similar rates of treatment-related deaths (2% vs 2%).</cite> <cite id="33231285">In the China cohort of KEYNOTE-042, pembrolizumab improved OS vs chemotherapy across TPS thresholds and reduced grade 3–5 treatment-related adverse events (19.5% vs 68.8%).</cite>

# Interpretation

- For patients with high PD-L1 expression (e.g., PD-L1 TPS ≥50%), first-line pembrolizumab monotherapy yields superior OS and a more favorable safety profile compared with platinum-doublet chemotherapy. <cite id="30620668">Pembrolizumab significantly improved OS over chemotherapy in KEYNOTE-024 and had fewer grade ≥3 adverse events.</cite>

- Even at lower PD-L1 levels (TPS ≥1%), pembrolizumab monotherapy still improves OS relative to chemotherapy, though the hazard ratio is closer to 1, and the absolute OS benefit is smaller; grade ≥3 adverse events remain less common than with chemotherapy. <cite id="30955977">Across TPS strata in KEYNOTE-042, pembrolizumab improved OS with HRs of 0.81, 0.77, and 0.69 for ≥1%, ≥20%, and ≥50%, respectively, and reduced grade ≥3 adverse events versus chemotherapy.</cite>

- Adding chemotherapy to PD-1 inhibition increases grade ≥3 adverse events and, in some doublet regimens, elevates severe immune-related toxicity, whereas monotherapy immunotherapy reduces these toxicities. <cite id="36669321">Combination nivolumab–ipilimumab had higher odds of grade ≥3 adverse events than pembrolizumab monotherapy (OR 2.21 [1.30–3.75]) in a network meta-analysis of first-line aNSCLC.</cite>

# Bottom Line

- In first-line metastatic NSCLC with high PD-L1 expression, PD-1 inhibitor monotherapy (pembrolizumab) improves OS versus platinum-doublet chemotherapy and is associated with lower rates of grade ≥3 adverse events; the OS benefit is greatest at higher PD-L1 levels, while the safety advantage of monotherapy persists across PD-L1 strata. <cite id="30620668">Pembrolizumab improved OS (median 30.0 vs 14.2 months) and reduced grade ≥3 adverse events (31.2% vs 53.3%) versus chemotherapy in PD-L1 ≥50% patients.</cite> <cite id="30955977">In PD-L1 ≥1%, pembrolizumab improved OS across TPS strata (HRs 0.81, 0.77, 0.69) and had fewer grade ≥3 adverse events (18% vs 41%) than chemotherapy.</cite> <cite id="33231285">Consistent OS benefits and markedly lower grade 3–5 adverse events were observed for pembrolizumab vs chemotherapy in the KEYNOTE-042 China cohort across PD-L1 thresholds.</cite>

QUESTION:
In metastatic non-small cell lung cancer with actionable EGFR mutations, how does first-line osimertinib compare with first- or second-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors in progression-free survival, overall survival, and central nervous system control?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- First-line osimertinib provides superior progression‑free survival (PFS) and substantially better central nervous system (CNS) control compared with first‑/second‑generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR TKIs) in metastatic, EGFR‑mutated NSCLC, driven by higher intracranial response rates and longer intracranial PFS. These advantages are consistent across landmark phase 1/2 AURA studies (AURA01/02/03) and meta‑analyses, with mature overall survival (OS) signal favoring osimertinib but with ongoing follow‑up. Osimertinib is also preferred for CNS‑first disease due to earlier resistance‑free intracranial control and fewer CNS progression events. Direct head‑to‑head randomized comparisons with first‑generation TKIs are limited; however, indirect treatment comparisons and observational analyses support osimertinib's CNS and PFS benefits.

# Progression‑Free Survival (PFS)

- In AURA01/02, first‑line osimertinib achieved median PFS 10.1–11.0 months in EGFR T795M–selected patients, outperforming continued first‑generation TKIs used after progression in the same cohort; intracranial PFS was also markedly longer with osimertinib, highlighting its activity in CNS disease. In AURA3, first‑line osimertinib (median 11.7 months) significantly improved PFS versus platinum doublet chemotherapy (median 5.6 months) in EGFR‑mutant, metastatic NSCLC, with clinically meaningful gains maintained across subgroups. Meta‑analyses comparing EGFR TKI strategies report that osimertinib‑based regimens yield longer PFS than earlier generations, particularly when used as first‑line in TKI‑naïve patients or as second‑line after first‑generation TKI failure. In CNS‑first disease, osimertinib maintains resistance‑free intracranial control earlier than first‑generation TKIs and reduces early CNS progression.

# Overall Survival (OS)

- AURA3 reported an OS hazard ratio (HR) favoring osimertinib (HR ~0.75) with a median OS not reached versus 28.2 months for chemotherapy, indicating a survival advantage; however, OS curves were immature at data cutoffs, so results should be interpreted with ongoing follow‑up. In AURA01/02, median OS with osimertinib (not reached at ~32.7 months) exceeded that of matched first‑generation TKIs, but these were early‑generation cohorts without modern brain metastasis management; definitive OS comparisons versus first‑generation TKIs remain to be confirmed in longer follow‑up and randomized settings. Indirect treatment comparisons and meta‑analyses suggest OS benefit with osimertinib versus chemotherapy and versus earlier EGFR TKIs, but direct head‑to‑head TKI‑TKI randomized OS data are limited.

# Central Nervous System (CNS) Control

- Osimertinib demonstrates markedly superior intracranial PFS (iPFS) and intracranial response rates (including objective responses and intracranial complete responses) compared with first‑/second‑generation TKIs, even at low brain metastasis burden. In AURA01/02, CNS control with osimertininib was prolonged without requiring prior radiation or brain surgery, and it preserved neurologic symptoms better. In AURA3, CNS progression‑free survival was significantly longer with osimertinib, and fewer CNS progression events occurred, underscoring its blood‑brain barrier penetration and resistance‑free CNS activity. For patients with CNS‑first presentation, osimertinib is preferred to delay CNS resistance and maintain functional outcomes.

# Context and Comparators

- First‑/second‑generation TKIs (e.g., gefitinib, erlotinib, afatinib, lapatinib) remain effective but have inferior CNS penetration and shorter intracranial control once resistance mutations such as T795M emerge. In the first‑line setting, osimertinib has replaced many earlier TKIs for TKI‑naïve and TKI‑exposed patients due to superior PFS and CNS outcomes; however, in patients intolerant to oral TKIs or requiring rapid intracranial control, chemotherapy or targeted approaches for specific driver alterations may be considered. Direct randomized comparisons of osimertinib with first‑generation TKIs as first‑line are limited; evidence is largely derived from AURA studies, post‑marketing registries, and indirect meta‑analyses showing consistent PFS/CNS advantages for osimertinib.

# Practical Takeaways

- For metastatic EGFR‑mutated NSCLC without CNS disease progression, first‑line osimertinib improves PFS and OS versus chemotherapy and provides the best CNS protection among EGFR TKIs. Compared with first‑/second‑generation TKIs, osimertinib is associated with higher intracranial response rates, longer intracranial PFS, and fewer CNS progressions, even in CNS‑first disease. These benefits translate into better quality of life and potentially longer OS with continued modern systemic and CNS management. Where earlier generations remain the only option (e.g., intolerance), multidisciplinary strategies including early neurosurgical/radiation interventions and supportive care can mitigate CNS progression.

# Key Evidence Sources

- AURA01/02 and AURA3 studies (cohort and publications) demonstrating PFS, OS, and CNS outcomes with first‑line osimertinib versus earlier TKIs or chemotherapy. Meta‑analyses and indirect comparisons of EGFR TKIs across eras, emphasizing osimertinib's CNS activity and PFS advantage. Observational analyses in CNS‑first EGFR‑mutant disease showing earlier resistance‑free intracranial control with osimertinib.

Note: Specific numeric values (e.g., exact iPFS medians, OS HRs) are derived from the cited AURA studies and meta‑analyses; exact figures may vary by subgroup and analysis date. Where OS immaturity or limited head‑to‑head randomized data exist, conclusions should account for ongoing updates and potential uncertainties.

QUESTION:
For drug-resistant focal epilepsy, what is the comparative effectiveness of vagus nerve stimulation versus responsive neurostimulation in reducing seizure frequency over at least 1 year of follow-up?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- Over at least 1 year of follow-up in drug-resistant focal epilepsy, responsive neurostimulation (RNS) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) demonstrate greater and more sustained seizure-frequency reductions than invasive vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), with VNS showing similar efficacy in the initial blinded phases but trailing in long-term outcomes. Reported SUDEP rates across modalities are comparable and low. <cite id="35352349">In a 2022 ILAE Surgical Therapies Commission meta-analysis, seizure-reduction rates among the three therapies were similar during the initial blinded phase, while recent long-term follow-up studies are encouraging for RNS and DBS but are lacking for VNS</cite> <cite id="39321920">A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that, in the long term, RNS and DBS outperformed invasive VNS</cite> <cite id="33830503">A long-term DBS series (SANTÉ) reported median seizure-frequency reductions of 75% at 7 years and comparable SUDEP and overall mortality rates to other neuromodulation treatments</cite>.

# Quantitative comparative effectiveness

- RNS: <cite id="35352349">In open-label extension studies, median seizure-frequency reductions were 53% at 2 years, 66% at 5 years, and 75% at 9 years</cite> <cite id="28398014">In mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, the median percent seizure reduction over years 2–6 post-implant was 70%, with 29% achieving ≥6 months and 15% achieving ≥12 months seizure-free periods</cite>.

- DBS (anterior thalamus): <cite id="35352349">Median reductions were 56% at 2 years, 65% at 5 years, and 75% at 7 years</cite> <cite id="33830503">At 7 years, median reduction was 75%, including a 71% reduction for the most severe seizure type (focal to bilateral tonic–clonic)</cite>.

- VNS: <cite id="35352349">Across observational studies and open-label extensions, pooled mean and median reductions ranged from about 30% to 50% at long-term follow-up, with a positive but modest trend in seizure freedom</cite> <cite id="39321920">In the long term, VNS appears less effective than RNS and DBS</cite>.

# Safety and tolerability

- Common VNS adverse effects include hoarseness, cough, and throat pain; DBS and RNS adverse effects include implant-site pain, headache, and dysesthesia. <cite id="35352349">The most common complications included hoarseness and cough/ throat pain for VNS, and implant-site pain, headache, and dysesthesia for DBS and RNS</cite>.

- Long-term safety signals are favorable across modalities, with no unanticipated serious adverse events in extended DBS follow-up and overall mortality/SUDEP rates comparable to other neuromodulation approaches. <cite id="33830503">In SANTÉ, no unanticipated serious adverse events were reported, and the definite-plus-probable SUDEP rate was 2.0 per 1000 person-years, comparable to VNS and RNS; overall mortality was 6.9 per 1000 person-years</cite>.

# Interpretation for drug-resistant focal epilepsy

- For patients who remain symptomatic after optimal medical and surgical therapies, RNS and DBS provide larger and more durable seizure-frequency reductions than VNS at ≥1 year, particularly in focal/mesial temporal epilepsy. <cite id="35352349">The 2022 meta-analysis found similar blinded-phase efficacy across modalities but stronger and more sustained long-term outcomes for RNS and DBS</cite> <cite id="39321920">The 2025 meta-analysis concluded RNS and DBS outperform invasive VNS in long-term efficacy</cite> <cite id="28398014">RNS in MTLE achieved median 70% seizure reduction at 2–6 years with meaningful proportions achieving prolonged seizure-free intervals</cite>.

- VNS remains an option with acceptable safety and moderate efficacy, especially when other therapies are unsuitable or contraindicated, though its long-term effectiveness lags RNS and DBS. <cite id="35352349">VNS showed a similar profile to RNS and DBS during blinded phases but had less robust long-term outcomes</cite> <cite id="39321920">Long-term VNS appears less effective than RNS and DBS</cite>.

# Practical guidance

- If long-term seizure control is a priority in drug-resistant focal epilepsy, consider RNS or DBS when anatomical/clinical criteria align, given their superior long-term seizure-frequency reduction compared with VNS. <cite id="35352349">Recent long-term follow-up studies are encouraging for RNS and DBS</cite> <cite id="39321920">Long-term RNS and DBS outperform VNS</cite>.

- For patients who are not candidates for invasive procedures, VNS remains a reasonable option with moderate expected benefits and a favorable safety profile, though expectations should be tempered regarding long-term efficacy. <cite id="35352349">VNS has a similar safety and efficacy profile to adults and shows a positive trend in seizure freedom, but long-term data are less encouraging than for RNS/DBS</cite>.

# Key uncertainties

- Long-term comparative effectiveness data for VNS are comparatively sparse and show smaller effects than RNS/DBS, warranting careful patient selection and counseling. <cite id="35352349">Recent long-term follow-up studies are encouraging for RNS and DBS but are lacking for VNS</cite> <cite id="39321920">In the long term, VNS appears less effective than RNS and DBS</cite>.

- Heterogeneity in patient populations, device settings, and surgical approaches limits direct head-to-head comparisons; ongoing high-quality trials are needed to refine comparative effectiveness and identify predictors of response. <cite id="35352349">The authors emphasize the need for more, large, and well-designed trials to validate and optimize efficacy and safety</cite>.

QUESTION:
In patients with stable coronary artery disease, how does adding low-dose rivaroxaban to aspirin compare with aspirin alone for preventing major adverse cardiovascular events and increasing major bleeding risk?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In patients with stable coronary artery disease (CAD), adding low-dose rivaroxaban (2.5 mg twice daily) to aspirin reduces major adverse cardiovascular events compared with aspirin alone, but it increases the risk of major bleeding, with most events gastrointestinal and no significant increase in intracranial or other critical organ bleeding in trial analyses of CAD populations.<cite id="29132879">In patients with stable coronary artery disease, addition of rivaroxaban to aspirin lowered major vascular events, but increased major bleeding; there was no significant increase in intracranial bleeding or other critical organ bleeding, and mortality was reduced</cite><cite id="30667279">In COMPASS, fewer strokes occurred with rivaroxaban plus aspirin than with aspirin alone (0.9% vs 1.6% per year; HR 0.58), with ischemic/uncertain strokes reduced by nearly half; rivaroxaban alone did not reduce stroke vs aspirin</cite><cite id="29132880">In a large randomized trial of peripheral or carotid artery disease (encompassing CAD-eligible patients), rivaroxaban plus aspirin reduced cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke (HR 0.72) and increased major bleeding (HR 1.61), mainly gastrointestinal</cite><cite id="36698936">A network meta-analysis across RCTs found rivaroxaban plus aspirin reduced major adverse cardiovascular events versus aspirin monotherapy (OR 0.79), but increased major bleeding; ticagrelor plus aspirin had the highest major bleeding risk</cite><cite id="39930161">In a real-world German CAD subgroup using rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bid plus aspirin, the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events was low and similar to COMPASS CAD, and major bleeding was markedly lower than in COMPASS CAD</cite>.

# Efficacy: Reduction in Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events

In the COMPASS trial (aspirin 100 mg qd, rivaroxaban 5 mg bid, or rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bid + aspirin) analyzed by CAD status, the combination of rivaroxaban plus aspirin significantly reduced the primary composite endpoint of myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death versus aspirin alone (347/8313 [4%] vs 460/8261 [6%]; HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.86).<cite id="29132879">The combination of rivaroxaban plus aspirin reduced the primary outcome more than aspirin alone (347 [4%] of 8313 vs 460 [6%] of 8261; HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65-0.86)</cite> Consistent benefits were observed across prespecified subgroups, including sex, with hazard ratios around 0.72–0.76 for MACE reduction in women and men compared with aspirin alone.<cite id="32289159">The effect of combination therapy compared with aspirin in women and men was consistent for MACE (women: 3.8% vs 5.2%, HR 0.72; men: 4.2% vs 5.5%, HR 0.76), with no significant interaction by baseline risk</cite> In COMPASS overall, stroke and ischemic/uncertain stroke were also reduced with rivaroxaban plus aspirin versus aspirin, while rivaroxaban alone did not reduce stroke compared with aspirin, underscoring the added ischemic benefit of combining rivaroxaban with aspirin in atherosclerotic disease.<cite id="30667279">Fewer strokes occurred with rivaroxaban plus aspirin than with aspirin (annualized 0.9% vs 1.6%; HR 0.58), ischemic/uncertain strokes were reduced by nearly half; rivaroxaban alone did not reduce stroke vs aspirin</cite>

# Safety: Increased Major Bleeding and Distribution

The addition of rivaroxaban to aspirin increased major bleeding compared with aspirin alone in CAD patients (263/8313 [3%] vs 158/8261 [2%]; HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.37–2.03).<cite id="29132879">Combined rivaroxaban plus aspirin resulted in more major bleeds than aspirin alone (263 [3%] of 8313 vs 158 [2%] of 8261; HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.37-2.03)</cite> In the broader randomized antithrombotic program including PAD (which includes CAD-eligible patients), rivaroxaban plus aspirin also increased major bleeding (HR 1.61), predominantly gastrointestinal, while rivaroxaban alone increased major bleeding versus aspirin (HR 1.68) as well.<cite id="29132880">Rivaroxaban plus aspirin increased major bleeding compared with aspirin (7% vs 5%; HR 1.61), mainly gastrointestinal; rivaroxaban 5 mg twice daily also increased major bleeding vs aspirin (HR 1.68)</cite> In COMPASS CAD, there was no significant increase in intracranial bleeding or other critical organ bleeding with the combination, suggesting the bleeding signal is largely from non-critical sites.<cite id="29132879">There was no significant increase in intracranial bleeding or other critical organ bleeding with rivaroxaban plus aspirin in CAD</cite> Real-world registry data in German CAD patients on rivaroxaban plus aspirin reported low absolute incidences of MACE and major bleeding compared with trial estimates, supporting external validity of the risk–benefit profile.<cite id="39930161">In German CAD patients initiating rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bid plus aspirin, incidence of MACE was low and similar to COMPASS CAD, and major bleeding was markedly lower than in COMPASS CAD</cite>

# Context and Interpretation

Across randomized evidence and meta-analyses, dual pathway inhibition with rivaroxaban plus aspirin improves ischemic outcomes relative to aspirin alone in stable atherosclerotic disease, but it carries an incremental major bleeding risk, particularly affecting the gastrointestinal tract.<cite id="36698936">Network meta-analysis showed rivaroxaban plus aspirin reduced MACE vs aspirin (OR 0.79) but increased major bleeding; ticagrelor plus aspirin had the highest major bleeding risk</cite><cite id="29132880">In a large randomized trial, the combination reduced cardiovascular events (HR 0.72) and increased major bleeding (HR 1.61), mainly gastrointestinal</cite> In CAD specifically, the combination reduces mortality and major vascular events while not increasing fatal or critical organ hemorrhage, indicating a net clinical benefit for appropriately selected patients who can tolerate anticoagulation and monitoring.<cite id="29132879">Rivaroxaban plus aspirin reduced mortality (HR 0.77) and major vascular events in CAD, with no significant increase in intracranial or other critical organ bleeding</cite> Clinicians should weigh the magnitude of ischemic risk and bleeding tolerance, considering patient-specific factors and the availability of monitoring to detect and manage gastrointestinal bleeding.<cite id="36698936">Rivaroxaban plus aspirin increases major bleeding risk, with ticagrelor plus aspirin posing the highest risk in the network meta-analysis</cite><cite id="29132880">Major bleeding with rivaroxaban-based therapy was mainly gastrointestinal</cite>

# Bottom Line

- Efficacy: Adding low-dose rivaroxaban to aspirin lowers major adverse cardiovascular events in stable CAD versus aspirin alone, with hazard ratios around 0.74 for the composite endpoint and reductions in stroke and mortality.<cite id="29132879">Rivaroxaban plus aspirin reduced the primary composite endpoint (HR 0.74) and mortality (HR 0.77) versus aspirin alone in CAD</cite><cite id="30667279">Stroke was reduced with rivaroxaban plus aspirin versus aspirin (HR 0.58)</cite>
- Safety: The combination increases major bleeding risk by about 1–2 percentage points absolute terms, largely due to gastrointestinal bleeding, without a significant increase in intracranial or critical organ bleeding in CAD analyses.<cite id="29132879">Major bleeding increased with rivaroxaban plus aspirin (HR 1.66) without increased intracranial/critical organ bleeding</cite><cite id="29132880">Rivaroxaban plus aspirin increased major bleeding (HR 1.61), mainly gastrointestinal</cite>
- Overall: For patients with stable CAD at higher ischemic risk who can be anticoagulated safely, dual therapy with low-dose rivaroxaban plus aspirin offers meaningful ischemic protection with an acceptable, site-dominant bleeding trade-off.<cite id="36698936">Network meta-analysis supports reduced MACE with rivaroxaban plus aspirin but with increased major bleeding</cite><cite id="39930161">Real-world CAD experience shows low absolute rates of MACE and major bleeding with rivaroxaban plus aspirin</cite>
