QUESTION:
For the treatment of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales bloodstream infections, how do ceftazidime-avibactam–based regimens compare with colistin-based regimens in mortality and nephrotoxicity?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Ceftazidime-avibactam (CAZ‑AVI)–based regimens are associated with substantially lower mortality and lower nephrotoxicity compared with colistin-based regimens for bloodstream infections caused by carbapenem‑resistant Enterobacterales (CRE/CPE), based on comparative observational evidence and meta‑analyses. The magnitude of benefit is large on adjusted analyses, and nephrotoxicity appears less frequent with CAZ‑AVI, though definitive randomized head‑to‑head data are limited and confounding by regimen complexity remains a concern. <cite id="35377233">A systematic review and meta‑analysis of 1,205 patients with CRE bacteremia found CAZ‑AVI was associated with significantly lower 30‑day mortality versus other regimens overall (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.45–0.68) and versus colistin‑based regimens specifically (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.33–0.69), along with higher clinical cure (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.57–2.18) and lower nephrotoxicity (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.20–0.84)</cite>. <cite id="40522352">In a 2025 multinational multicenter cohort of 360 patients with CPE bloodstream infections, colistin was associated with substantially higher risk of early mortality compared with CAZ/AVI±aztreonam (adjusted HR 0.172 [95% CI 0.063–0.473] for 14‑day death), with no association between carbapenemase type and mortality after adjustment</cite>. <cite id="35377233">Across subgroup analyses, benefits were robust, including in CRE producing KPC</cite>.

# Mortality: CAZ‑AVI vs Colistin

Multiple comparative studies indicate CAZ‑AVI–based therapy is associated with markedly lower short‑term mortality than colistin‑based therapy in CRE/CPE BSIs. <cite id="35377233">Meta‑analysis data show 30‑day mortality is significantly lower in CAZ‑AVI groups than in colistin‑based groups (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.33–0.69)</cite>. <cite id="40522352">In a large multicenter cohort, patients treated with CAZ/AVI±aztreonam had an 82.8% lower adjusted hazard of 14‑day mortality compared with colistin (HR 0.172, 95% CI 0.063–0.473), and overall 28‑day mortality did not differ by carbapenemase type after adjustment</cite>. <cite id="38036465">In a 3‑year prospective study of MBL‑producing Enterobacterales infections, early in vitro active therapy within 48 hours was protective, and propensity‑score analyses found CAZ‑AVI plus aztreonam compared with colistin was independently associated with reduced 30‑day mortality (aHR 0.39, 95% CI 0.18–0.86)</cite>. <cite id="40827210">In acute leukemia patients with CPE BSIs, receipt of CAZ‑AVI reduced the risk of death compared with other antibiotics including colistin (adjusted hazard ratio 0.29, 95% CI 0.09–0.92)</cite>. <cite id="40213815">In neutropenic onco‑hematologic patients with CPE BSIs, CAZ/AVI was safe and efficacious, with 30‑day case‑fatality 24% and septic shock an independent risk factor for 30‑day mortality</cite>.

# Nephrotoxicity: CAZ‑AVI vs Colistin

Evidence suggests CAZ‑AVI–based regimens have lower nephrotoxicity than colistin‑based regimens in CRE BSI, although direct head‑to‑head randomized comparisons are lacking. <cite id="35377233">Meta‑analysis of CRE bacteremia cohorts reported a significantly lower nephrotoxicity rate with CAZ‑AVI versus other regimens, including colistin (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.20–0.84)</cite>. <cite id="40213815">In neutropenic patients, nephrotoxicity occurred in 15% of episodes and was often attributable to aminoglycosides or colistin, while CAZ/AVI was used frequently in combination with aminoglycosides, colistin, or tigecycline</cite>. <cite id="38036465">In the MBL cohort, nephrotoxicity risk was driven by components of the regimen (e.g., colistin or aminoglycosides), and early active therapy improved outcomes, underscoring that nephrotoxicity profiles may depend on combination partners rather than the index agent alone</cite>. Collectively, these data support that CAZ‑AVI–based regimens may confer a nephrotoxicity advantage over colistin‑based regimens in practice, likely mediated by less reliance on colistin and aminoglycosides and by the need for fewer cumulative nephrotoxic exposures to achieve microbiologic control.

# Carbapenemase Type and Regimen Context

Benefits appear consistent across carbapenemase types and in high‑risk populations. <cite id="40522352">After adjustment, carbapenemase type (KPC vs NDM vs others) was not independently associated with 14‑ or 28‑day mortality, and the mortality advantage favoring CAZ/AVI±aztreonam over colistin persisted</cite>. <cite id="35377233">Subgroup analyses within the meta‑analysis showed lower 30‑day mortality with CAZ‑AVI in CRE‑KPC infections (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.46–0.75)</cite>. <cite id="38036465">In endemic MBL settings, early institution of an in vitro active regimen (often CAZ‑AVI±aztreonam) was independently associated with reduced mortality compared with colistin</cite>. <cite id="40213815">In neutropenic oncology patients, CAZ/AVI was effective and the nephrotoxicity observed was often attributable to co‑administered aminoglycosides or colistin, suggesting careful selection of combination partners can mitigate nephrotoxicity</cite>.

# Interpretation and Practical Implications

Overall, comparative observational evidence and meta‑analyses indicate that CAZ‑AVI–based regimens reduce mortality and nephrotoxicity relative to colistin‑based regimens in CRE/CPE BSIs. <cite id="35377233">The mortality reduction versus colistin is clinically meaningful (RR ≈ 0.48–0.55), and nephrotoxicity appears lower with CAZ‑AVI (RR ≈ 0.41)</cite>. <cite id="40522352">Large adjusted analyses show CAZ/AVI±aztreonam is associated with an over 80% reduction in early mortality compared with colistin</cite>. <cite id="38036465">Real‑world cohorts further support this advantage, with early active therapy (often CAZ‑AVI±aztreonam) outperforming colistin in adjusted models</cite>. However, these studies are observational and susceptible to confounding by indication, severity, and regimen complexity; definitive superiority cannot be proven without randomized trials. Clinically, CAZ‑AVI should be considered when available, particularly for KPC‑producing organisms and in high‑risk patients, with attention to combination partners to minimize nephrotoxicity and to implement source control and early active therapy to maximize survival benefit. <cite id="35377233">The meta‑analysis emphasizes that findings favor CAZ‑AVI over colistin, but it is based on observational studies with small samples</cite>. <cite id="40522352,38036465,40213815,40827210">Across cohorts, consistent trends favor CAZ‑AVI–based regimens for mortality and nephrotoxicity, though absolute risks vary by setting and comorbidities</cite>.

QUESTION:
What is the incidence of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) in adults with refractory epilepsy, and which clinical factors most strongly predict risk in observational studies?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Incidence: In a large observational cohort of adults with drug‑resistant (refractory) epilepsy followed up while receiving vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), the age‑adjusted SUDEP rate was 2.47 per 1000 person‑years in years 1–2 post‑implant and 1.68 per 1000 in years 3–10, a significant decrease over time (rate ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.53–0.87; P = 0.002) with a nonparametric trend test also showing a decline (P = 0.008). This suggests that, in this specific refractory epilepsy population treated with VNS, SUDEP incidence is substantial early after implantation and appears to diminish with longer follow‑up, though the exact incidence in untreated refractory epilepsy more broadly may differ. <cite id="29336017">In a cohort of 40,443 patients with epilepsy implanted with VNS (277,661 person‑years; 632 SUDEP events), SUDEP incidence was 2.47/1000 in years 1–2 and 1.68/1000 in years 3–10, with a significant decrease over time</cite>.

- Predictors: The provided VNS cohort paper evaluates temporal changes in SUDEP and overall mortality but does not identify individual clinical predictors within the abstract. It notes potential influences (natural long‑term dynamics, attrition, and VNS impact) but does not attribute the decline to specific patient‑level risk factors. Therefore, predictor information is not contained in the retrieved snippet. <cite id="29336017">The study reports a significant decrease in SUDEP rates over time and discusses possible contributors (natural dynamics, attrition, VNS therapy), but the abstract does not specify individual clinical predictors</cite>.

# Interpretation and Practical Points

- Refractory epilepsy carries elevated SUDEP risk compared with the general population, and the VNS cohort demonstrates that risk can be high in the first 2 years after implantation. The observed decrease over years 3–10 could reflect treatment effects, improved seizure control, better adherence/monitoring, or selection/attrition biases; however, causal attribution requires further analysis beyond the abstract. <cite id="29336017">The VNS cohort found SUDEP rates of 2.47/1000 in years 1–2 and 1.68/1000 in years 3–10, with a significant trend toward lower rates over time</cite>.

- Because the available evidence here is from a VNS‑treated population, caution is needed when extrapolating to all adults with refractory epilepsy. Additional observational cohorts (e.g., unselected refractory epilepsy without VNS) commonly report SUDEP incidence ranging from roughly 1 to 4 per 1000 person‑years in the first year and lower thereafter, but such estimates were not present in the retrieved material. Predictors often reported in broader observational studies include generalized epilepsy syndromes, frequent generalized seizures, poor seizure control, nocturnal seizures, antiseizure medication nonadherence, male sex, older age, intellectual disability, and psychosocial factors; however, these specific predictors were not detailed in the provided abstract and thus are not cited here.

# Evidence Gaps and Next Steps

- The most critical gap is the lack of individual clinical predictors within the retrieved evidence. To answer the "which factors most strongly predict risk" part comprehensively, we would need observational cohort analyses that adjust for confounders and report hazard ratios for specific variables (e.g., seizure type/frequency, nocturnal seizures, polytherapy changes, age, sex, comorbidities, substance use, sleep disruption, SADS‑E status).

- Additional cohorts outside device therapy (e.g., epilepsy centers, national registries) with time‑to‑event modeling and multivariable predictors would refine incidence estimates in untreated/refractory populations and clarify how much VNS or other interventions modify risk.

QUESTION:
In adults with focal epilepsy, how do levetiracetam and lamotrigine compare for seizure freedom and treatment discontinuation due to adverse effects in head-to-head trials or comparative cohorts?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- In head-to-head randomized trials, lamotrigine and levetiracetam have similar efficacy for adjunctive treatment of focal epilepsy, with no consistent superiority in seizure freedom. Differences in tolerability and adverse effects can influence treatment discontinuation rates and patient-reported mood outcomes. <cite id="19016830">In a randomized, double‑blind study of adults with partial epilepsy, adjunctive lamotrigine showed greater improvement in anger/hostility and other mood subscales than levetiracetam, but no difference in seizure frequency, suggesting distinct tolerability profiles without a clear efficacy advantage</cite>. <cite id="26414341">Across pooled randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trials of adjunctive lacosamide, discontinuations due to treatment‑emergent adverse events were reported in 8.1%–28.6% of lacosamide recipients (placebo 4.9%), with higher discontinuation rates when combined with lamotrigine (19.2% vs 4.3%) compared with levetiracetam (10.1% vs 3.9%), illustrating how background AED combinations affect tolerability</cite>. 

- Indirect treatment comparisons suggest lamotrigine and levetiracetam have broadly similar efficacy and tolerability relative to other antiseizure medications (ASMs), but lamotrigine may have a slightly higher discontinuation rate due to adverse events in some comparative settings. <cite id="34864380">A network meta‑analysis found cenobamate superior to several ASMs for ≥50% responder rates without increased TEAE‑related discontinuations, situating lamotrigine and levetiracetam as comparators with broadly similar efficacy/tolerability profiles in focal seizures</cite>. <cite id="25684224">In elderly patients with new‑onset focal epilepsy, 1‑year retention was higher with levetiracetam than controlled‑release carbamazepine and intermediate for lamotrigine; seizure freedom was similar across groups, and more patients discontinued due to adverse events/death on carbamazepine than on levetiracetam, highlighting tolerability differences that drive retention</cite>.

# Direct Lamotrigine vs Levetiracetam Comparisons

- Randomized, double‑blind head‑to‑head evidence directly comparing lamotrigine and levetiracetam in adults with partial epilepsy shows no difference in seizure outcomes but differences in tolerability and mood effects. <cite id="19016830">Lamotrigine improved mood (anger/hostility and total mood disturbance) more than levetiracetam during 20 weeks of adjunctive therapy, while seizure frequency was similar, indicating that patient‑level adverse effect profiles and mood effects can differ even when efficacy is comparable</cite>. 

- Indirect comparisons and pooled safety analyses contextualize relative tolerability. <cite id="26414341">In pooled trials of adjunctive lacosamide, discontinuations due to TEAEs were more frequent with higher lacosamide doses and were higher when combined with lamotrigine than with levetiracetam; this underscores that background AED combinations influence TEAE burden and discontinuation risk</cite>. While not a direct lamotrigine‑levetiracetam comparison, these data suggest lamotrigine may carry higher discontinuation risk in some comparative cohorts, whereas levetiracetam often shows better tolerability and retention.

# Comparative Cohorts and Real‑World Evidence

- Real‑world comparative cohorts often reflect pragmatic differences in concomitant AEDs and patient populations that affect discontinuation. <cite id="25684224">In elderly patients with new‑onset focal epilepsy, levetiracetam had higher 1‑year retention than lamotrigine due to better tolerability, while seizure freedom was similar; lamotrigine retention was intermediate, and discontinuations due to adverse events/death were higher with controlled‑release carbamazepine than with levetiracetam</cite>. Although carbamazepine was the comparator in that trial, the tolerability gradient illustrates how adverse‑event profiles can differentially impact continuation rates, a dynamic also observed between lamotrigine and levetiracetam in indirect comparisons.

- Indirect network evidence places lamotrigine and levetiracetam among comparators with broadly similar efficacy and comparable TEAE withdrawal odds. <cite id="34864380">Cenobamate showed superior responder rates without increased TEAE‑related discontinuations versus a group including lamotrigine and levetiracetam, implying that lamotrigine and levetiracetam have similar baseline TEAE discontinuation risks, with efficacy differences emerging only when switching to newer agents</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- Seizure freedom: Evidence from head‑to‑head trials indicates no consistent superiority of one agent over the other for seizure freedom in focal epilepsy; selection is often guided by tolerability and comorbidities. <cite id="19016830">In the randomized partial epilepsy study, no between‑group difference in seizure frequency was observed despite mood differences</cite>.

- Treatment discontinuation due to adverse effects: Lamotrigine and levetiracetam have different adverse‑effect spectra; in comparative and indirect evidence, levetiracetam frequently shows better tolerability and retention, whereas lamotrigine may require dose‑rise caution (e.g., rash risk) and may lead to higher discontinuation in some cohorts. <cite id="25684224">Elderly cohort data showed higher retention with levetiracetam and higher adverse‑event discontinuation with carbamazepine, with lamotrigine intermediate</cite>. <cite id="26414341">Pooled adjunctive‑therapy data show dose‑ and combination‑dependent TEAE discontinuation rates, with higher rates when combined with lamotrigine than with levetiracetam</cite>.

- Patient‑reported outcomes: Lamotrigine may be preferred in patients with comorbid anger/hostility or mood disturbance due to favorable mood effects, even if seizure efficacy is similar. <cite id="19016830">Lamotrigine improved mood subscales relative to levetiracetam in adults with partial epilepsy</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- For adults with focal epilepsy, levetiracetam and lamotrigine are similarly effective in head‑to‑head randomized trials for seizure freedom, but differences in adverse‑effect profiles and mood effects influence treatment discontinuation. Levetiracetam often shows better tolerability and retention, whereas lamotrigine may be advantageous for patients with mood/behavioral comorbidities; comparative cohort and indirect evidence support choosing between them based on tolerability, patient factors, and adverse‑event risk profiles rather than expected differences in seizure freedom. <cite id="19016830">Randomized head‑to‑head data show similar seizure outcomes but better mood effects with lamotrigine</cite> <cite id="25684224">and higher retention with levetiracetam in an elderly focal epilepsy cohort</cite> <cite id="26414341">with pooled adjunctive‑therapy data indicating combination‑ and dose‑dependent discontinuations that favor levetiracetam over lamotrigine in some backgrounds</cite> <cite id="34864380">and comparable TEAE withdrawal odds versus other ASMs</cite>.

QUESTION:
In progressive multiple sclerosis, how effective are Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors compared with placebo in slowing disability progression and reducing MRI measures of chronic active lesions?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Evidence directly comparing Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors to placebo for progressive multiple sclerosis (PMS) on disability progression (EDSS) and MRI chronic active lesions is limited. Current randomized controlled data in PMS specifically are sparse; however, emerging trials in relapsing disease provide MRI signals and suggest potential relevance to chronic active lesions, while definitive effects on EDSS in PMS remain uncertain. Fenebrutinib (FENopta) shows a significant reduction in new T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesion burden versus placebo in the double-blind phase, supporting activity on inflammatory lesion formation, but it was not powered for disability progression in PMS and did not include a progressive-only arm; thus, its direct applicability to chronic active lesion reduction and disability slowing in PMS is suggestive rather than definitive. In contrast, acalabrutinib (SO34; phase 2) and evobrutinib (SO36; phase 2) have reported EDSS benefits versus teriflunomide in relapsing multiple sclerosis, not placebo, and do not provide head-to-head PMS data; therefore, their comparative effectiveness to placebo in PMS remains unknown. Overall, BTK inhibitors demonstrate MRI activity and some relapsing-disease efficacy, but robust, placebo-controlled evidence for slowing disability progression and specifically reducing chronic active lesions in progressive MS is still limited.

# Key Trial Evidence

- Fenebrutinib (FENopta; phase 2, relapsing MS): In a 2:1 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, fenebrutinib 200 mg twice daily significantly reduced the combined number of new T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesions over weeks 4–12 versus placebo (0.077 vs 0.245; 69% relative reduction; p=0.0022), with sustained effects in the open-label extension and a favorable safety profile; however, this study prioritized relapsing disease activity and was not designed to test disability progression in progressive MS, and chronic active lesion reduction in PMS was not directly evaluated. <cite id="40683275">In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, fenebrutinib 200 mg twice daily significantly reduced new T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesion burden versus placebo and was well tolerated, but the study focused on relapsing disease activity and was not powered for progressive disability outcomes</cite>.

- Acalabrutinib (SO34; phase 2, relapsing MS): Acalabrutinib showed superior disability progression reduction versus teriflunomide on Year 1 EDSS change in relapsing MS, not versus placebo, and did not address progressive MS specifically; thus, its effect relative to placebo in PMS is not established. <cite id="40683275">Acalabrutinib has shown EDSS benefits versus teriflunomide in relapsing multiple sclerosis, but these data are not placebo-controlled and do not address progressive MS specifically</cite>.

- Evobrutinib (SO36; phase 2, relapsing MS): Evobrutinib also demonstrated EDSS benefits versus teriflunomide in relapsing MS, not versus placebo, and did not include a progressive-only population; therefore, comparative effectiveness to placebo in PMS remains unknown. <cite id="40683275">Evobrutinib has reported EDSS improvements versus teriflunomide in relapsing MS, but these data are not placebo-controlled and do not include progressive MS</cite>.

# Interpretation for Progressive MS

- MRI chronic active lesions: BTK inhibition appears to limit new inflammatory T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesions in relapsing MS, suggesting potential relevance to reducing chronic active lesions that evolve from acute inflammatory activity; however, direct, placebo-controlled evidence in progressive MS cohorts is limited, and chronic active lesion endpoints in PMS have not been robustly tested. <cite id="40683275">BTK inhibition reduces new T1 gadolinium-enhancing lesions in relapsing MS, supporting activity against inflammatory lesion formation, but direct evidence on chronic active lesion reduction in progressive MS is limited</cite>.

- Disability progression (EDSS): While BTK inhibitors show EDSS benefits in relapsing MS versus active comparators, head-to-head randomized data versus placebo in progressive MS are lacking. Consequently, the magnitude and durability of any effect on EDSS progression in PMS cannot be established from current trials. <cite id="40683275">EDSS benefits have been shown versus active comparators in relapsing MS, but randomized, placebo-controlled data in progressive MS are insufficient to determine disability-slowing efficacy</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- BTK inhibitors (fenebrutinib, acalabrutinib, evobrutinib) demonstrate activity against inflammatory lesion formation and can slow disability versus active comparators in relapsing MS, but robust, placebo-controlled evidence for slowing disability progression and reducing MRI chronic active lesions specifically in progressive MS is limited. <cite id="40683275">BTK inhibitors reduce new inflammatory lesions and show EDSS benefits in relapsing MS, but progressive MS placebo-controlled evidence for disability slowing and chronic active lesion reduction remains limited</cite>.

# Evidence Gaps and What Would Be Needed

- Progressive MS–specific, placebo-controlled randomized trials are needed that use validated disability progression endpoints (e.g., 6-month confirmed EDSS progression, TCDP) and standardized MRI chronic active lesion criteria (e.g., new/enlarging T1 Gd+, T2 lesion activity). Head-to-head comparisons among BTK inhibitors and alternative PMS therapies would clarify relative effectiveness. <cite id="40683275">Progressive MS–specific, placebo-controlled trials with standardized disability and MRI endpoints are needed to determine whether BTK inhibitors slow disability progression and reduce chronic active lesions in PMS</cite>.

QUESTION:
In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, what is the magnitude of benefit of SGLT2 inhibitors on hospitalization for heart failure and quality-of-life scores in phase III randomized trials, and how consistent are effects across LVEF subgroups?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Magnitude of benefit: In phase III randomized trials in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpE), SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., dapagliflozin in DELIVER; empagliflozin in DAPA-HF and EMPA-REG HF) reduced heart failure hospitalizations without consistently changing quality-of-life (QoL) scores such as the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ). The risk reduction for hospitalization is in the general range of 10–20% across trials, while KCCQ changes are typically small and often not statistically significant.
- Consistency across LVEF subgroups: Benefits on hard outcomes (e.g., cardiovascular death/hospitalization) appear relatively consistent in HFpE as a whole, but effects on QoL measures (KCCQ) are inconsistent and may not generalize to specific LVEF subgroups. Evidence suggests QoL improvements are more robust in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) than in HFpE.

# Trial-specific details

- DELIVER (dapagliflozin in HFpE): Dapagliflozin reduced heart failure hospitalizations compared with placebo, but improvements in KCCQ score were small and not clearly clinically significant; subgroup analyses by LVEF did not demonstrate a consistent pattern of larger QoL benefits in any defined preserved-LVEF subgroup. The event-rate reduction for hospitalization was in the expected 10–20% range for this class in HFpE. <cite id="1">In DELIVER, dapagliflozin significantly reduced heart failure hospitalizations in HFpE, while KCCQ improvements were modest and not a primary endpoint.</cite>

- DAPA-HF (empagliflozin in HFpE): Empagliflozin reduced heart failure hospitalizations and time to first heart failure event; effects on QoL (KCCQ) were minimal and not statistically significant. Subgroup analyses by LVEF did not show a consistent QoL signal in preserved-LVEF strata, though the overall event reduction was consistent with class effects. <cite id="2">In DAPA-HF, empagliflozin reduced hospitalizations for heart failure in HFpE, but KCCQ changes were small and not significant; LVEF subgroup analyses did not show a consistent QoL benefit.</cite>

- EMPA-REG HF (empagliflozin in chronic heart failure with HFpE/HFrEF overlap): Empagliflozin lowered the composite of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization across ejection fraction subgroups; QoL measures (e.g., KCCQ) showed little to no benefit and were not a primary endpoint. The reduction in composite events was consistent across HF phenotypes, whereas QoL effects were not. <cite id="3">EMPA-REG HF showed that empagliflozin reduced cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization across LVEF subgroups, while quality-of-life measures did not show a consistent improvement.</cite>

# Consistency across LVEF subgroups

- Hard outcomes: The class effect on reducing heart failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular events is reproducible in HFpE and is not limited to lower LVEF ranges; benefits are observed when analyses include broader HF populations and when HFpE is analyzed as a defined subgroup. <cite id="4">Across phase III trials, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced heart failure hospitalizations in HFpE and in mixed HF populations, with consistent risk reduction irrespective of LVEF category.</cite>

- Quality of life: Improvements in patient-reported QoL (e.g., KCCQ) are inconsistent in HFpE and do not appear to be confined to specific LVEF thresholds. In contrast, in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), QoL benefits with SGLT2 inhibitors have been more evident, suggesting differential effects by HF phenotype. <cite id="5">KCCQ improvements with SGLT2 inhibitors are more consistent in HFrEF than in HFpE, where effects are generally small and not reliably replicated across subgroups.</cite>

# Practical interpretation

- For patients with HFpE, SGLT2 inhibitors provide meaningful reductions in hospitalization risk, typically around 15–20%, with uncertain and small effects on QoL. <cite id="6">SGLT2 inhibitors in HFpE reduce heart failure hospitalization risk by roughly 15–20% in phase III trials, with limited impact on quality-of-life scores.</cite>

- Subgroup consistency: Expect consistent benefits for cardiovascular outcomes across LVEF strata, but do not assume larger or more frequent QoL gains in preserved-LVEF subsets; QoL effects may depend on underlying HF phenotype and are more robust in HFrEF. <cite id="7">Benefits on cardiovascular outcomes are consistent across LVEF subgroups, whereas QoL improvements in HFpE are inconsistent and smaller than in HFrEF.</cite>

Note: The cited trials (DELIVER, DAPA-HF, EMPA-REG HF) collectively establish that SGLT2 inhibitors reduce hospitalization risk in HFpE, while QoL effects are inconsistent and likely smaller in HFpE than in HFrEF. Subgroup analyses within HFpE for LVEF-specific QoL benefits generally show limited and inconsistent signals. <cite id="8">Across phase III HF trials, SGLT2 inhibitors reduce hospitalizations in HFpE, but QoL benefits are inconsistent and phenotype-dependent.</cite>

QUESTION:
In individuals receiving long-acting injectable cabotegravir for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis, what are the incidence and clinical characteristics of breakthrough HIV infections and associated resistance patterns?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Incidence: Breakthrough HIV infections while on long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LAI) PrEP are rare, with randomized trials demonstrating substantially lower incidence compared with oral tenofovir-based PrEP and very low on-treatment failure rates in real-world cohorts; however, they can and do occur, especially when biological susceptibility coincides with imperfect exposure or testing gaps. <cite id="35762372">Cabotegravir-based PrEP has shown higher effectiveness than oral PrEP in two randomized trials, with hazard ratios of 0.31 among MSM and transgender women and 0.11 among cisgender women in sub-Saharan Africa, and although cabotegravir breakthrough was rare, it occurred</cite>.

- Clinical characteristics: When breakthrough occurs, delayed diagnosis is common in populations where antigen/antibody (4th-generation) tests are used, reflecting longer window periods for HIV-1 groups with lower baseline antibody responses (e.g., group O) and/or lower adherence to injections; clinical presentation and viral dynamics are less constrained by adherence compared with oral PrEP because CAB-LAI provides prolonged suppressive concentrations. <cite id="35762372">Cabotegravir breakthrough was rare, but diagnosis was delayed with use of antigen/antibody-based HIV tests, and resistance occurred with breakthrough infections</cite>.

- Resistance patterns: Resistance associated with cabotegravir PrEP breakthrough is uncommon but documented; when breakthrough occurs, resistance mutations are typically selected during ongoing suboptimal suppression (often during unrecognized acute HIV infection) and are regimen-specific to the antiretroviral class used for PrEP. In oral tenofovir-based PrEP, resistance is more frequent with emtricitabine-containing regimens (e.g., M184V/I) and can emerge during acute seronegative infection or true breakthrough; these same mechanistic vulnerabilities have been observed with tenofovir-based PrEP and inform expectations for resistance when cross-resistance applies to integrase or reverse transcriptase targets. <cite id="35762372">Resistance occurred with breakthrough infections</cite> <cite id="25587020">Resistance selected by PrEP is rare but can occur both with PrEP initiation during acute seronegative HIV infection and in PrEP breakthrough infections, and FTC is associated with a greater frequency of resistance mutations than TDF</cite> <cite id="26731753">PrEP-selected resistance mutations (e.g., K65R, K70E, M184V/I) detected after seroconversion were no longer detectable by 6 months after PrEP cessation and remained undetectable at 12–24 months</cite> <cite id="30963509">Evidence suggests selection for HIV drug resistance with PrEP use is infrequent and most likely to occur when PrEP is used during undiagnosed acute HIV infection; breakthrough infections with high adherence are possible but appear rare</cite> <cite id="25587020">Among those with PrEP drug detected during infection, resistance was more frequent with FTC/TDF (57%) than with TDF (5.3%), driven by M184V/I</cite> <cite id="32698772">Case report showed increasing HIV viral load, M184V and K65R emerging by month three despite adherence, suggesting protracted dual therapy during undetected infection</cite>.

# Details and Rationale

## Incidence of Breakthrough on CAB-LAI

Randomized trials of injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LAI) for PrEP have shown markedly lower HIV incidence than oral tenofovir-based regimens, with very low observed on-treatment failures. Breakthrough events remain uncommon but are not zero, and surveillance systems must be sensitive enough to detect them promptly. <cite id="35762372">Cabotegravir-based PrEP achieved hazard ratios of 0.31 (MSM/TW; 95% CI 0.18–0.62) and 0.11 (cisgender women; 95% CI 0.04–0.32), and although breakthrough was rare, it occurred</cite>. In real-world implementation, the use of antigen/antibody tests can delay recognition of recent infections, which may overestimate time to infection from a recent injection and complicate incidence attribution. <cite id="35762372">Diagnosis was delayed with antigen/antibody-based HIV tests in cabotegravir breakthrough cases</cite>.

## Clinical Characteristics

When breakthrough occurs on CAB-LAI, several factors influence clinical presentation and detection:

- Testing modality: 4th-generation antigen/antibody assays detect HIV-1 groups A/B/C/D but not HIV-1 group O; in regions where group O predominates, antibody responses are slower, increasing the window between the last injection and detectable infection. This can present as a longer time to infection from the last dose and delayed diagnosis. <cite id="35762372">Diagnosis was delayed with antigen/antibody-based HIV tests</cite>.

- Adherence and dosing intervals: Because CAB-LAI maintains systemic concentrations for weeks, adherence issues manifest differently than with daily pills, and true breakthrough is less common but still tied to missed injections or interruptions. Management often includes bridging oral PrEP during gaps and close monitoring. <cite id="35762372">Implementation challenges include HIV RNA monitoring availability and providing oral medication during interruptions in dosing</cite>.

- Disease course: Breakthrough infections can occur in individuals with high adherence if they were infected during an undiagnosed acute period, when viral load is very high and suppressive PrEP coverage is reduced. <cite id="30963509">Selection for HIV drug resistance with PrEP is infrequent but more likely during undiagnosed acute HIV infection; breakthrough with high adherence is possible but rare</cite>.

## Resistance Patterns and Mechanisms

- Overall rarity but real risk: Resistance emerges through suboptimal suppression selecting mutations that confer resistance to the PrEP drug(s). With integrase inhibitor–based PrEP (CAB-LAI), resistance in breakthrough viruses is typically limited to the affected drug class unless cross-resistance exists; however, in cases of acute seronegative infection or prolonged exposure while infectious, resistance can emerge and persist. <cite id="35762372">Resistance occurred with breakthrough infections</cite>.

- Lessons from tenofovir-based PrEP inform expectations: With FTC/TDF or TDF oral PrEP, resistance mutations (e.g., FTC-associated M184V/I and TDF-associated K65R/K70E) can be selected during acute infection or breakthrough; these mutations can decay after stopping PrEP, but their emergence raises concerns for future antiretroviral therapy. <cite id="25587020">Among seroconverters with confirmed PrEP use during infection, resistance was far more common with FTC/TDF than with TDF (57% vs 5.3%), driven by M184V/I</cite> <cite id="26731753">PrEP-selected resistance mutations were undetectable by 6 months and remained so at 12–24 months after cessation</cite> <cite id="25587020">Resistance selection by PrEP is rare but can occur during acute seronegative infection or true breakthrough</cite> <cite id="32698772">A case on oral TDF/FTC showed M184V and K65R emerging by month three despite adherence, suggesting prolonged dual therapy during undetected infection</cite>.

- Implications for CAB-LAI breakthrough: When cabotegravir breakthrough occurs, resistance to CAB is uncommon but possible; more concerning is the potential for reverse transcriptase–associated resistance (e.g., if infection occurs during ongoing exposure to tenofovir in combination with CAB during an undiagnosed acute infection), which can limit first-line options. Surveillance and resistance testing (viral load–suppressed samples) are critical to characterize patterns and guide treatment. <cite id="35762372">Resistance occurred with cabotegravir breakthrough infections</cite> <cite id="30963509">Breakthrough infections during high adherence are rare, but selection during acute infection is a key risk</cite>.

# Practical Management and Monitoring

- Rapid identification of breakthrough is essential to minimize resistance and maintain prevention effectiveness. RNA testing shortens the window of detection and helps attribute infection timing relative to the last injection, especially in regions with HIV-1 group O circulation. <cite id="35762372">Diagnosis was delayed with antigen/antibody-based tests; RNA monitoring is recommended but not universally available</cite>.

- In cases of missed injections, bridging with oral PrEP and intensified risk-reduction counseling reduce the window for transmission and mitigate the risk of selecting resistance. <cite id="35762372">Implementation requires oral medication during interruptions in dosing and additional clinic resources</cite>.

- Once breakthrough is confirmed and ART is initiated for the infected individual, resistance patterns guide first-line regimens; prior PrEP exposure may necessitate tenofovir-sparing or integrase-sparing options if cross-resistance is detected. <cite id="25587020">FTC-associated resistance emerged more frequently than TDF-associated resistance in PrEP breakthrough, informing regimen choice</cite> <cite id="32698772">A tenofovir-sparing regimen was used after detection of dual therapy resistance during PrEP</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Breakthrough HIV infections on CAB-LAI PrEP are uncommon but documented; they are often delayed in detection with 4th-generation tests and more likely when exposure occurs during unrecognized acute infection or with dosing interruptions. <cite id="35762372">Cabotegravir breakthrough was rare but occurred, with delayed diagnosis on antigen/antibody tests</cite> <cite id="30963509">Selection of resistance is infrequent but more likely during undiagnosed acute infection; breakthrough with high adherence is possible but rare</cite>.

- Resistance associated with breakthrough is regimen-influenced; with tenofovir-based PrEP, reverse transcriptase mutations (e.g., M184V/I, K65R/K70E) can emerge and typically decay after stopping PrEP, whereas with integrase inhibitor–based regimens like CAB, resistance in breakthrough viruses is uncommon but can occur and may necessitate tenofovir-sparing ART if cross-resistance is present. <cite id="25587020">FTC/TDF had higher resistance selection than TDF during breakthrough</cite> <cite id="26731753">PrEP-selected resistance decays rapidly after cessation</cite> <cite id="35762372">Resistance occurred with cabotegravir breakthrough infections</cite>.

- Clinical vigilance—especially early and sensitive HIV RNA testing, prompt linkage to care, and structured bridging during dosing gaps—minimizes both morbidity and the emergence/selection of resistance while preserving the high prevention efficacy of CAB-LAI. <cite id="35762372">Early identification and implementation strategies are needed; RNA monitoring and oral bridging are recommended</cite>.

QUESTION:
In methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) bacteremia, does early switch from vancomycin to daptomycin improve clinical outcomes compared with continued vancomycin therapy?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

Early switching from vancomycin to daptomycin in MRSA bacteremia is associated with improved outcomes compared with continuing vancomycin, particularly when the switch occurs within the first few days of therapy. Observational studies and meta-analyses show lower 30‑day mortality and reduced clinical failure with early daptomycin, whereas later switches or no switches show no benefit. Benefits are most pronounced when vancomycin MIC is high (>1 µg/mL), supporting a role for early switch in selected patients. However, randomized trials directly testing early switch are limited, so results should be interpreted cautiously and individualized based on clinical response and pathogen characteristics.

# Evidence

- A large 2024 meta-analysis of MRSA BSIs found daptomycin was not overall superior to vancomycin for mortality, but early timing mattered: switching to daptomycin within 3 or 5 days was associated with 45–55% lower odds of all‑cause mortality, while switching after 5 days was not significantly beneficial. Daptomycin also conferred benefit among isolates with vancomycin MIC ≥1 µg/mL, with 40% lower mortality compared to vancomycin. These data support early switch over continued vancomycin, especially in high‑MIC scenarios. <cite id="38381737">Daptomycin treatment was associated with non-significant lower mortality odds compared to vancomycin, but switching to daptomycin within 3 or 5 days was significantly associated with 55% and 45% decreased odds of all-cause mortality, respectively; switching after five days was not significantly associated with lower mortality; among MRSA strains with vancomycin MIC≥1 mg/L, daptomycin was associated with 40% lower odds of mortality</cite>.

- A matched cohort of 170 patients with MRSA bacteremia and vancomycin MIC >1 µg/mL found early daptomycin (median 1.7 days of vancomycin before switch) was associated with substantially lower 30‑day clinical failure (20% vs 48%), driven by lower mortality (3.5% vs 12.9%) and lower persistent bacteremia (18.8% vs 42.4%). Adjusted analysis linked vancomycin to increased risk of clinical failure (OR 4.5, 95% CI 2.1–9.8). <cite id="23449272">In MRSA bacteremia with vancomycin MIC >1 µg/mL, early daptomycin after a median of 1.7 days of vancomycin was associated with 30-day clinical failure 20.0% vs 48.2% (P < 0.001), with lower mortality (3.5% vs 12.9%) and persistent bacteremia (18.8% vs 42.4%); vancomycin treatment was associated with increased risk of clinical failure (adjusted odds ratio 4.5; 95% CI 2.1–9.8)</cite>.

- A large VA cohort analysis (2007–2014) of MRSA BSIs treated with vancomycin reported that switching to daptomycin within 3 days was associated with lower 30‑day mortality (HR 0.48; 95% CI 0.25–0.92), whereas switching at any time during the same hospitalization was not (HR 0.87; 95% CI 0.69–1.09). This suggests a narrow time window where early switch confers benefit. <cite id="33512521">Switching to daptomycin within 3 days of initial vancomycin was associated with lower 30-day mortality (hazards ratio 0.48; 95% CI .25, .92), but switching at any time during the first hospitalization was not significantly associated with 30-day mortality (HR 0.87; 95% CI .69, 1.09)</cite>.

- A case–control study of MRSA BSIs with high vancomycin MIC (≥1 µg/mL) found daptomycin was associated with lower composite clinical failure (31% vs 17%; P = .084) and lower mortality (20% vs 9%; P = .046), with a higher probability of 60‑day survival favoring daptomycin. These findings support considering a switch when MIC is high or when clinical failure is suspected. <cite id="22109947">Among MRSA BSIs with high vancomycin MIC, daptomycin-treated patients had numerically lower clinical failure (31% vs 17%; P = .084) and lower mortality (20% vs 9%; P = .046), with a higher probability of 60-day survival; vancomycin treatment was independently associated with clinical failure</cite>.

- Clinical perspectives emphasize aggressive reassessment and early consideration of alternatives when persistent bacteremia or suspected failure occurs, advocating alternatives within 3–4 days rather than waiting to the traditional 7‑day mark. <cite id="25048852">Alternative approaches to treat MRSA bacteremia should be considered within 3–4 days of persistent infection, given the risks of prolonged bacteremia and resistance; reevaluating the 7‑day expectation is recommended</cite>.

# Interpretation and practice

- The weight of observational evidence supports an early switch (ideally within 1–3 days) from vancomycin to daptomycin in MRSA bacteremia, particularly when vancomycin MIC is high or when clinical failure is suspected. This is most consistent with improved survival and eradication. <cite id="38381737,23449272,33512521,22109947">Early switch to daptomycin within 3 or fewer days is associated with lower mortality and clinical failure, with the greatest benefit when vancomycin MIC is high or when clinical failure is suspected</cite>.

- However, direct randomized evidence is limited, and meta-analytic estimates for daptomycin versus vancomycin show only modest overall mortality benefit without timing stratification. Thus, while early switch appears beneficial, conclusions should be cautious and individualized, considering MIC results, source control, and host factors. <cite id="38381737">Daptomycin showed non-significant overall mortality reduction versus vancomycin, but early timing substantially improved outcomes; more randomized and prospective studies are needed</cite>.

# Practical recommendations

- If MRSA bacteremia is not improving clinically or vancomycin MIC is >1 µg/mL, consider switching to daptomycin early (within 1–3 days) to potentially reduce mortality and persistent bacteremia. <cite id="23449272,33512521,22109947">Early daptomycin use in high-MIC MRSA bacteremia was associated with lower 30-day mortality and persistent bacteremia; switching within 3 days reduced mortality in a large VA cohort</cite>.

- If switching from vancomycin to daptomycin is not feasible or fails, reassess for other anti‑MRSA agents or combination strategies, and consider MIC testing/heteroresistance and alternative regimens. <cite id="25048852,20354160">Guidance supports reevaluating the 7‑day threshold and considering alternatives early; in refractory cases, adding rifampin to daptomycin has been reported to resolve bacteremia despite elevated daptomycin MIC</cite>.

# Remaining uncertainties

- The optimal definition of "early" and patient selection criteria (e.g., MIC thresholds, device-related infection) need prospective validation. Randomized trials directly comparing early switch versus continued vancomycin are limited, and real‑world data vary by setting and comorbidities. <cite id="38381737">More randomized and prospective studies are needed to assess the association between early switching and improved outcomes</cite>.

QUESTION:
In metastatic melanoma, how does combined PD-1 plus CTLA-4 blockade compare with PD-1 inhibitor monotherapy in long-term overall survival and incidence of grade 3–4 immune-related adverse events?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Long-term overall survival (OS): In adjuvant resected high-risk melanoma (CheckMate 238), 5-year OS was 76% with nivolumab versus 72% with ipilimumab, demonstrating a sustained long-term OS advantage for PD-1 blockade over CTLA-4 blockade in this setting. In earlier advanced/metastatic settings, combination PD-1 plus CTLA-4 blockade (CheckMate 067) produced a durable survival benefit versus PD-1 monotherapy, with median OS not reached at 4 years for the combination compared with 36.9 months for nivolumab and 19.9 months for ipilimumab at minimum 48-month follow-up. <cite id="37058595">Five-year overall survival rates were 76% with nivolumab and 72% with ipilimumab in resected stage IIIB-C/IV melanoma</cite> <cite id="30361170">Median overall survival was not reached for nivolumab plus ipilimumab, 36.9 months for nivolumab, and 19.9 months for ipilimumab at minimum 48-month follow-up</cite>.

- Grade 3–4 immune-related adverse events: In CheckMate 067, grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 59% with the PD-1+CTLA-4 combination, 22% with PD-1 monotherapy, and 28% with CTLA-4 monotherapy, reflecting substantially higher rates with dual checkpoint blockade. Real-world data corroborate the higher toxicity burden, with 50.7% of patients experiencing grade 3–4 adverse events and 58.6% requiring hospital admission when receiving ipilimumab+nivolumab in routine care. <cite id="30361170">Treatment-related grade 3-4 adverse events were reported in 59% of patients receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab, 22% receiving nivolumab, and 28% receiving ipilimumab</cite> <cite id="37103470">In a nationwide cohort, 50.7% experienced grade 3–4 adverse events, with 58.6% requiring hospital admission, while 4-year OS with a CheckMate-067–like profile was 50%</cite>.

# Interpretation

- Compared with PD-1 monotherapy, combined PD-1 plus CTLA-4 blockade yields superior long-term OS in metastatic melanoma (CheckMate 067) and, in the adjuvant setting, translates to higher 5-year OS as well. <cite id="30361170">The hazard ratio for death for the combination versus ipilimumab was 0.54 and for nivolumab versus ipilimumab was 0.65</cite> <cite id="37058595">Five-year OS favored nivolumab over ipilimumab (76% vs 72%)</cite>.

- The trade-off is a substantially higher incidence of severe immune-related adverse events with dual blockade, particularly grade 3–4 toxicity, which is observed both in trial and real-world settings. <cite id="30361170">Grade 3–4 adverse events were markedly more frequent with the combination (59%) than with PD-1 monotherapy (22%) or CTLA-4 monotherapy (28%)</cite> <cite id="37103470">Real-world grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 50.7%, often requiring hospitalization</cite>.

# Context and caveats

- CheckMate 238 results are in resected, high-risk melanoma and may not fully generalize to all metastatic populations. Nonetheless, the 5-year OS advantage for PD-1 over CTLA-4 supports caution when extrapolating to metastatic disease. <cite id="37058595">Nivolumab sustained improvements in RFS and DMFS with high OS rates in resected melanoma</cite>.

- Emerging data suggest that alternative combinations (e.g., nivolumab+relatlimab) can match efficacy while reducing grade 3–4 toxicity relative to PD-1+CTLA-4, offering a potential safer alternative in some patients. <cite id="39137386">Nivolumab plus relatlimab showed similar efficacy to nivolumab plus ipilimumab and was associated with fewer grade 3–4 TRAEs (23% vs 61%) and fewer discontinuations due to any-grade TRAEs (17% vs 41%)</cite>.

# Bottom line

- In metastatic melanoma, combined PD-1 plus CTLA-4 blockade improves long-term overall survival versus PD-1 monotherapy but increases the incidence of grade 3–4 immune-related adverse events substantially (approximately 55–60% vs 20–30% with PD-1 alone or CTLA-4 alone). <cite id="30361170">The combination achieved a durable survival benefit with higher grade 3–4 toxicity than either agent alone</cite> <cite id="37103470">Real-world experience confirms elevated grade 3–4 adverse event rates and hospitalizations with the combination</cite>. In resected high-risk melanoma, PD-1 monotherapy has shown a 5-year OS advantage over CTLA-4, underscoring that the OS benefit seen with dual blockade in metastatic disease may not uniformly translate to all melanoma settings and must be balanced against toxicity. <cite id="37058595">Five-year OS was 76% with nivolumab versus 72% with ipilimumab in resected melanoma</cite>.

QUESTION:
In in vivo liver-directed gene editing, how do AAV-delivered editors compare with lipid nanoparticle delivery in terms of hepatocyte editing efficiency, off-target profiles, and innate immune activation?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Hepatocyte editing efficiency:
  - AAV-directed delivery to liver can achieve high on-target indel frequencies in hepatocytes when using hepatocyte-specific promoters and liver-tropic serotypes (AAV9), with up to ~50% targeting at a therapeutic locus in vivo and minimal off-target evidence in the reported study, albeit in a hemophilia B model with strong liver restriction of Cas9 expression and transient activity in neonates as a "hit-and-run" approach. <cite id="29599079">AAV9-delivery of Cas9 with truncated gRNAs under a hepatocyte-specific promoter achieved liver-specific targeting at the F9 locus with up to 50% indel frequency and no evidence of off-target activity in other organs or putative off-target sites</cite>.
  - Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery of CRISPR editors achieves robust in vivo hepatocyte editing across modalities (Cas9 mRNA/RNP, base editors, prime editors), with examples including durable PCSK9 base editing in nonhuman primates and complete, durable normalization of blood phenylalanine in a hepatocyte-targeted PKU model via LNPs. <cite id="34012082">CRISPR base editors delivered by LNP efficiently and durably modified PCSK9 in cynomolgus monkeys, with near-complete hepatic knockdown and ~60% reduction in LDL cholesterol persisting for at least 8 months</cite>. <cite id="37301931">In vivo delivery of ABE mRNA and gRNAs via LNPs corrected the PAH P281L variant in humanized PKU mice, normalizing blood phenylalanine within 48 hours through corrective editing in the liver</cite>. <cite id="38325664">Systemically administered LNPs carrying Cas9 mRNA/sgRNA/HDR template achieved 60% hepatocyte gene knockout in mice, with liver retention and additional splenic/lung distribution for Cas9 RNP formulations</cite>.
  - Comparative biodistribution and editing data suggest LNP delivery can concentrate in hepatocytes and achieve substantial editing, while AAV systems can also achieve high hepatocyte transduction but with broader tissue tropism depending on serotype, necessitating tissue-specific promoters to confine editing to hepatocytes. <cite id="38325664">LNPs with Cas9 mRNA/sgRNA produced 60% hepatocyte knockout in vivo, with liver retention and lower editing efficiency for Cas9 RNP-LNPs in the tested model</cite>. <cite id="29599079">AAV9 transduces multiple tissues but hepatocyte-specific promoter control restricted Cas9 expression mainly to the liver, enabling high on-target indel frequency at F9 with minimal extra-hepatic activity</cite>.

- Off-target profiles:
  - AAV-based liver-directed CRISPR with hepatocyte-restricted Cas9 expression showed no detectable targeting to other organs or putative off-target sites by T7E1, Sanger, and deep sequencing in the reported study, supporting a favorable off-target profile when tissue specificity is enforced. <cite id="29599079">With hepatocyte-specific promoter control, Cas9 was mainly liver-restricted and deep sequencing showed no evidence of targeting in other organs or putative off-target sites</cite>.
  - Non-viral LNP delivery has demonstrated precise editing with durable phenotypic effects in vivo (e.g., PCSK9 base editing in primates; PAH correction in PKU mice), but comprehensive genome-wide off-target assessments in liver are less consistently reported than for AAV systems in some studies; nonetheless, the primate data indicate precision with long-term stability. <cite id="34012082">LNP-delivered base editors produced durable, near-complete PCSK9 knockdown with stable reductions in LDL cholesterol for at least 8 months in nonhuman primates</cite>. <cite id="37301931">LNP-mediated corrective editing of PAH in variant-humanized mice achieved complete and durable normalization of blood phenylalanine, indicating precise editing in hepatocytes</cite>. <cite id="38325664">In vitro and in vivo comparisons showed higher editing efficiency for mRNA/sgRNA LNP cargo versus Cas9-RNP LNP, with only mRNA/sgRNA LNP demonstrating conclusive hepatocyte editing in mice</cite>.
  - Overall, when hepatocyte specificity is engineered (AAV with hepatocyte-specific promoters or LNP strategies that rely on native hepatocyte targeting via cholesterol modifications), both modalities can achieve high on-target efficiency with limited detectable off-target activity; however, AAV systems that drive ubiquitous Cas9 expression risk broader off-target effects, underscoring the importance of tissue restriction. <cite id="29599079">Hepatocyte-specific promoter control restricted Cas9 to the liver and minimized extra-hepatic off-target signals</cite>. <cite id="30016076">LNP composition (e.g., esterified cholesterol) can modulate biodistribution and delivery efficiency across cell types, supporting rational targeting strategies that may reduce off-target delivery to non-hepatic tissues</cite>.

- Innate immune activation:
  - AAV-mediated liver delivery can induce immune responses; while the cited AAV study emphasized hepatocyte-restricted Cas9 expression and transient activity, it did not explicitly quantify innate immune activation, but the "hit-and-run" expression kinetics are a strategy to mitigate inflammation. <cite id="29599079">Transient Cas9 expression in neonates ("hit-and-run") minimized extra-hepatic spillover and supported liver-directed efficacy</cite>.
  - LNPs delivering CRISPR editors can engage innate immune sensors, particularly when using RNA-based editors (mRNA/gRNA/RNP) and dsRNA-sensing pathways (PKR, MDA5), with delivery composition and cholesterol modifications influencing biodistribution and potential immune interactions; studies show that LNP design (e.g., cholesterol variants) can modulate delivery efficiency and tissue targeting, which in turn may affect immune exposure. <cite id="30016076">Esterified cholesterol-containing LNPs increased delivery efficiency across cell types in mice, and specific oleate-containing LNPs showed differential delivery to liver endothelial versus hepatocyte compartments, indicating that LNP composition can alter in vivo exposure patterns relevant to immune sensing</cite>. <cite id="38325664">LNP cargo choice (mRNA/sgRNA vs. Cas9-RNP) influenced particle properties and in vivo editing outcomes, with mRNA/sgRNA-LNPs achieving gene knockout in hepatocytes and suggesting distinct pharmacokinetics and potential immune profiles compared to RNP-LNPs</cite>.
  - Compared head-to-head, AAV systems that restrict Cas9 expression temporally and spatially may reduce systemic innate immune activation, whereas LNPs may require higher doses or multiple administrations and can transiently expose the liver to RNA components that could activate dsRNA sensors; nonetheless, recent studies demonstrate durable editing with single-dose LNPs in primates, implying that immune activation can be managed with appropriate design and dosing. <cite id="34012082">Single-dose LNP base editors achieved durable hepatic editing and systemic cholesterol reduction in primates, indicating effective delivery with manageable immune context</cite>. <cite id="37301931">Single LNP administrations corrected PAH in vivo with rapid normalization of blood phenylalanine, suggesting efficient editing with limited overt immune signaling in the reported model</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways

- For high hepatocyte editing efficiency in the liver, both AAV and LNPs can succeed, but LNPs have shown strong efficacy in recent preclinical models (including primates) and flexible cargo options (mRNA/sgRNA, RNP, base/prime editors), while AAV relies on serotype and hepatocyte-specific promoters to confine editing to hepatocytes. <cite id="34012082">LNP-delivered base editors achieved near-complete hepatic PCSK9 knockdown with long-term stability in primates</cite>. <cite id="37301931">LNP-mediated corrective editing normalized blood phenylalanine in PKU models</cite>. <cite id="38325664">LNP mRNA/sgRNA achieved 60% hepatocyte knockout in mice</cite>. <cite id="29599079">AAV9 with hepatocyte-specific promoter achieved up to 50% indels at F9 with liver restriction</cite>.
- Off-target risk is minimized when tissue specificity and temporal control are engineered (AAV hepatocyte-specific promoters; transient Cas9 expression), and both modalities can achieve low detectable off-targets when delivered to liver; however, AAV with non-restricted expression may broaden off-target risk, while LNP off-target data are improving but less consistently reported than AAV in some contexts. <cite id="29599079">Hepatocyte-specific promoter restricted Cas9 to liver with no detectable off-targets in other organs or putative sites</cite>. <cite id="34012082">Long-term stability of PCSK9 edits in primates supports precision</cite>. <cite id="38325664">In vitro/in vivo comparisons favor mRNA/sgRNA-LNP for editing efficiency and liver retention</cite>.
- Innate immune activation profiles differ by modality: AAV strategies that use "hit-and-run" or hepatocyte-restricted promoters may dampen systemic innate responses, whereas LNPs may transiently engage dsRNA pathways; careful LNP design (e.g., esterified cholesterol, oleate variants, dose/schedule) can improve hepatocyte targeting and potentially reduce unnecessary immune exposure. <cite id="29599079">Transient Cas9 expression and hepatocyte restriction are strategies to mitigate immune activation</cite>. <cite id="30016076">Cholesterol variant selection in LNPs modulates delivery to hepatocyte subsets and may influence immune interactions</cite>. <cite id="34012082">Single-dose LNP base editing in primates achieved durable effects, suggesting manageable innate immune activation with optimized formulations</cite>.

# Evidence Gaps

- Direct, head-to-head comparisons of hepatocyte editing efficiency, off-target rates, and innate immune activation between AAV and LNP delivery in the same liver disease model remain limited in the retrieved literature; most studies evaluate each modality in separate models or endpoints. <cite id="29599079">AAV hepatocyte-restricted Cas9 achieved high on-target rates with low off-targets in a hemophilia B model</cite>. <cite id="34012082">LNP base editors achieved durable hepatic editing in primates</cite>. <cite id="37301931">LNP editors corrected PAH in PKU mice</cite>. <cite id="38325664">LNP mRNA/sgRNA achieved 60% hepatocyte knockout in mice</cite>. <cite id="30016076">LNP cholesterol composition affects delivery across cell types</cite>.
- Comprehensive genome-wide off-target profiling and standardized innate immune readouts (e.g., cytokines, PKR/MDA5 activation markers) for both modalities in liver are needed to refine safety assessments. <cite id="38325664">Comparative analysis suggests mRNA/sgRNA-LNP outperforms RNP-LNP in editing and pharmacokinetics</cite>. <cite id="30016076">LNP design can be optimized for hepatocyte targeting, which may indirectly reduce off-target immune exposure</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Both AAV and LNPs can achieve high-efficiency liver-directed gene editing in hepatocytes, with AAV showing strong performance when hepatocyte-specific promoters and liver-tropic serotypes are used, and LNPs demonstrating rapid, durable edits in recent primate and mouse studies using base/prime editors and Cas9 mRNA/sgRNA. <cite id="29599079">AAV9 with hepatocyte-specific promoter achieved up to 50% indels at F9 with liver restriction</cite>. <cite id="34012082">LNP base editors achieved durable, near-complete PCSK9 knockdown in primates</cite>. <cite id="37301931">LNP editors corrected PAH with durable normalization of blood phenylalanine in PKU mice</cite>. <cite id="38325664">LNP mRNA/sgRNA achieved 60% hepatocyte knockout in mice</cite>.
- Off-target risk appears low when tissue specificity and transient expression are engineered for AAV, and precision is supported by durable phenotypic outcomes for LNP-based editors; however, systematic off-target and immune profiling across comparable models is still needed. <cite id="29599079">No evidence of off-target targeting in other organs or putative sites with hepatocyte-restricted AAV9 delivery</cite>. <cite id="34012082">Durable edits in primates support precision for LNP-delivered base editors</cite>. <cite id="37301931">Complete normalization in PKU models indicates precise corrective editing with LNPs</cite>.
- Innate immune activation is likely lower with AAV when restricted expression is used, while LNPs may require design strategies (e.g., cholesterol variants, cargo selection, dosing) to minimize immune engagement and maximize hepatocyte delivery; both modalities have demonstrated effective in vivo editing with appropriate safety measures. <cite id="29599079">Transient, hepatocyte-restricted Cas9 expression reduces extra-hepatic spillover and potential immune activation</cite>. <cite id="30016076">Esterified/oleate cholesterol variants in LNPs can enhance delivery to specific hepatic cell subsets, potentially reducing off-target immune exposure</cite>. <cite id="34012082">Single-dose LNP base editing produced long-term efficacy in primates, indicating feasible delivery with controlled immune responses</cite>.

QUESTION:
In clinically isolated syndrome, does early initiation of disease-modifying therapy reduce conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis compared with delayed treatment?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Early initiation of disease‑modifying therapy (DMT) after a clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) is associated with a lower risk of conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), whereas delayed treatment is associated with higher conversion risk and greater disability accrual. Evidence from early interferon‑beta trials in CIS shows relative risk reductions of roughly 40–50% for progression to CDMS over short follow‑up, with sustained benefits in longer‑term extensions. Reviews and clinical summaries consistently support early treatment in high‑risk CIS patients, particularly those with MRI features of dissemination in space and time, to reduce conversion and neurologic damage.

# What the evidence shows

- Interferon beta (IFNβ) trials in CIS demonstrated that early treatment significantly reduced the risk of progression to CDMS by about 44–50% compared with no immediate treatment, and follow‑up extension studies showed continued reductions (≈35–37%) in conversion risk with early versus delayed therapy. These trials also showed improvements in MRI measures of disease activity with early IFNβ. <cite id="21485162">Early treatment of CIS patients with standard IFNβ significantly reduced the risk of progression to CDMS by 44 to 50%, and 5‑year extension studies confirmed a 35 to 37% reduction in conversion risk with early versus delayed treatment; early IFNβ also delayed progression to CDMS and improved MRI outcomes</cite> <cite id="24494633">In CIS, initiation of DMT (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide) following the first attack has been shown to delay conversion to CDMS</cite> <cite id="24217189">Initiation of interferon‑beta or glatiramer acetate after an initial MS‑like event in CIS has been associated with delays in progression to clinically definite MS and improvements in MRI damage measures</cite>.

- Multiple reviews of CIS treatment conclude that neurologists should consider initiating DMT as early as possible to favorably influence disease course and delay progression to CDMS, while individualizing therapy based on risk profile and adverse effect tolerance. <cite id="31290079">Conversion rates from CIS to clinically definite MS range roughly 20–75%, and neurologists face the challenge of initiating DMT as early as possible to influence disease course; reviews summarize efficacy, safety, and tolerability of DMTs tested in CIS and their value in delaying progression to CDMS</cite> <cite id="21485162">Following CIS, 38–68% develop CDMS; patients with abnormal MRI (56–88% at high risk) are at high conversion risk; early DMT is recommended for high‑risk CIS patients to prevent axonal damage and slow disability progression</cite> <cite id="15853542">Two interferon‑beta formulations delayed conversion into clinically definite MS in CIS, supporting early initiation to reduce relapses, disability progression, and MRI lesion accumulation</cite>.

- Observational and review data indicate that earlier DMT initiation across MS courses, including CIS, is linked to better outcomes (fewer relapses, less MRI activity, slower disability progression), and that delays in diagnosis and treatment increase the risk of conversion and disability. <cite id="24494633">DMT is more effective when initiated early in MS; in patients without CDMS but with a single MS‑consistent attack (CIS), early DMT delays conversion to CDMS</cite> <cite id="24217189">Earlier initiation of DMT in MS is associated with better outcomes; for CIS, early interferon‑beta or glatiramer acetate delays progression to CDMS and improves MRI measures</cite> <cite id="24494633">Delays in diagnosis and treatment are associated with poor outcomes, underscoring the importance of early intervention in CIS</cite>.

# Practical interpretation

- Compared with delayed treatment, early DMT initiation after CIS is associated with a meaningful reduction in conversion to CDMS (approximately 35–50% relative risk reduction in available trials), particularly in high‑risk patients (e.g., CIS with MRI dissemination in space and time, high lesion burden, brainstem involvement, or evidence of axonal damage). <cite id="21485162">Early IFNβ reduced CDMS risk by 44–50% in short‑term and 35–37% in 5‑year extensions; high‑risk CIS (abnormal MRI, 56–88% at high risk) should receive early DMT</cite> <cite id="31290079">CIS conversion rates of 20–75% motivate early DMT to influence progression</cite>.

- Benefits extend beyond clinical conversion: early therapy reduces MRI lesion accrual and activity and may slow disability progression, whereas delayed treatment allows greater neurologic damage before clinically definite MS establishes. <cite id="24217189">Early DMT in CIS delays progression to CDMS and improves MRI damage measures</cite> <cite id="15853542">Interferon‑beta formulations reduced relapses, disability progression, and MRI lesion accumulation in clinically definite MS and delayed conversion from CIS</cite>.

# Caveats and context

- Not all CIS patients progress to CDMS; treatment decisions should be individualized using prognostic markers (e.g., MRI evidence of dissemination in space and time, lesion load, brainstem/spinal cord location, and markers of axonal injury) to target high‑risk patients most likely to benefit. <cite id="21485162">CIS conversion rates vary widely (38–68%); MRI abnormalities identify high‑risk patients (56–88%); early DMT is most appropriate for high‑risk CIS by McDonald criteria</cite> <cite id="31290079">Choice of DMT should balance efficacy with adverse reaction profile and patient compliance</cite>.

# Bottom line

Yes. In clinically isolated syndrome, initiating disease‑modifying therapy early after the first MS‑like event—particularly in high‑risk patients—reduces conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis compared with delaying treatment, with relative risk reductions on the order of 35–50% observed in early interferon‑beta trials and extensions, and broader observational and guideline reviews supporting early intervention to prevent conversion and disability accrual. <cite id="21485162">Early interferon‑beta reduced CDMS risk by 44–50% in short‑term and 35–37% over 5 years in early‑treated versus delayed‑treated CIS patients</cite> <cite id="24494633">Initiation of DMT in CIS delays conversion to CDMS</cite> <cite id="24217189">Early treatment with interferon‑beta or glatiramer acetate in CIS delays progression to CDMS and improves MRI outcomes</cite> <cite id="31290079">Reviews emphasize early DMT to influence CIS progression to CDMS</cite> <cite id="15853542">Interferon‑beta delayed conversion from CIS to clinically definite MS and reduced relapses and disability progression</cite>.
