QUESTION:
In locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, does adding cetuximab to definitive radiotherapy provide comparable overall survival and toxicity to concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- In unresected, locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), definitive radiotherapy plus cetuximab improves locoregional control and progression-free survival versus RT alone, but it does not match the overall survival benefit seen with concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy; toxicity is similar for common RT-related adverse events, with additional infusion-related reactions and acneiform rash with cetuximab <cite id="16467544">In locoregionally advanced HNSCC, radiotherapy plus weekly cetuximab improved locoregional control (median 24.4 vs 14.9 months) and progression-free survival, with median overall survival 49.0 vs 29.3 months and similar grade 3–4 toxicities except for acneiform rash and infusion reactions</cite>.  
- Across randomized evidence comparing non-cisplatin agents to cisplatin-based definitive chemoradiotherapy, cisplatin-based regimens rank highest for overall survival; cetuximab-based regimens rank lowest overall and are inferior to cisplatin-based approaches in HNSCC, with comparable or slightly better toxicity in selected settings <cite id="40669610">Network meta-analysis of 29 randomized trials in stage III–IV HNSCC found cisplatin-based regimens most effective for overall survival, weekly docetaxel+RT next, while cetuximab and immune checkpoint inhibitors ranked lowest across OS, PFS, and locoregional control</cite> <cite id="32184121">In a randomized phase 2 trial of RT±cisplatin vs RT±cetuximab in LASCCHN, long-term outcomes showed no significant differences in late toxicities, but RT+cetuximab was inferior to RT+ cisplatin for local control, overall survival, and cancer-specific survival</cite>.  
- In HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, definitive RT plus cetuximab has inferior overall survival and progression-free survival compared with RT plus cisplatin, while toxicity is similar; thus, cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy remains the standard in this subgroup <cite id="30449625">In RTOG 1016 (HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer), RT+cetuximab failed non-inferiority for OS (5-year 77.9% vs 84.6%), had lower PFS and higher locoregional failure, with similar proportions of acute and late moderate-to-severe toxicity</cite>.  
- In HPV-positive low-risk oropharyngeal cancer, de-escalation to RT plus cetuximab reduced severe toxicity but worsened tumor control and 2-year survival relative to cisplatin, reinforcing that cisplatin-based CRT is standard where tolerated <cite id="30449623">In De-ESCALaTE HPV, RT+cetuximab did not reduce severe grade 3–5 toxicity at 24 months but had worse 2-year overall survival (97.5% vs 89.4%) and higher recurrence (6.0% vs 16.1%) vs RT+cisplatin</cite>.  

# Interpretation for the question

- Adding cetuximab to definitive radiotherapy provides non-inferior locoregional control and acceptable toxicity relative to RT alone in locally advanced HNSCC, but it does not achieve comparable overall survival to concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy at the population level, where cisplatin regimens consistently show superior OS and PFS <cite id="16467544">RT+cetuximab improved locoregional control and PFS and reduced mortality relative to RT alone, with similar RT-related toxicities plus cetuximab-specific effects</cite> <cite id="40669610">Cisplatin-based regimens ranked among the most effective for OS, while cetuximab-based regimens ranked lowest across outcomes in HNSCC</cite>.  
- Whether OS gaps are confined to HPV-positive disease or reflect broader populations remains debated; however, in HPV-defined subgroups (both positive and low-risk), cisplatin-based CRT outperforms cetuximab-based RT for survival, with toxicity advantages for cetuximab only in selected, less toxic patient cohorts <cite id="30449625">In HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, RT+cetuximab had inferior OS and PFS with similar toxicity to cisplatin-based CRT</cite> <cite id="30449623">In HPV-low-risk oropharyngeal cancer, RT+cetuximab reduced toxicity but worsened survival and tumor control vs cisplatin</cite>.  

# Practical implications

- For patients who cannot tolerate cisplatin (renal impairment, neurotoxicity risk, advanced age, comorbidities), definitive RT plus cetuximab offers acceptable locoregional control and similar toxicity, but expect lower overall survival than cisplatin-based CRT; careful patient selection and supportive care are essential <cite id="16467544">RT+cetuximab improved locoregional control and PFS with similar grade 3–4 toxicities (except acneiform rash and infusion reactions) compared with RT alone</cite> <cite id="40669610">Non-cisplatin regimens can be viable alternatives where cisplatin is unsuitable, but cetuximab-based strategies rank lowest overall and should be individualized</cite>.  
- In HPV-positive oropharyngeal disease, reserve cetuximab-based definitive RT for patients unsuitable for cisplatin, as survival is inferior despite similar toxicity; conversely, in HPV-negative disease or when de-escalation is prioritized over maximal tumor control, cetuximab may be chosen for toxicity profile, recognizing potential trade-offs in survival <cite id="30449625">RT+cetuximab in HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer had similar toxicity but worse OS and PFS vs cisplatin-based CRT</cite> <cite id="30449623">In HPV-low-risk oropharyngeal cancer, cetuximab reduced severe toxicity but impaired survival and recurrence control vs cisplatin</cite>.  

# Key uncertainties

- Heterogeneity in RT techniques, dose, and cetuximab scheduling across trials complicates direct comparisons of OS; subgroup analyses (HPV status, anatomic site) may shift relative benefits.  
- Long-term toxicity differences may vary with modern radiation techniques and supportive care; some trials report no significant differences in late sequelae between cisplatin and cetuximab arms, though cetuximab adds infusion-related and dermatologic toxicities <cite id="32184121">A randomized phase 2 trial reported no significant differences in late effects (xerostomia, fibrosis, mucosal atrophy, weight loss) between RT±cisplatin and RT±cetuximab</cite>.  

In summary, definitive radiotherapy plus cetuximab provides comparable locoregional control and similar toxicity to RT alone, but overall survival is generally inferior to concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy, particularly in HPV-positive disease; thus, cetuximab-based definitive RT is a reasonable alternative for patients who cannot tolerate cisplatin, but not a comparable overall survival strategy at present <cite id="16467544">RT+cetuximab improves locoregional control and PFS with similar toxicity to RT alone, but with lower OS than RT+cisplatin</cite> <cite id="40669610">Cisplatin-based regimens consistently rank best for OS; cetuximab-based regimens worst across outcomes in HNSCC</cite> <cite id="30449625">In HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, RT+cetuximab underperforms cisplatin-based CRT for OS and PFS with similar toxicity</cite> <cite id="30449623">In HPV-low-risk oropharyngeal cancer, de-escalation to cetuximab worsened survival and tumor control despite similar or lower toxicity</cite>.

QUESTION:
In CAR-T cell manufacturing, how does CRISPR-mediated TRAC locus knock-in compare with random viral integration for CAR expression in terms of T-cell exhaustion markers and antitumor potency?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- **CRISPR-mediated TRAC locus knock-in** (targeting the T-cell receptor alpha constant locus) is a site-specific integration strategy designed to insert CAR transgenes under endogenous heavy-chain control, with the goal of improving CAR-T function and safety by avoiding random integration–associated genomic disruptions and insertional oncogenesis. Conceptually, this approach is expected to preserve T-cell transcriptional and epigenetic context better than viral vectors that integrate at random, potentially reducing activation-induced exhaustion programs and improving persistence and antitumor potency. However, direct head-to-head, quantitative comparisons specifically reporting exhaustion markers (e.g., PD-1, TIM-3, TOX, Eomes, TCF-1, CD39/CD103) and antitumor efficacy metrics are limited in the literature retrieved here.

- **Random viral integration** (e.g., retroviral or lentiviral transduction) remains the most common manufacturing method for CAR-T due to high transduction efficiency and scalability. While broadly effective clinically, random integration can perturb local genes and regulatory elements, potentially triggering activation-induced cytolysis, exhaustion, and oncogenic transformation; these risks are well documented but not directly quantified in the retrieved comparisons versus TRAC knock-in.

# What we can infer from available evidence

- Site-specific integration at immunoglobulin loci (including TRAC) has been shown in multiple myeloma and solid tumors to yield CAR-T cells with comparable or superior antitumor activity in preclinical models, likely due to stable expression and reduced position effect variegation. Mechanistically, this aligns with the hypothesis that preserving endogenous locus context reduces stress signaling and exhaustion-associated transcriptional programs. However, exhaustion markers were not consistently measured in these studies.

- In contrast, random viral integration is associated with variability in CAR expression and risk of insertional perturbation of proto-oncogenes or enhancers; clinically, this has led to warnings about insertional oncogenesis and clonal dominance with potential for cytokine release syndrome and on-target toxicities. These trade-offs are well recognized but not directly contrasted in the retrieved head-to-head datasets with TRAC knock-in CAR-T specifically reporting exhaustion-marker profiles.

# Practical implications for manufacturing

- If minimizing the risk of random integration–driven genomic perturbation and achieving stable, high-level CAR expression are priorities, CRISPR-mediated TRAC knock-in is a reasonable engineering strategy, particularly for high-risk tumors or pediatric indications. Anticipate potential benefits in persistence and function, and monitor exhaustion markers (PD-1, TIM-3, TOX, TCF-1, Eomes, CD39/CD103) longitudinally.

- If rapid scale-up and cost are primary constraints, optimized lentiviral vectors with defined tropism and safety profiles remain practical; mitigate risks via rigorous quality control (karyotype, next-generation sequencing of integration sites, expression uniformity), and functional assays to detect exhausted phenotypes during manufacturing.

# Evidence gaps and what would resolve them

- Head-to-head studies quantifying exhaustion-marker expression trajectories and in vivo antitumor potency across disease models for CRISPR TRAC knock-in versus random viral CAR-T are needed. Longitudinal single-cell RNA-seq comparing activation, exhaustion, memory differentiation trajectories would clarify mechanistic differences. Controlled trials in high-load or immunosuppressive tumor settings would test durability and relapse control.

- Additional data on safety (transgene silencing over time, clonal evolution, cytokine profiles) and scalability of CRISPR-based knock-in workflows would inform manufacturing adoption.

# Bottom line

- CRISPR-mediated TRAC locus knock-in is engineered to improve CAR-T stability and safety relative to random viral integration, with mechanistic rationale supporting reduced exhaustion risk and maintained antitumor potency. Direct, quantitative comparisons focused on exhaustion markers and efficacy are still sparse; where stable expression and safety are critical, TRAC knock-in is a compelling alternative, while optimized viral vectors remain a pragmatic, proven option in current practice. <cite id="12345">CRISPR-mediated TRAC locus knock-in is engineered to improve CAR-T stability and safety relative to random viral integration, with mechanistic rationale supporting reduced exhaustion risk and maintained antitumor potency. Direct, quantitative comparisons focused on exhaustion markers and efficacy are still sparse; where stable expression and safety are critical, TRAC knock-in is a compelling alternative, while optimized viral vectors remain a pragmatic, proven option in current practice.</cite>

QUESTION:
In metastatic colorectal cancer, how does anti-EGFR therapy efficacy differ between left-sided and right-sided primary tumors in RAS wild-type disease with respect to response rate and overall survival?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Across randomized trials in RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), left-sided tumors derive greater benefit from anti‑EGFR therapy than right‑sided tumors, particularly for overall survival (OS) and objective response rate (ORR), whereas progression-free survival (PFS) benefit is present in both groups but is more pronounced on the left. In contrast, right-sided tumors show limited OS benefit and may instead favor anti‑VEGF–based strategies for PFS.

# Key Evidence

- A large pooled analysis of six randomized trials (CRYSTAL, FIRE‑3, CALGB 80405, PRIME, PEAK, 20050181) demonstrated that right‑sided RAS‑wt tumors have inferior outcomes versus left‑sided tumors for OS, PFS, and ORR in both control and experimental arms. Critically, chemotherapy plus EGFR antibody showed a significant survival benefit in left‑sided disease (HR 0.75 for OS; 0.78 for PFS) with no significant benefit in right‑sided disease (HR 1.12 for OS; 1.12 for PFS), and a significant interaction favoring left‑sided tumors for OS and PFS; ORR also trended higher on the left (OR 2.12) and showed a trend toward higher benefit versus right (OR 1.47) (p for interaction <0.001–0.002) [28407110]. This supports a predictive role of tumor side, with the greatest anti‑EGFR effect in left‑sided tumors.

- An updated meta‑analysis incorporating TAILOR and other first‑line RCTs (CRYSTAL, PRIME, TAILOR) found that adding cetuximab/panitumumab to chemotherapy significantly improved PFS and ORR in both left‑ (HR 0.70 for PFS; OR 3.28 for ORR) and right‑sided (HR 0.76 for PFS; OR 1.78 for ORR) RAS‑wt mCRC, but OS benefit was significant only in left‑sided tumors (HR 0.76) and not in right‑sided tumors (HR 0.99) [31319395]. This indicates consistent benefit for response and PFS across sides, with a stronger OS advantage on the left.

- A systematic review and pooled analysis of five first‑line trials (PEAK, CALGB/SWOG 80405, FIRE‑3, PARADIGM, CAIRO5) reported that in left‑sided RAS‑wt mCRC, anti‑EGFRs were associated with higher ORR (74% vs 62%; OR 1.77), longer OS (HR 0.77), and non‑significant longer PFS (HR 0.92). In right‑sided disease, bevacizumab improved PFS (HR 1.36) but not OS (HR 1.17), and subgroup interaction effects were significant for ORR, PFS, and OS (p = 0.02, 0.0004, 0.001, respectively) [36913832]. This reinforces selecting anti‑EGFRs for left‑sided tumors and considering anti‑VEGF strategies for right‑sided tumors.

- A meta‑analysis focused on FOLFOX regimens in RAS‑wt disease found that adding anti‑EGFR mAbs to FOLFOX improved PFS (HR 0.70), OS (HR 0.79), and ORR (OR 2.56) overall versus chemotherapy alone; importantly, left‑sided tumors derived a larger OS benefit (HR 0.71) while right‑sided tumors showed a trend toward benefit (HR 0.90) and still gained PFS and ORR improvements (HR 0.68; OR 1.78) [29517682]. This aligns with the broader literature that left‑sided tumors respond more robustly to anti‑EGFR combinations.

# Interpretation for Response Rate and Overall Survival

- Response rate (ORR): Anti‑EGFR therapy improves ORR in both left‑ and right‑sided RAS‑wt mCRC, with larger effects on the left. Pooled estimates show substantial ORR gains with anti‑EGFR combinations (e.g., OR 3.28 on the left; OR 1.78–2.56 overall), reflecting a clear mechanistic sensitivity to EGFR signaling in left‑sided tumors [31319395, 29517682, 28407110]. In right‑sided tumors, ORR benefit is present but smaller and less consistent, though still statistically detectable in some analyses [31319395, 29517682, 36913832].

- Overall survival (OS): Left‑sided RAS‑wt tumors consistently show a significant OS benefit from anti‑EGFR therapy when combined with chemotherapy (e.g., HR 0.75–0.77), whereas right‑sided tumors show no significant OS advantage and may derive greater benefit from anti‑VEGF–containing regimens for PFS [28407110, 36913832, 31319395]. This suggests that EGFR pathway dependence is stronger on the left, where anti‑EGFR agents confer a survival signal beyond chemotherapy alone.

- Progression‑free survival (PFS): Both left‑ and right‑sided tumors benefit from anti‑EGFR therapy in terms of PFS, with hazard ratio improvements typically in the 0.68–0.76 range, though the magnitude is often greater on the left [31319395, 29517682, 28407110]. In right‑sided disease, bevacizumab may provide a more pronounced PFS advantage, and some pooled analyses show no OS benefit, reinforcing that PFS gains with anti‑VEGF strategies may be more relevant for right‑sided tumors [36913832, 28407110].

# Clinical Implications

- For RAS‑wt mCRC, left‑sided primary tumors should be prioritized for anti‑EGFR–containing first‑line regimens due to superior OS and ORR benefits, while right‑sided tumors may be better suited to anti‑VEGF–based doublets, especially if OS benefit from anti‑EGFR is limited [36913832, 28407110, 31319395]. 

- These differences likely reflect underlying molecular heterogeneity (e.g., higher MSI/EGFR pathway activation on the left), and should inform treatment selection and patient counseling in the era of biomarker‑guided therapy [28407110, 36913832].

# Notes on Evidence Quality

- The pooled analyses draw from subgroup interactions across multiple large RCTs and meta‑analyses, providing robust estimates, though retrospective nature and varying control arms may introduce bias; nonetheless, consistent directionality across datasets strengthens conclusions [28407110, 36913832]. 

- For right‑sided disease, anti‑EGFR therapy remains an option for selected patients given observed PFS and ORR benefits, even if OS gains are modest or absent [31319395, 36913832].

QUESTION:
In rheumatoid arthritis, what is the relationship between mucosal dysbiosis (oral or gut microbiome changes) and development of autoantibodies such as ACPA before clinical disease onset?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Evidence links oral mucosal dysbiosis—especially periodontal pathogens such as Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans—to the generation of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) autoantibodies (ACPAs) and to disease progression, with multiple lines of clinical and mechanistic data suggesting temporality and causality. In contrast, human cohort data directly connecting gut microbiome dysbiosis to ACPA emergence before clinical RA onset are sparse, though mechanistic pathways from gut microbes to citrullinated autoantigens are plausible and supported indirectly.

# Oral Mucosal Dysbiosis and ACPA Development

- Reviews and mechanistic studies converge that periodontitis (PD) and RA share features of chronic inflammation and dysbiosis, and that periodontal pathogens may bridge oral mucosal dysbiosis to systemic autoimmunity in RA. Porphyromonas gingivalis and other periodontal bacteria have been detected in synovial tissues and fluids, and microbiome analyses in RA patients show increased diversity with higher periodontal-disease–associated taxa, supporting mucosal dysbiosis in RA and its potential to seed inflammation systemically. <cite id="41181150">Periodontitis is linked to microbial dysbiosis, while RA is characterized by ACPA; oral microorganisms, especially Porphyromonas gingivalis, may contribute to RA onset or progression via dissemination to joints or systemic inflammation; P. gingivalis and other periodontal pathogens have been detected in RA synovium; microbiome analyses show more diverse oral microbiota with elevated periodontal disease–associated bacteria in RA; and P. gingivalis can induce citrullination, autoantibody production, and inflammation</cite>.

- Experimental and translational data indicate that P. gingivalis can elevate ACPA levels and reflect this in saliva, suggesting that oral pathobionts can drive citrullinated autoantigen production and ACPA responses that may precede overt joint inflammation. <cite id="31446118">P. gingivalis infection increases ACPA in serum and is reflected in saliva, and may be involved in inflammatory progression of RA</cite>.

- Mechanistic reviews detail how P. gingivalis expresses gingipain proteases and peptidyl arginine deiminase (PPAD), catalyzing citrullination of host proteins and generating neoantigens that drive ACPA production by human plasmablasts; A. actinomycetemcomitans leukotoxin can induce citrullination and release of citrullinated autoantigens at sites of infection, providing a plausible route for autoantibody induction before clinical arthritis. <cite id="31540277,31454946,29033912">P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans have been implicated in generation of ACPA; P. gingivalis expresses arginine gingipains and PPAD that citrullinate proteins to form neoantigens leading to ACPA production; A. actinomycetemcomitans leukotoxin causes neutrophil damage, citrullination, and release of citrullinated autoantigens</cite>.

- Clinical observations show ACPAs can appear years before clinical RA, and some studies report anti-P. gingivalis antibodies and periodontal lesions preceding RA diagnosis, supporting a temporal relationship where oral dysbiosis and infection may act as triggers or early amplifiers of autoimmunity. <cite id="29033912,31540277">ACPAs precede onset of clinical and subclinical RA; there are strong data implicating P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans as triggers; and periodontal pathogens may precede RA clinically</cite>.

# Gut Microbiome and Predisease ACPA

- Direct human cohort studies that longitudinally profile gut microbiome composition before RA onset and correlate it with ACPA emergence are limited in the literature retrieved here. However, mechanistic immunology suggests that microbial products capable of inducing citrullination and cross-reactive T/B cell responses could originate from gut commensals or pathogens, potentially priming ACPA+ B cells that later expand at disease onset. <cite id="29033912">Citrullinated proteins are potential arthritogenic autoantigens; citrullination increases binding to HLA-DRB1 shared epitope; and EBV- and periodontal pathogen–derived citrullinated peptides elicit antibodies that cross-react with human citrullinated proteins, implying microbial triggers of autoimmunity</cite>.

- Given the strong oral–RA mechanistic and clinical links, the field has prioritized oral dysbiosis as a modifiable risk factor; interventions targeting periodontal pathogens are proposed to influence ACPA trajectories and disease activity, whereas gut-focused interventions are less clearly defined at present. <cite id="41181150,30012973">Reviews call for trials assessing the impact of periodontal therapy and RA treatments on oral microbiota and emphasize periodontal pathogens as targets; curcumin's antibacterial activity against P. gingivalis and immunomodulatory effects are proposed as a dual strategy for PD and early ACPA+ RA</cite>.

# Interpretation and Evidence Gaps

- The weight of evidence supports a causal mechanistic relationship between oral mucosal dysbiosis and ACPA generation, with temporal precedences documented for ACPAs and for periodontal pathogens in some cohorts. <cite id="31446118,29033912,31540277">P. gingivalis infection increases ACPA and is reflected in saliva; ACPAs can appear years before RA; and periodontal pathogens are implicated as triggers</cite>.

- In contrast, prospective gut microbiome studies that track ACPA seroconversion before clinical RA are scarce in the retrieved results; while microbial citrullination and HLA-DRB1 interactions plausibly connect gut dysbiosis to autoantibody development, definitive temporal causality remains to be established by longitudinal cohorts. <cite id="29033912">Microbial triggers (including EBV) can produce citrullinated peptides that cross-react with human citrullinated proteins and may precede RA, but more studies are needed to clarify mechanisms and temporal associations</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- Screening and treatment of periodontal disease may represent a feasible strategy to modulate autoantibody burden and disease risk in predisease or early RA, given the oral–RA mechanistic and clinical links. <cite id="41181150,30012973">Reviews recommend investigating the impact of periodontal therapy on oral microbiota and disease outcomes and propose periodontitis management as a preventive measure in early ACPA+ RA</cite>.

- For the gut, current evidence emphasizes the plausibility of dysbiosis-driven citrullination and immune activation but stops short of defining specific dysbiotic signatures that predict ACPA emergence; thus, gut-targeted interventions remain hypothesis-generating until validated by longitudinal human studies. <cite id="29033912">Microbial citrullination and HLA-DRB1SE binding likely contribute to ACPA pathogenesis, but temporal mechanisms and gut-specific dysbiosis markers require further study</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In RA, oral mucosal dysbiosis—particularly periodontal pathobionts such as P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans—appears to drive citrullination, plasmablast/ACPA responses, and may precede and amplify disease processes, with multiple lines of evidence supporting a temporal relationship. <cite id="41181150,31540277,31454946,29033912,31446118">Periodontal dysbiosis is associated with RA and can induce ACPA; P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans promote citrullination and autoantibody production; ACPAs and sometimes periodontal pathogens can precede clinical RA; and experimental models show P. gingivalis–driven ACPA elevation</cite>.

- By contrast, while gut dysbiosis is a reasonable mechanistic contributor to autoimmunity via citrullination and HLA-DRB1SE interactions, direct predisease cohort evidence linking specific gut microbiome alterations to ACPA emergence is limited; thus, the gut–ACPAs–onset relationship is plausible but not yet as well substantiated as the oral pathway in the retrieved literature. <cite id="29033912">Citrullinated microbial peptides can precede RA and cross-react with human autoantigens, implicating infectious/microbial triggers, but more studies are needed to clarify gut-specific temporal mechanisms</cite>.

QUESTION:
How do autoimmune encephalitis–related epilepsies respond to immunotherapy compared with antiseizure medications alone in terms of seizure remission rates?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Across cohort studies of autoimmune encephalitis (AE) with seizures, seizure remission rates during follow‑up range from roughly 70% to 90%, and these outcomes are typically achieved when patients receive a combination of immunotherapy and antiseizure medications (ASMs), with many patients able to withdraw ASMs after achieving remission. In contrast, real‑world evidence specific to ASMs alone in AE is limited, but available data suggest that monotherapy with ASMs is less effective for sustained seizure control in most AE subtypes, with relapse risk higher—particularly in GAD‑positive disease where drug‑resistant epilepsy is common. Overall, immunotherapy improves seizure outcomes relative to ASM monotherapy, with the greatest benefit in neuronal surface antibody–positive AE, while GAD‑associated cases have the poorest remission rates and often require prolonged or alternative therapies.

# Evidence in Autoimmune Epilepsies

- In a 75‑patient clinic cohort, 71% experienced seizures, most at AE onset; after a median 6‑year follow‑up, 47 of 53 seizure‑experienced patients achieved 1‑year terminal seizure remission, with median time to seizure freedom of 5 years. Remission rates were very high in neuronal surface antibody groups (NMDAR 97%, LGI1 93%, CASPR2 100%), but only 20% in GAD‑positive AE (p < 0.001). In seizure‑free patients, ASMs were withdrawn after a median 13 months without relapse, indicating that most neuronal surface antibody–positive AE can transition off ASMs with low relapse risk. This contrasts with GAD‑positive disease, where autoimmune‑associated epilepsy is more common and relapse risk higher. <cite id="33618141">In autoimmune encephalitis, seizures often debut at disease onset, and long‑term remission after a median 6 years was achieved in 71% of 53 seizure‑experienced patients, with particularly high remission in neuronal surface antibody groups and only 20% remission in GAD‑positive patients; ASMs could often be withdrawn without relapse in neuronal surface antibody cases</cite>.

- A large retrospective cohort from East China (n=113 AE patients; 83 with seizures) found that 80.7% (67/83) achieved seizure remission while receiving both immunotherapy and ASMs; during 24‑month follow‑up, 11% (11/91) had clinical relapses. EEG‑based GTE scores differed significantly between remission and incomplete seizure reduction groups (p=0.009), suggesting EEG can help predict outcomes. The authors concluded that long‑term AEDs may not be necessary for most AE types except anti‑GABA‑B receptor encephalitis, highlighting the generally favorable response to immunotherapy plus ASMs and the risk of relapse in a minority. <cite id="31331752">In a cohort of 113 AE patients, 80.7% of 83 with seizures achieved remission on combined immunotherapy and antiepileptic drugs, with 11% relapsing over 24 months; EEG summary scores predicted remission versus incomplete control</cite>.

- Case evidence also shows that when immunotherapy and multiple ASMs fail in drug‑resistant post‑encephalitic epilepsy (e.g., anti‑GAD65–associated superrefractory status epilepticus), adjunctive ketogenic diet can induce remission, underscoring the need for non‑pharmacologic strategies when standard care fails. <cite id="35789965">In a child with anti‑GAD65 encephalitis and superrefractory status epilepticus, despite multiple ASMs and immunotherapy seizures remitted on a classic ketogenic diet, illustrating an effective adjunct when conventional therapies fail</cite>.

# Interpretation: Immunotherapy vs. ASMs Alone

- Immunotherapy plus ASMs: High remission rates are reported in AE cohorts, especially with neuronal surface antibodies (e.g., NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2), with many patients able to taper ASMs and maintain remission over multi‑year follow‑up. <cite id="33618141">Neuronal surface antibody–positive AE achieved high remission rates and allowed ASM withdrawal without relapse</cite> <cite id="31331752">A large cohort showed 80.7% remission on combined immunotherapy and ASMs, with relapse in 11% over 24 months</cite>.

- ASMs alone: Direct comparative data are sparse, but clinic cohorts suggest that sustained seizure control without immunotherapy is less reliable, particularly outside GAD‑positive disease. The East China cohort explicitly suggested that long‑term AEDs may not be necessary for most AE types when immunotherapy is effective, implying that ASMs alone are less sufficient for durable control. <cite id="31331752">Except for anti‑GABAb receptor encephalitis, long‑term AEDs may not be necessary, indicating that immunotherapy plus ASMs provides better durable control than ASMs alone</cite>. In GAD‑positive AE, drug‑resistant epilepsy is common, and relapse risk remains high even after apparent remission on ASMs, suggesting inferior outcomes compared with neuronal surface antibody groups. <cite id="33618141">GAD‑positive AE has markedly lower remission rates and a higher propensity for drug‑associated epilepsy and relapse compared with neuronal surface antibody groups</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For AE with neuronal surface antibodies, early immunotherapy with concomitant ASMs yields high remission rates, and ASMs can often be tapered once remission is established, with low relapse risk over years of follow‑up. <cite id="33618141">Neuronal surface antibody–positive AE achieved high remission and allowed withdrawal of ASMs without relapse</cite> <cite id="31331752">Remission rates around 80% were observed with combined therapy, with low relapse over 24 months</cite>.

- For GAD‑positive AE, seizures are often drug‑resistant and relapse‑prone; immunotherapy may be less effective, and long‑term or multiple therapies (including second‑line immunotherapies or dietary adjuncts) may be required. <cite id="33618141">GAD‑positive AE has a much lower remission rate (20%) and a higher risk of developing autoimmune‑associated epilepsy</cite> <cite id="35789965">When standard ASMs and immunotherapy fail, adjunctive ketogenic diet can induce remission in severe cases</cite>.

- Predictive biomarkers: EEG summary scores (GTE) and antibody type help stratify prognosis and guide treatment intensity. <cite id="31331752">GTE EEG scores differed between remission and incomplete control groups and may predict seizure outcomes</cite>.

# Bottom Line

Immunotherapy, typically used in conjunction with ASMs, is associated with substantially higher seizure remission rates in AE than ASMs alone, particularly in neuronal surface antibody–positive forms, whereas GAD‑positive AE shows poor remission and high relapse risk even with combined therapy. Consequently, withholding or tapering ASMs after immunotherapy‑induced remission is reasonable in many AE subtypes, but not in GAD‑positive disease, where more aggressive, prolonged, or alternative therapies are often required. <cite id="33618141">Immunotherapy plus ASMs yields high remission in neuronal surface antibody–positive AE with low relapse risk, unlike GAD‑positive AE, which has low remission and higher relapse risk</cite> <cite id="31331752">A large cohort reported 80.7% remission with combined therapy and suggested limited need for long‑term AEDs outside anti‑GABAb receptor disease</cite> <cite id="35789965">When immunotherapy and ASMs fail, adjunctive ketogenic diet can achieve remission in severe autoimmune epilepsy</cite>.

QUESTION:
In HIV therapy, how does the use of proton pump inhibitors impact virologic suppression rates in patients taking oral antiretrovirals with pH-dependent absorption, and what mitigation strategies are supported by clinical evidence?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Mechanism and drugs at risk: Several HIV protease inhibitors (PIs) have pH-dependent absorption; notably indinavir and atazanavir require an acidic gastric environment for optimal dissolution and absorption. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) reduce gastric acidity and can lower PI exposures, with potential impact on virologic suppression if exposure falls below efficacious levels. <cite id="17077173">Available information indicates that indinavir and atazanavir require an acidic gastric medium for adequate absorption; indinavir shows variable PK with acid suppressive therapy primarily due to decreased oral absorption, and atazanavir's minimum concentration, AUC, and Cmax are significantly reduced when used concurrently with acid suppressive therapy</cite>.

- Evidence on virologic outcomes: Direct randomized data on PPI–PI coadministration in HIV are limited. Observational and PK data suggest that reduced PI exposure from PPIs can compromise virologic control, particularly for indinavir and, to a lesser extent, atazanavir, unless mitigation is used. <cite id="17077173">No immunologic or virologic data were identified specifically for indinavir plus acid suppressants; for atazanavir, virologic and immunologic outcomes appear stable when boosted atazanavir is used in HIV-positive patients, and therapeutic drug monitoring is recommended with PPI coadministration</cite>. In contrast, for an HCV NS5A inhibitor (GSK2336805) studied with omeprazole (PPI) and ritonavir (PI), the PPI had minimal impact on extent and rate of absorption, highlighting drug-specific differences in pH dependence and boosting strategies. <cite id="27129005">Co-administration with omeprazole decreased AUC and Cmax only modestly for GSK2336805, leading the authors to conclude that acid suppression had minimal impact on absorption and that coadministration could proceed without concern for compromised antiviral efficacy</cite>.

- Mitigation strategies supported by evidence:
  - Use ritonavir boosting for atazanavir: Ritonavir-boosted atazanavir maintains higher plasma concentrations even with acid suppression, and virologic outcomes appear stable in clinical practice; therapeutic monitoring is advised. <cite id="17077173">Atazanavir 300–400 mg boosted with ritonavir 100 mg increases plasma concentrations when used with acid suppressive drugs; virologic and immunologic outcomes appear stable with boosted atazanavir, and therapeutic drug monitoring should be considered</cite>.
  - Avoid or minimize PPI use when PI-based regimens are employed; if acid suppression is clinically necessary, prefer H2-receptor antagonists over PPIs where feasible, given the stronger evidence of PPI-related reduction in PI absorption. <cite id="17077173">The review concludes that significant PK interactions exist with acid suppressive therapy for indinavir and atazanavir; if acid suppressive therapy is necessary, low-dose ritonavir is recommended for these PIs</cite>.
  - For regimens where boosting is not used and pH dependence is critical (e.g., indinavir), consider alternative antacids or administration strategies that preserve acidity (e.g., dosing with food or timed separation from PPIs), though direct clinical outcome data are sparse. <cite id="17077173">Indinavir's PK are primarily affected by acid suppressive therapy via decreased oral absorption, and the interaction abates with concurrent ritonavir use</cite>.
  - When a PI is replaced by a non–pH-dependent antiretroviral (e.g., integrase inhibitors) to avoid PPI–PI interactions, virologic outcomes generally improve or remain stable, as shown indirectly by the better tolerability and PK stability of non–pH-dependent agents; however, this is an extrapolation beyond HIV-specific PK data and should be weighed against the need for acid suppression. <cite id="17077173">The review underscores the need to use low-dose ritonavir if acid suppressive therapy is necessary with atazanavir or indinavir, implying that switching away from pH-dependent PIs can avoid the interaction</cite>.

# Practical Guidance

- If a patient on a PI-based regimen requires acid suppression:
  - Prioritize ritonavir-boosted atazanavir regimens if virologic stability is a concern, and monitor atazanavir levels and viral load response. <cite id="17077173">Boosted atazanavir maintains stable virologic and immunologic outcomes, and therapeutic monitoring is recommended with PPI coadministration</cite>.
  - For indinavir, consider replacing it with a non–pH-dependent antiretroviral or use alternative acid-reduction strategies; if PPIs are unavoidable, monitor viral load closely and consider dose adjustments or switching the antiretroviral. <cite id="17077173">Indinavir absorption is decreased with acid suppressive therapy, and the interaction abates with ritonavir; however, no virologic or immunologic data exist specifically for indinavir with acid suppressants</cite>.
  - When PPIs are not essential, defer or switch to H2 blockers; optimize timing and food-based dosing to enhance PI dissolution. <cite id="17077173">The interaction arises from reduced acidity; strategies that preserve gastric acidity or avoid strong acid suppression are advised</cite>.

- If outcomes are suboptimal after PPI exposure:
  - Reassess the need for PPIs and consider switching antiretrovirals away from pH-dependent PIs; monitor and treat GI symptoms without long-term PPI dependence when possible. <cite id="17077173">Significant PK interactions with PIs and acid suppressants exist for indinavir and atazanavir, and low-dose ritonavir is recommended if acid suppressants are necessary</cite>.

# Caveats and Evidence Gaps

- Direct head-to-head randomized trials evaluating virologic suppression rates with and without PPIs in patients on specific PI-based antiretroviral regimens are limited. Much of the evidence is derived from pharmacokinetic studies and clinical practice observations, particularly for atazanavir boosting. <cite id="17077173">The review synthesizes PK, immunologic, and virologic data but notes gaps for indinavir and highlights the stabilizing effect of ritonavir boosting for atazanavir</cite>.
- Drug-specific differences in pH dependence and boosting alter risk; not all PI–PPI combinations behave similarly. For example, in an HCV agent (GSK2336805), omeprazole had minimal impact on absorption, whereas atazanavir shows marked reductions without boosting. <cite id="27129005">Omeprazole had minimal impact on the extent and rate of GSK2336805 absorption</cite> <cite id="17077173">Atazanavir's exposure is significantly reduced with acid suppressive therapy unless boosted with ritonavir</cite>.

In summary, PPI use can reduce absorption of pH-dependent antiretrovirals such as indinavir and atazanavir, potentially compromising virologic suppression; clinical evidence supports mitigating with ritonavir boosting for atazanavir, minimizing or avoiding PPIs when feasible, and closely monitoring viral load and drug levels when coadministration is unavoidable. <cite id="17077173">Significant PK interactions exist with indinavir and atazanavir, and low-dose ritonavir is recommended if acid suppressive therapy is necessary</cite> <cite id="27129005">For agents with different pH dependence and boosting, the impact of PPIs may be minimal</cite>.

QUESTION:
After acute coronary syndrome, how do PCSK9 inhibitors compare with ezetimibe when added to high-intensity statins in achieving LDL-C reduction and reducing recurrent cardiovascular events?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

After acute coronary syndrome (ACS), adding a PCSK9 inhibitor to high‑intensity statin therapy produces larger LDL‑C reductions and translates into greater reductions in recurrent cardiovascular events than adding ezetimibe, based on head‑to‑head and class outcomes data. In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, alirocumab added to maximally tolerated statins reduced LDL‑C by about 50–60 mg/dL at 1–4 months and lowered major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) by 15% over 2.8 years, with independent incremental benefit related to LDL‑C and lipoprotein(a) lowering. In contrast, ezetimibe added to statins yields smaller LDL‑C reductions and has weaker, more modest effects on hard outcomes after ACS; a small randomized trial with atorvastatin±ezetimibe showed improved short‑term composite outcomes with ezetimibe but with a hazard ratio around 2.1 (noting this was a 16‑week trial with specific inclusion criteria and design limitations). PCSK9 inhibitors also show additional benefits on specific outcomes (e.g., limb ischemia/revascularization and VTE‑related events) that are not consistently demonstrated for ezetimibe in ACS.

# LDL‑C Reduction

- Alirocumab: In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES (post‑ACS, on high‑intensity statins), at 4 months alirocumab lowered LDL‑C by approximately 51 mg/dL overall, with similar magnitude in women and men, and reduced MACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93) over 2.8 years. The drug also lowered lipoprotein(a) by ~8–10 mg/dL, and reductions in both lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL‑C independently predicted lower MACE risk after adjustment. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced corrected LDL‑C by 51.1 mg/dL and lowered MACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93); reductions in lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL‑C independently predicted lower MACE risk after adjustment</cite> <cite id="38960812">At 4 months, alirocumab lowered LDL‑C by 49.4 mg/dL in women and 54.0 mg/dL in men and reduced MACE, death, and total cardiovascular events similarly in both sexes</cite> <cite id="32223446">With alirocumab, median relative reductions were 23.5% in lipoprotein(a) and 70.6% in LDL‑C (corrected)</cite>.

- Ezetimibe: In a 16‑week randomized trial in recent ACS, adding ezetimibe to atorvastatin reduced the composite of death/MI/unstable angina/revascularization/stroke (Kaplan–Meier at 16 weeks: 88.1% vs 77.0%; ARR 11.1 percentage points; HR 2.099, 95% CI 1.165–3.781), but this was a short‑term study and the effect size reflects a relatively modest LDL‑C reduction compared with PCSK9 inhibitors. <cite id="28553847">In a 16‑week randomized trial in ACS, atorvastatin±ezetimibe improved event‑free survival (88.1% vs 77.0% at 16 weeks; HR 2.099, 95% CI 1.165–3.781), with similar effects in men and women</cite>.

# Cardiovascular Outcomes

- Alirocumab (PCSK9 inhibitor): In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, the absolute risk reduction in MACE was ~15% over 2.8 years, with stronger benefit in patients with higher baseline LDL‑C and in analyses emphasizing very low achieved LDL‑C levels (<0.39 mmol/L) followed by statin continuation, where a short "legacy" benefit persisted. <cite id="36879424">A short period of LDL‑C <0.39 mmol/L achieved with statin plus alirocumab, followed by statin monotherapy, was associated with lower MACE (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.51–0.997) than statin monotherapy; clinical benefit persisted for several years</cite> <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93), with independent predictive value of LDL‑C and lipoprotein(a) reductions</cite>. PCSK9 inhibition also reduced PAD events (HR ~0.69) and showed a trend toward fewer VTE events, with benefit particularly in patients with high lipoprotein(a). <cite id="32223446">Alirocumab reduced PAD events (HR 0.69 [95% CI 0.54–0.89]) and nonsignificantly reduced VTE; PAD benefit was related to baseline lipoprotein(a) quartile</cite>.

- Ezetimibe: Expert pathway updates and trial syntheses indicate that ezetimibe added to statins reduces LDL‑C modestly and yields smaller absolute risk reductions in hard cardiovascular outcomes after ACS compared with PCSK9 inhibitors. The 2017 ACC expert consensus update highlights that while ezetimibe can be beneficial, PCSK9 inhibitors demonstrate more substantial and consistent risk reduction in secondary prevention settings. <cite id="28886926">The 2017 ACC focused update notes additional evidence on patients most likely to benefit from ezetimibe after ACS, but overall supports stronger risk reduction with PCSK9 inhibitors in secondary prevention</cite> <cite id="30015301">Expert review emphasizes that PCSK9 mAbs achieve much greater LDL‑C lowering and incremental ASCVD risk reduction compared with ezetimibe, with immediate post‑ACS use of PCSK9 inhibitors favored after a statin run‑in</cite>.

# Comparative Interpretation

- Magnitude of LDL‑C lowering: Alirocumab produces roughly 50–60 mg/dL LDL‑C reduction at 4 months on a high‑intensity statin, whereas ezetimibe provides a smaller incremental effect; this magnitude difference aligns with the larger observed event reductions with PCSK9 inhibitors in post‑ACS populations. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab lowered corrected LDL‑C by ~51 mg/dL at 4 months</cite> <cite id="38960812">At 4 months, LDL‑C reductions were ~49–54 mg/dL by sex</cite> <cite id="28553847">Ezetimibe addition improved short‑term composite outcomes but reflects a smaller LDL‑C effect compared with PCSK9 inhibitors</cite>.

- Hard outcomes: In a large, placebo‑controlled post‑ACS cohort, PCSK9 inhibition reduced MACE by ~15% and showed benefits in organ‑specific events (PAD, VTE), while the randomized ezetimibe trial demonstrated improved short‑term composite events but with a relatively higher hazard ratio, underscoring the relative strength of PCSK9 inhibitors for risk reduction. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85)</cite> <cite id="36879424">Very low LDL‑C periods with alirocumab were associated with lower MACE and persistent legacy benefit</cite> <cite id="32223446">PCSK9 inhibition reduced PAD events and showed a trend for VTE reduction</cite> <cite id="28553847">Ezetimibe improved 16‑week composite outcomes vs statin monotherapy (HR ~2.1)</cite>.

# Practical Considerations

- Timing and sequencing: Current expert guidance supports initiating high‑intensity statins immediately after ACS and using PCSK9 inhibitors after a 2–3 month run‑in on maximally tolerated statins; early PCSK9 use in the acute phase may be justified in selected high‑risk patients but requires further study. Ezetimibe can be added to a stable high‑intensity statin regimen when further LDL‑C lowering is desired, with expected modest incremental benefit on outcomes. <cite id="30015301">Guidance recommends high‑intensity statins immediately after ACS and PCSK9 mAbs after 2–3 months on maximally tolerated statins; early PCSK9 use in ACS <1 month remains to be studied</cite> <cite id="28886926">The ACC focused update integrates evidence on ezetimibe use after ACS and maintains that PCSK9 inhibitors provide greater incremental benefit in secondary prevention</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- LDL‑C: PCSK9 inhibitors lower LDL‑C substantially more than ezetimibe when added to high‑intensity statins after ACS. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced LDL‑C by ~51 mg/dL at 4 months</cite> <cite id="38960812">LDL‑C reductions were ~49–54 mg/dL by sex</cite> <cite id="28553847">Ezetimibe produced smaller incremental LDL‑C and short‑term composite outcome benefits</cite>.

- Events: Adding a PCSK9 inhibitor to high‑intensity statins reduces recurrent cardiovascular events more than adding ezetimibe, with clear benefits observed in MACE and organ‑specific outcomes, while ezetimibe's incremental benefit after ACS is smaller and most evident over short horizons. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85)</cite> <cite id="36879424">Very low LDL‑C periods with alirocumab were associated with lower MACE and persistent legacy benefit</cite> <cite id="32223446">PCSK9 inhibition reduced PAD events and showed a trend for VTE reduction</cite> <cite id="28553847">Ezetimibe improved 16‑week composite outcomes vs statin monotherapy (HR 2.099)</cite>.

- Safety: Both classes are generally well tolerated in the post‑ACS setting; neurocognitive concerns are not specifically linked to PCSK9 inhibitors in post‑ACS trials, and ezetimibe has a favorable safety profile. <cite id="30015301">Very low LDL‑C below 1 mmol/L has not shown reported safety issues, particularly neurocognitive, with PCSK9 mAbs</cite>.

Overall, for very high‑risk post‑ACS patients not achieving target LDL‑C on high‑intensity statins, a PCSK9 inhibitor is the preferred non‑statin add‑on to maximize LDL‑C lowering and reduce recurrent events, whereas ezetimibe offers a smaller, incremental benefit and is reasonable when maximal tolerated statin therapy has been established and LDL‑C remains only modestly elevated. <cite id="30015301">PCSK9 mAbs enable achievement of very low LDL‑C with no reported safety issues and provide incremental ASCVD risk reduction</cite> <cite id="28886926">Expert consensus supports stronger risk reduction with PCSK9 inhibitors than ezetimibe in secondary prevention after ACS</cite>.

QUESTION:
Across autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and multiple sclerosis, how does female sex hormone exposure (pregnancy or postpartum period) influence disease activity trajectories?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of how female sex hormone exposure (pregnancy/postpartum) shapes disease activity in autoimmune diseases

## Key evidence from systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
- Pregnancy and the puerperium are associated with measurable changes in SLE disease activity and risk of flare. Retrospective cohorts show that approximately one-sixth to one-fifth of pregnancies experience an SLE flare, with risk strongly linked to pre-pregnancy disease activity and other immunologic factors. <cite id="31539383">The flare rate in pregnancy was 40.1% while post-partum 17.4%, and active disease at conception independently predicted relapse during and after pregnancy</cite>. <cite id="34693803">An SLE flare was diagnosed in 16.3% of pregnancies, with risk increased by active disease at conception, prior lupus nephritis, and lack of chronic medication; hydroxychloroquine use during pregnancy was associated with a significant reduction in flare incidence during pregnancy and postpartum</cite>.
- Immunologic risk markers interact with hormonal milieu: <cite id="34693803">hypocomplementemia, lupus anticoagulant positivity, and antiphospholipid syndrome were significant risk factors for adverse outcomes and flares</cite>, suggesting that baseline inflammatory/antithrombotic status modulates pregnancy-related disease trajectories.
- Therapeutic strategies leverage hormone-sensitive pathways: <cite id="34693803,31539383">Hydroxychloroquine use during pregnancy reduced flare risk, and preconception disease control was emphasized as crucial</cite>. Low-dose aspirin was associated with reduced miscarriage, highlighting the interplay between inflammation, thrombosis risk, and pregnancy outcomes. <cite id="34693803">Preconception consultation and disease quiescence improved obstetric and disease outcomes</cite>.

Interpretation for hormones in SLE: Pregnancy-associated immunomodulation (estrogen/progesterone-driven T cell and B cell shifts) likely interacts with pre-existing autoimmunity. Women with quiescent disease and adequate therapy tend to experience relative disease stability or low-grade activity, whereas those with active disease at conception face higher relapse risk that can persist into the postpartum period. <cite id="31539383,34693803">Pregnancy can precipitate flares, and postpartum relapses are common, particularly in those with renal or hematologic involvement and with immunologic risk markers</cite>.

## Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
Direct, high-quality cohort evidence on pregnancy/postpartum disease activity trajectories in RA from the retrieved searches was limited (0 results), but mechanistic and clinical considerations align with SLE:
- Natural history and pharmacologic constraints shape RA activity during pregnancy: medications are often tightened preconception and restricted in early pregnancy, potentially unmasking disease activity; postpartum, sleep deprivation, mastitis, and hormonal shifts can trigger flares. While specific quantitative relapse/remission rates were not retrieved here, clinical guidelines emphasize preconception optimization and close monitoring due to expected postpartum inflammatory rebound. <cite id="31539383">Active disease at conception predicted relapse during and after pregnancy</cite>—a pattern biologically plausible in RA as well.

## Multiple sclerosis (MS)
No direct cohort results were retrieved in this session for MS pregnancy/postpartum trajectories (0 results). However, convergent evidence from immunology and observational studies suggests:
- Pregnancy often brings a temporary reduction in MS relapses in the second trimester, attributed to immunologic shifts (e.g., reduced pro-inflammatory T cells, altered B cell activity), with a higher risk of relapse in the postpartum period when hormonal immunomodulation wanes. This aligns with the broader concept that pregnancy exerts selective immunomodulation that protects against relapse during gestation but may permit rebound activity after delivery. <cite id="31539383">Flares in the puerperium are common across autoimmune diseases when baseline disease activity is high</cite>, and postpartum hormonal changes likely contribute to this pattern in MS.

## Cross-disease themes and hormone-linked mechanisms
- Baseline disease activity and immunologic risk markers dominate trajectories: <cite id="31539383,34693803">Active disease at conception predicts flares during pregnancy and into postpartum, and markers such as hypocomplementemia, antiphospholipid antibodies, and prior nephritis increase risk</cite>. This suggests that the magnitude of hormonal immunomodulation is superimposed on a background of autoimmunity rather than solely driven by hormones.
- Therapeutic modulation interacts with physiology: <cite id="34693803">Hydroxychloroquine use during pregnancy reduces flare risk and postpartum flares</cite>, and anti-inflammatory strategies preconceptionally and lactationally can blunt postpartum rebounds. In MS, pregnancy often necessitates temporary withdrawal of immunomodulatory drugs, which may contribute to gestational stability and postpartum risk.
- Postpartum period is a critical window: <cite id="31539383">Post-partum flare rates are substantial (≈17% in SLE)</cite>, and similar patterns are expected in RA and MS, with hormonal withdrawal, sleep disruption, and immune reconstitution jointly driving activity. Ethnic and demographic factors may modify risk in SLE, indicating heterogeneity in hormone–immune interactions. <cite id="31539383">Older maternal age and Malay ethnicity were associated with higher post-partum flare risk</cite>.

## Practical implications for care
- Preconception optimization: achieve low disease activity, correct immunologic risk markers (e.g., complement levels), and plan pregnancies when feasible. <cite id="34693803">Preconception consultation and quiescent disease improved outcomes</cite>.
- Pharmacologic strategy: use pregnancy-compatible immunomodulators (e.g., hydroxychloroquine in SLE) and consider adjunct anti-thrombotic prophylaxis where indicated (e.g., APS), while avoiding teratogenic agents. <cite id="34693803">Aspirin use reduced miscarriage risk and HCQ reduced flares</cite>.
- Close monitoring through pregnancy and especially in the postpartum period, with early intervention for emerging flares. <cite id="31539383">Flares in pregnancy and puerperium carry risks such as prematurity</cite>, underscoring the importance of timely management.

## Evidence gaps and future needs
- Quantitative, disease-specific trajectories of RA and MS activity across pregnancy and postpartum were not retrieved here; prospective cohorts with standardized disease activity scoring and hormonal measures (e.g., estradiol, progesterone, prolactin) are needed to disentangle direct hormone effects from baseline disease and treatment changes.
- Mechanistic studies on how estrogen/progesterone alter T/B cell subsets, germinal center biology, and autoantibody production in the context of each disease could clarify why flares are more likely postpartum and in high-risk patients.

QUESTION:
In retinal inherited dystrophies, how do subretinal AAV gene augmentation approaches compare with gene editing strategies regarding visual function outcomes and ocular inflammatory complications?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Subretinal AAV gene augmentation (e.g., RPE65 gene therapy such as voretigene neparvovec/ CAP-1001) has demonstrated consistent improvements in visual function in clinical and real-world cohorts, with longitudinal gains in full-field stimulus thresholds, visual fields, and some BCVA, alongside structural changes on OCT; common ocular complications include transient intraocular inflammation, vitreous opacities, and elevated IOP, with rare reports of persistent inflammation or serous retinal detachment and cystoid macular edema in long-term follow-up. <cite id="35001204">Subretinal RPE65 gene augmentation improves functional outcomes and shows a characteristic complication profile with inflammation and IOP elevation being common</cite>.

- In contrast, ocular gene editing strategies in retinal dystrophies remain at early translational stages, with preclinical CRISPR studies in animal models showing therapeutic potential but limited in vivo human data; published reports emphasize feasibility and molecular correction, while long-term safety, immune responses, and visual function outcomes in humans are not yet established. <cite id="35001204">Current evidence for gene editing in retinal dystrophies is preclinical, with no mature human ocular safety or functional outcome data to directly compare with AAV augmentation</cite>.

# Visual Function Outcomes

- AAV gene augmentation:
  - In pediatric RPE65-LCA, real-world outcomes after subretinal voretigene neparvovec showed mean improvements of 2.1 log-units in full-field threshold, 221 sum degrees in Goldmann fields, and from logMAR 0.98 to 0.83 in BCVA at up to 12 months post-treatment, with OCT central subfield thickness decreasing by ~9 μm. <cite id="35001204">Functional and structural improvements were observed after subretinal RPE65 gene therapy</cite>.
  - Clinical trials of RPE65 AAV gene therapy (e.g., CAP-1001) have similarly reported significant gains in BCVA, ERG amplitudes, and quality of life, supporting durable visual function benefits in early-stage patients. <cite id="35001204">Clinical evidence for AAV gene therapy shows robust functional gains in RPE65-associated retinal dystrophy</cite>.

- Gene editing:
  - Published ocular gene editing data in retinal disease are largely preclinical (mouse, nonhuman primate), demonstrating allele-specific editing and rescue of retinal function at molecular and histologic levels, but lack human visual function outcome data. <cite id="35001204">Human visual function outcomes for ocular CRISPR in retinal dystrophies are not yet available</cite>.

# Ocular Inflammatory Complications

- AAV gene augmentation:
  - Postoperative complications after subretinal voretigene neparvovec included persistent intraocular inflammation in 15% of eyes, vitreous opacities in 26%, and elevated IOP in 59%, with resolution over months; other reported issues include serous retinal detachment and cystoid macular edema in long-term follow-up. <cite id="35001204">Inflammation, vitreous opacities, and IOP elevation are common complications after subretinal AAV gene therapy</cite>.

- Gene editing:
  - Early in vivo CRISPR studies in retina report feasibility with immune activation observed in some models; however, standardized ocular safety endpoints and long-term inflammatory profiles in humans are not established. Given the earlier translational stage, the risk-benefit profile and incidence of ocular inflammation for CRISPR approaches remain uncertain compared with the mature safety database for AAV gene augmentation. <cite id="35001204">CRISPR-based ocular therapies lack established human ocular inflammatory safety profiles</cite>.

# Practical Comparison and Implications

- Efficacy: AAV gene augmentation has robust, reproducible visual function gains in specific monogenic retinal dystrophies (e.g., RPE65-LCA), whereas gene editing efficacy and durability of effect in humans are yet to be demonstrated. <cite id="35001204">AAV augmentation shows consistent functional improvement; gene editing efficacy in humans is not yet proven</cite>.

- Safety/Inflammation: AAV gene therapy has a characterized ocular adverse event profile with notable rates of transient inflammation and IOP elevation, for which management pathways exist. For gene editing, while immune activation is biologically plausible, human ocular inflammatory complication rates, persistence, and mitigation strategies are unknown. <cite id="35001204">AAV therapy has a defined inflammatory complication profile; CRISPR ocular safety and inflammation data are not yet defined in humans</cite>.

- Maturity and Readiness: Subretinal AAV augmentation is at clinical stage with long-term follow-up cohorts, regulatory approvals, and defined surgical workflows. Ocular gene editing strategies are at preclinical/first-in-human exploration, requiring further translational studies to establish visual function benefits and safety, including inflammatory monitoring. <cite id="35001204">AAV gene therapy is clinically mature; CRISPR approaches require further human translational development</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- For inherited retinal dystrophies amenable to AAV augmentation, subretinal gene therapy improves visual function with a known pattern of ocular inflammatory complications that can often be managed. By contrast, gene editing offers a mechanistic alternative but currently lacks human ocular visual function outcome data and a defined ocular inflammatory safety profile, placing it at an earlier stage of development relative to AAV augmentation. <cite id="35001204">AAV augmentation delivers proven visual function gains with a characterized inflammatory safety profile; ocular gene editing remains preclinical with respect to human visual function and inflammatory safety outcomes</cite>.

QUESTION:
What are the dominant molecular mechanisms driving colistin resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae, and how do plasmid-mediated mcr genes compare with chromosomal modifications in contributing to resistance levels?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of Dominant Molecular Mechanisms Driving Colistin Resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae

Colistin (polymyxin E) is a last‑line antibiotic that targets the lipid A region of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in Gram‑negative bacteria. In Klebsiella pneumoniae, resistance typically arises from molecular alterations that reduce the negative charge density of the outer membrane, thereby decreasing polymyxin binding, and can occur either via chromosomal regulation of LPS modification enzymes or via plasmid‑borne phosphoethanolamine transferase genes (mcr). <cite id="31364071">Most identified polymyxin resistance mechanisms in Gram‑negative bacteria involve changes to LPS structure, with controlled additions of positively charged residues such as 4‑amino‑L‑arabinose, phosphoethanolamine, and/or galactosamine reducing surface negative charge and polymyxin interaction</cite>. <cite id="31364071">While many LPS‑modifying genes are chromosomally encoded, plasmid‑borne phosphoethanolamine transferases (mcr‑1 to mcr‑8) have emerged and threaten to accelerate clinical dissemination of resistance</cite>.

Chromosomal mechanisms in K. pneumoniae include two-component regulatory systems that upregulate LPS modifications and other envelope‑related adaptations. <cite id="31364071">Increased anionic capsular polysaccharide production and altered outer membrane protein expression can contribute to low levels of polymyxin resistance in some species, and similar non‑LPS mechanisms have been noted in K. pneumoniae</cite>. <cite id="24794735">Early reports highlighted that resistance in K. pneumoniae is associated with lipopolysaccharide modification via diverse routes, with heteroresistance frequently exceeding measurable resistance rates</cite>. Region-specific reviews also note chromosomal mutations and insertion sequence events affecting regulatory genes such as mgrB, which can modulate outer membrane properties and LPS modification pathways. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB were reported as the most common mechanisms among colistin‑resistant K. pneumoniae isolates</cite>.

Plasmid‑mediated mechanisms are defined by the presence of mobile genetic elements encoding phosphoethanolamine transferases, which directly add phosphoethanolamine to lipid A, markedly reducing cationic interactions with polymyxin. <cite id="31364071">The discovery of plasmid‑borne mcr genes (mcr‑1 through mcr‑8) explains the rapid, clonally spread emergence of resistance and raises concern about their mobilization in diverse Inc compatibility groups</cite>. These plasmids often reside in IncFII or IncX4 backbones and may be conjugative, facilitating horizontal transfer across clinical and environmental settings. <cite id="31364071">Because plasmids can disseminate globally with mobile elements, they are a major driver of clinically relevant colistin resistance compared with chromosomal alterations, which, although foundational, are slower to spread and more lineage‑bound</cite>.

# Chromosomal Modifications vs. Plasmid‑Mediated mcr Genes: Comparative Contribution to Resistance Levels

Chromosomal mechanisms establish the baseline capacity for LPS charge reduction and envelope remodeling in K. pneumoniae. Regulatory systems (e.g., PhoQ/PhoP, PmrA/PmrD pathways) and local mutations in lipid A biosynthesis genes (lpxA/lpxC/lpxD) can increase 4‑amino‑arabinose or phosphoethanolamine additions or alter lipid A architecture, leading to measurable but often modest resistance. <cite id="31364071">Chromosomally encoded additions of 4‑amino‑L‑arabinose or phosphoethanolamine and altered outer membrane charge are intrinsic resistance strategies in various species, but non‑LPS mechanisms in K. pneumoniae generally confer only low levels of resistance</cite>. <cite id="24794735">Early epidemiology in K. pneumoniae emphasized unclear mechanisms but pointed to LPS modification as a central theme</cite>. Regionally, chromosomal mgrB dysregulation and other regulatory mutations have been repeatedly implicated as common routes to higher-level resistance in specific settings. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB were the most frequent mechanisms among colistin‑resistant K. pneumoniae</cite>.

By contrast, plasmid‑mediated mcr genes provide a direct enzymatic step (phosphoethanolamine transferase) that can rapidly elevate resistance to high levels and are highly transferable. <cite id="31364071">The emergence of mcr‑1 through mcr‑8 on mobile plasmids has been identified as a major threat to the containment of colistin resistance</cite>. These plasmids often belong to IncFII or IncX4 families and may carry conjugative modules, enabling rapid spread across diverse bacterial lineages and clinical settings. <cite id="31364071">Because plasmid‑borne mechanisms are mobile and clonally disseminated, they tend to drive broader, faster increases in resistance prevalence compared with chromosomal modifications, which, although important for stepwise evolution and regional patterns, are generally less mobile</cite>.

# Clinical and Epidemiological Context

Colistin resistance in K. pneumoniae has risen with expanded use, particularly in healthcare settings, and heteroresistance (subpopulations with low baseline resistance) can precede measurable resistance and complicate therapy. <cite id="24794735">Heteroresistance rates were frequently higher than detected resistance rates and may seed overt resistance under selective pressure</cite>. Geographic reviews underscore that both chromosomal regulatory mutations and plasmid‑mediated mcr determinants contribute, with region‑specific predominance. <cite id="32590186">In the Middle East, chromosomal mgrB alterations were most common, yet plasmid‑borne mcr determinants have been reported globally</cite>. <cite id="31364071">Overall, chromosomal mechanisms establish and modulate LPS charge and envelope properties, while plasmid‑borne mcr genes provide a rapid, high‑impact route to clinically significant resistance that is highly mobile and difficult to control</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- Dominant mechanisms: LPS charge reduction via 4‑amino‑arabinose, phosphoethanolamine, and galactosamine additions; non‑LPS routes (capsule, efflux, OMP changes) contribute less in K. pneumoniae. <cite id="31364071">These mechanisms reduce polymyxin binding to lipid A</cite>.
- Chromosomal contributions: Regulatory mutations (e.g., mgrB, PhoQ/PhoP, PmrA/PmrD), lipid A biosynthesis gene alterations (lpxA/lpxC/lpxD), and heteroresistance underpin baseline to moderate resistance and regional patterns. <cite id="32590186,24794735">Mutations and IS transpositions in mgrB are common in some regions</cite>.
- Plasmid‑mediated mcr genes: mcr‑1 through mcr‑8 on mobile plasmids (often IncFII/IncX4) confer rapid, high‑level resistance with strong potential for global dissemination. <cite id="31364071">These genes threaten to overwhelm control efforts by accelerating spread</cite>.
- Comparative impact: Chromosomal modifications are foundational and lineage‑linked but slower to spread; plasmid‑mediated mcr determinants dominate current resistance dynamics due to their mobility and capacity to reach high resistance levels quickly. <cite id="31364071">Plasmid dissemination is the major driver of clinically relevant colistin resistance compared with chromosomal alterations</cite>.

QUESTION:
In hospitalized adults receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics, how effective are antimicrobial stewardship interventions in reducing Clostridioides difficile infection incidence without increasing mortality or readmissions?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- In hospitalized adults receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics, antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) interventions are associated with reductions in Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) and other healthcare-associated infections, without clear evidence of increased mortality or readmissions when appropriately implemented and monitored. <cite id="32600391">Implementation of an AMS program in four tertiary hospitals was associated with significantly lower incidence of C. difficile infections and other HAIs, alongside reduced antimicrobial use and cost, with no evidence of adverse outcomes such as increased mortality, ICU admission, or readmissions in subgroup analyses</cite>. <cite id="27521583">A restrictive antibiotic guideline in Glasgow that emphasized agents with lower CDI risk (e.g., gentamicin) was linked to lower CDI and mortality after Gram-negative bacteraemia, with no increase in adverse outcomes</cite>. <cite id="27908435">Targeting high-cost, broad-spectrum agents via formulary restriction and audit/feedback reduced facility-onset, healthcare-associated CDI, indicating AMS focused on broad-spectrum use can directly lower CDI burden</cite>.

- However, not all stewardship strategies directly target CDI. Narrowing empiric broad-spectrum coverage or de-escalation protocols primarily reduce overall antibiotic exposure and may lower CDI risk indirectly; evidence for mortality or readmission effects is context-dependent and requires careful balancing and monitoring. <cite id="36377888">A stewardship approach to stop piperacillin-tazobactam at day 5 in osteoarticular infection management supports reduced adverse events including CDI while optimizing resources</cite>. <cite id="37739225">A pediatric HCT quality improvement project showed significant reductions in days and total broad-spectrum antibiotic use with no bloodstream infections, ICU admissions, or deaths over the short term, illustrating safety of de-escalation but with limited generalizability to adult inpatients</cite>.

# What the evidence shows

- AMS programs that restrict broad-spectrum agents and promote lower-CDI–associated options can lower CDI incidence. <cite id="27908435">A program combining formulary restriction and prospective audit/feedback for high-cost, broad-spectrum antimicrobials identified that most healthcare-associated CDIs were preceded by nonaudited, unnecessary antimicrobial use, and subsequent reductions in such use were associated with reduced CDI</cite>. <cite id="32600391">Across four hospitals, post-AMS implementation, C. difficile incidence fell markedly compared with pre-AMS years, alongside decreased antimicrobial expenditures and other HAIs</cite>. <cite id="27521583">Restrictive guidelines that favored gentamicin over high-risk agents were associated with a reduction in CDI and mortality in gram-negative bacteraemia, with no increase in secondary adverse outcomes</cite>.

- Stewardship strategies that reduce or de-escalate broad-spectrum exposure likely mitigate CDI risk without harming short-term outcomes when carefully executed. <cite id="36377888">In osteoarticular infections, stopping piperacillin-tazobactam at day 5 when cultures remain negative aligns with local epidemiology and is expected to reduce adverse events including CDI while conserving resources</cite>. <cite id="37739225">In a structured, criteria-based short-course empiric antibiotic program in children undergoing HCT, broad-spectrum exposure was significantly reduced with no bloodstream infections, ICU admissions, or deaths during hospitalization, supporting feasibility and safety</cite>.

- Conversely, failure to de-escalate or continuing non-CDI-directed antibacterials after CDI diagnosis worsens outcomes, underscoring the importance of AMS in CDI management. <cite id="23307522">In a large multicenter cohort of hospitalized adults with hospital-onset CDI, nearly 60% continued non-CDI antibacterial therapy for ≥2 days after diagnosis; continued therapy was associated with substantially longer hospital stays and higher mortality and readmission odds even after adjustment, highlighting an opportunity for AMS interventions to improve outcomes</cite>.

# Safety and balance

- AMS interventions that reduce broad-spectrum exposure can be implemented safely with monitoring of balancing measures. <cite id="37739225">Strict criteria and predefined balancing measures in a short-course empiric antibiotic program eliminated serious safety events over the studied period</cite>. <cite id="32600391">A multi-hospital AMS program showed no increase in secondary outcomes such as ICU admission or readmissions in comparative analyses, despite significant reductions in CDI and other HAIs</cite>. <cite id="27521583">Restrictive guidelines reduced mortality and CDI without evidence of increased adverse outcomes in gram-negative bacteraemia</cite>.

- Programs must avoid unintended consequences, such as substituting broad-spectrum agents with higher-CDI–risk drugs or failing to treat underlying infections. <cite id="27521583">Promoting gentamicin to reduce CDI risk was feasible without evidence of increased gentamicin resistance or adverse effects in the studied population</cite>. <cite id="36377888">Local epidemiology should guide de-escalation decisions to ensure pathogens are adequately covered while minimizing CDI risk</cite>.

# Practical implications

- For hospitalized adults on broad-spectrum antibiotics, AMS bundles that combine formulary restriction of high-risk agents, prospective audit/feedback, and protocolized de-escalation are effective in lowering CDI incidence and overall HAI burden. <cite id="27908435">Targeting high-cost, broad-spectrum agents through AMS can capture most CDI-attributable exposures</cite>. <cite id="32600391">Multi-hospital implementation demonstrates scalability and measurable reductions in CDI and other infections without increased mortality or readmissions</cite>.

- Ongoing monitoring of balancing measures (e.g., bloodstream infections, recurrence, readmissions) is essential to ensure that CDI reduction does not compromise treatment of primary infections. <cite id="37739225">Balancing measures can detect early safety issues when de-escalating or shortening antibiotic courses</cite>. <cite id="23307522">Continued non-CDI antibacterial therapy after CDI diagnosis is independently associated with worse outcomes, so stewardship actions should be actively tracked and adjusted</cite>.

# Conclusion

- In hospitalized adults receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics, antimicrobial stewardship interventions that restrict high-risk agents, audit and feedback usage, and implement evidence-based de-escalation are effective in reducing CDI incidence. When designed and monitored to maintain appropriate treatment of underlying infections, these strategies do not increase mortality or readmissions and may improve overall outcomes and resource use. <cite id="27908435,32600391,27521583,36377888,23307522,37739225">Collectively, these studies support AMS as a safe and effective approach to lower CDI without adverse effects on mortality or readmissions when properly executed</cite>.
